conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: What blood film finding indicates haemolysis, and why does it occur?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back: Schistocytes (fragmented RBCs) — from mechanical shearing of RBCs.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: What does the direct Coombs test (DAT) detect, and how is it interpreted?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back: It detects antibody/complement on the RBC surface: positive = immune; negative = usually non-immune — but note ~5–10% of genuine autoimmune haemolytic anaemia is DAT-negative, so a negative test does not exclude AIHA.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: What are the Coombs-POSITIVE (immune) causes of haemolytic anaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back: AIHA (warm IgG / cold IgM) and alloimmune (transfusion reaction, HDN).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: What are the Coombs-NEGATIVE (non-immune) causes of haemolytic anaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back:
• MAHA (TTP/HUS, DIC, malignancy, pre-eclampsia)
  • PNH (complement, morning haemoglobinuria)
  • prosthetic valve haemolysis
  • and Zieve syndrome (alcohol).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: Which antibody mediates warm vs cold AIHA?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back:
• Warm AIHA = IgG
  • cold AIHA = IgM.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: At what temperature do warm vs cold AIHA act?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back:
• Warm AIHA: 37°C (body temp)
  • cold AIHA: <37°C (cold extremities).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: What is the site of haemolysis in warm vs cold AIHA?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back:
• Warm AIHA: extravascular, in the spleen
  • Cold AIHA: complement-mediated — mainly extravascular clearance of C3b-coated cells in the liver, with an intravascular component.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: What are the causes of warm vs cold AIHA?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back:
• Warm: idiopathic; SLE; CLL/lymphoma; methyldopa
  • Cold: EBV, Mycoplasma; lymphoma, leukaemia, SLE.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: What is the clue feature for warm vs cold AIHA?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back:
• Warm: spherocytes + reticulocytes on film
  • Cold: Raynaud's / acrocyanosis in cold.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: How is warm vs cold AIHA treated?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back:
• Warm: steroids first-line (± rituximab); treat underlying
  • Cold: avoid cold; treat underlying; rituximab.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: What is the mechanism of a transfusion reaction (alloimmune haemolysis)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back: Foreign RBC antigens → recipient antibodies attack transfused cells → acute haemolysis (ABO mismatch) or delayed (Kidd, Duffy antigens).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: What is the mechanism of haemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN), and how is it prevented?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back: Maternal IgG antibodies (e.g. anti-D, anti-Kell) cross the placenta → attack foetal RBCs → haemolysis in utero/neonate. RhD disease is prevented by anti-D prophylaxis in RhD-negative mothers; anti-D does NOT prevent HDN caused by other antibodies such as anti-Kell, which are detected by routine antenatal antibody screening.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: What is the mechanism of paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back: Somatic mutation in haematopoietic stem cells (PIG-A gene) → loss of GPI-anchor proteins (CD55, CD59) on the RBC surface → uncontrolled complement activation → intravascular haemolysis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: What are the clinical features of PNH?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back:
• Haemoglobinuria (morning dark urine)
  • anaemia
  • thrombosis (major cause of death — unusual sites: hepatic vein, cerebral sinus)
  • and smooth muscle dystonia (oesophageal spasm, erectile dysfunction).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: How is PNH managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back:
• Eculizumab — a monoclonal Ab targeting complement C5 → blocks MAC formation
  • Meningococcal vaccination (± antibiotic prophylaxis) is MANDATORY before starting: terminal complement blockade greatly increases the risk of fatal meningococcal sepsis
  • Also bone marrow transplant (curative) and anticoagulation for thrombosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: What is the mechanism of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA), and its film/Coombs findings?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back: Small vessel structural abnormalities/fibrin strands → RBCs sheared → schistocytes on film. Coombs negative.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: What are the causes of MAHA?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back:
• TTP
  • HUS
  • DIC
  • malignancy, pre-eclampsia (HELLP)
  • and SLE.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: What is the mechanism of prosthetic valve haemolysis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back: Turbulence around a mechanical/bioprosthetic valve → collision of RBCs → mechanical shearing → Coombs-negative haemolysis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: How is prosthetic valve haemolysis managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back:
• Monitoring
  • oral iron
  • transfusion if severe
  • valve revision surgery if refractory.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: What is the triad of Zieve syndrome, and what is it associated with?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back: Coombs-negative haemolysis + cholestatic jaundice + hyperlipidaemia — a triad associated with binge drinking. Resolves with alcohol abstinence.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: EXAM PEARL: 'MCV is the spine' — summarise the three buckets.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back:
• Micro = TAILS
  • Normo = acute loss / ACD / aplastic / haemolytic / CKD
  • Macro = megaloblastic (B12/folate) vs normoblastic (alcohol/liver/thyroid/myelodysplasia/drugs).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise the IDA vs ACD discriminators.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back:
Both have low serum iron. Key discriminators:
  • TIBC HIGH in IDA, LOW in ACD
  • Ferritin LOW in IDA, HIGH in ACD.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the rule for new unexplained IDA in an adult?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back: Men & post-menopausal women → bidirectional endoscopy (OGD + colonoscopy) to exclude GI cancer. 2WW cancer pathway if ≥60 or FIT-positive/alarm features. Never assume dietary in men or post-menopausal women; check coeliac serology.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the ferritin caveat?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back: Ferritin is an acute phase reactant — raised in inflammation. Normal ferritin does NOT exclude IDA if CRP is elevated.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: EXAM PEARL: Why treat B12 before folate?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back: Treat B12 BEFORE folate — giving folate first in combined deficiency corrects anaemia but precipitates/worsens SACD.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: EXAM PEARL: What are the B12 deficiency hallmarks?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back:
• Hypersegmented neutrophils
  • SACD (dorsal + lateral cord)
  • anti-IF antibody first-line test
  • IM hydroxocobalamin.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: EXAM PEARL: List the haemolysis markers.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back:
• Raised reticulocytes
  • raised LDH
  • raised unconjugated bilirubin
  • low haptoglobin
  • schistocytes on film.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: EXAM PEARL: Coombs positive = immune — contrast warm vs cold AIHA.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back: Warm AIHA (IgG, steroids) vs cold AIHA (IgM, Raynaud's, rituximab).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise G6PD deficiency.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back: X-linked, Mediterranean/African, fava beans + drugs (primaquine, sulfonamides, ciprofloxacin) → Heinz bodies + bite cells. Diagnose with enzyme assay (after crisis).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise hereditary spherocytosis.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back: Autosomal dominant, Northern European, aplastic crisis = Parvovirus B19. Treatment = folate for all; splenectomy only in moderate-to-severe disease, with prior vaccination and lifelong penicillin V prophylaxis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise PNH.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back: GPI-anchor defect → complement attacks RBCs → morning haemoglobinuria + thrombosis (unusual sites). Eculizumab (anti-C5).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.front: EXAM PEARL: What defines MAHA and what are its causes?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia (micro/.back: MAHA = schistocytes + Coombs negative: TTP / HUS / DIC / pre-eclampsia / malignancy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What is the decisive fork in sickle cell disease pathophysiology?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: HbS polymerises when deoxygenated. Deoxygenation → HbS polymerises → RBC sickles → two branches: (1) haemolysis (fragile RBC → anaemia, gallstones, folate demand, aplastic vulnerability) and (2) vaso-occlusion (rigid cells jam capillaries → infarcts, organ damage, crises). Every complication lives on one of these two branches — with hyposplenism/functional asplenia as the third, clinically separate consequence of repeated splenic vaso-occlusion.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: How does sickle cell disease compare to thalassaemia at the gene level?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Same β-chain, same chromosome 11, but sickle cell is a qualitative defect whereas thalassaemia is a quantitative one.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What type of condition is sickle cell disease and how is it inherited?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: A haemoglobinopathy — autosomal recessive.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What is the underlying mutation in sickle cell disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: A point mutation in β-globin (chromosome 11) → glutamate to valine at position 6 → HbS.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What is the RBC lifespan in sickle cell disease compared to normal?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Deoxy-HbS polymerises → RBC sickles; RBC lifespan is 10–20 days (normal 120).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: Is sickling reversible, and what happens with repeated cycles?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Sickling is initially reversible on reoxygenation but becomes irreversible with repeated cycles → progressive organ damage.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What is the epidemiology of sickle cell disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back:
• Africa
  • Caribbean
  • India
  • Middle East.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What is the heterozygote (trait) advantage in sickle cell disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Malaria protection → balanced polymorphism.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: How does sickle cell trait (HbAS) differ from disease (HbSS)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back:
Trait (HbAS) is asymptomatic under normal conditions and is NOT the same as disease (HbSS). Recognised exceptions:
  • painless haematuria and papillary necrosis
  • hyposthenuria
  • splenic infarction at extreme altitude or hypoxia
  • and exertional rhabdomyolysis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: How is sickle cell disease screened for antenatally and in newborns?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Antenatal screening plus newborn heel-prick screening (day 5).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What are the three branches and their complications?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back:
• Haemolysis branch → anaemia, pigment gallstones, folate deficiency, aplastic crisis
  • Vaso-occlusion branch → stroke, ACS, AVN, priapism, CKD, retinopathy
  • Hyposplenism branch → functional asplenia → encapsulated-organism sepsis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What is the definitive investigation for sickle cell disease and the expected findings?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back:
Hb electrophoresis (definitive):
  • 80–95% HbS
  • absent HbA
  • raised HbF.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What does the FBC show in sickle cell disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back:
• Low Hb
  • raised reticulocytes
  • raised WCC + CRP in crisis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What are the key blood film findings in sickle cell disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Sickle cells and Howell-Jolly bodies (which signal hyposplenism — a high-yield film finding).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What is the limitation of the sickle solubility test?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Screening only — it cannot distinguish trait from disease; electrophoresis/HPLC is still needed. It is also unreliable in the first ~6 months of life, because high HbF gives false negatives — which is why it is not used for newborn screening.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: When is newborn screening done and what does it enable?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Heel-prick day 5 — enables early prophylaxis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What is the key reticulocyte discriminator between sequestration and aplastic crisis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Reticulocytes are HIGH in sequestration (marrow compensating) but LOW in aplastic crisis (marrow suppressed by parvovirus B19) — classic SBA.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: Vaso-occlusive (painful) crisis: mechanism, key discriminator, and management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back:
• Mechanism: capillary occlusion → ischaemia
  • Discriminator: pain ± fever; dactylitis in children; clinical diagnosis
  • Management: strong opioid within 30 minutes plus regular paracetamol and an NSAID unless contraindicated; warmth and hydration; oxygen if SpO₂ is 95% or below on air, or below the patient's own baseline (NICE).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: Splenic sequestration crisis: mechanism, key discriminator, and management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back:
• Mechanism: RBC pooling in spleen
  • Discriminator: enlarged painful spleen + shock; raised reticulocytes
  • Management: IV fluids + transfusion; splenectomy if recurrent.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: Aplastic crisis: mechanism, key discriminator, and management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back:
• Mechanism: marrow shutdown — parvovirus B19
  • Discriminator: severe anaemia + low reticulocytes
  • Management: supportive ± transfusion; self-limiting ~1 week.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: Acute chest syndrome: mechanism, key discriminator, and management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back:
• Mechanism: pulmonary vaso-occlusion/infarct
  • Discriminator: a new CXR infiltrate (≥1 complete lung segment) plus at least one of fever, chest pain, tachypnoea, wheeze, cough or new hypoxia — fever is NOT obligatory — leading cause of death
  • Management: antibiotics with atypical cover, oxygen, analgesia, incentive spirometry, IV fluids without overload, and transfusion — simple top-up if Hb is falling, urgent exchange if severe or deteriorating; ± NIV/ITU.
Escalate early: urgent haematology/haemoglobinopathy team involvement and a critical-care review, because exchange and ventilatory support are decided there, not at the bedside.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What is the transfusion logic in sickle cell disease (simple vs exchange)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back:
• Simple top-up transfusion for symptomatic anaemia, aplastic crisis, splenic sequestration and pre-operative optimisation — an uncomplicated painful crisis is NOT an indication to transfuse, and do not push Hb above ~100 g/L (hyperviscosity worsens sickling)
  • Exchange transfusion (rapid HbS% reduction, target <30%) for acute stroke, severe or deteriorating acute chest syndrome, and multiorgan failure
  • Sequestration is treated with fluids and cautious small-volume simple transfusion, not exchange — the pooled cells auto-transfuse back as the spleen decompresses.
Use extended phenotype-matched (Rh and Kell) blood; chronic transfusion needs iron monitoring and chelation.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What are the ongoing chronic therapies in sickle cell disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back:
• Avoid triggers (dehydration, cold, hypoxia, infection)
  • folic acid
  • hydroxycarbamide (first-line disease-modifier, raises HbF)
  • transfusion for severe anaemia
  • and — potentially curative — allogeneic stem cell transplant or CRISPR gene therapy (exagamglogene autotemcel / Casgevy).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: Which triggers should be avoided in sickle cell disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back:
• Dehydration
  • cold
  • hypoxia, and infection.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: How does hydroxycarbamide work in sickle cell disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: It raises HbF → dilutes HbS → fewer crises; it is the first-line disease-modifying agent.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What are the potentially curative options in sickle cell disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Allogeneic stem cell transplant, and — newer — CRISPR gene therapy: exagamglogene autotemcel (Casgevy), approved in the UK (MHRA) for severe disease, which edits BCL11A to reactivate HbF.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What is the newer gene therapy for sickle cell disease (and what happened to crizanlizumab/voxelotor)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back:
• Exagamglogene autotemcel (Casgevy) — a CRISPR therapy editing BCL11A to raise HbF, approved in the UK (MHRA) as a world first, potentially curative for severe disease
  • Crizanlizumab (anti-P-selectin) no longer has a UK licence — it was withdrawn after a phase 3 trial failed to confirm benefit, and NHS supply has ended
  • Voxelotor (anti-sickling) was withdrawn worldwide over safety concerns.
Do not start either.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What infection prophylaxis is given for functional asplenia in sickle cell disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Penicillin V (phenoxymethylpenicillin) TWICE daily — 500 mg BD in adults; in children 62.5 mg BD (<1 yr), 125 mg BD (1–5 yr), 250 mg BD (6–17 yr) — started by 3 months of age and continued lifelong (erythromycin if penicillin-allergic); pneumococcal vaccine every 5 years; meningococcal, Hib, and annual flu vaccines.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What is the rationale for infection prophylaxis in sickle cell disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Recurrent splenic infarction → functional asplenia → encapsulated organism risk (Strep. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, N. meningitidis). The corollary: FEVER in a patient with sickle cell disease is an emergency, not a wait-and-see — assess urgently, take blood cultures and give broad-spectrum antibiotics promptly. Prophylactic penicillin does not exclude pneumococcal sepsis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What are the complications on the haemolysis branch?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back:
• Chronic anaemia
  • pigment gallstones
  • folate deficiency
  • and aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What are the complications on the vaso-occlusion branch?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back:
• Stroke (children)
  • avascular necrosis (hip, shoulder)
  • acute chest syndrome
  • priapism
  • CKD/papillary necrosis
  • pulmonary hypertension
  • and retinopathy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What are the features of the hyposplenism branch?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Functional asplenia, Howell-Jolly bodies on film, encapsulated organism sepsis — this drives the prophylaxis strategy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the commonest cause of death in sickle cell disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Acute chest syndrome — a new CXR infiltrate plus at least one of fever, chest pain, tachypnoea, wheeze, cough or hypoxia (fever is not required). Needs antibiotics, oxygen and transfusion — simple top-up if mild/moderate, urgent exchange transfusion if severe or deteriorating.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: EXAM PEARL: Why does functional asplenia produce Howell-Jolly bodies and drive prophylaxis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Functional asplenia → Howell-Jolly bodies on film → lifelong penicillin V + pneumococcal/Hib/meningococcal vaccines. And it makes any fever an emergency: blood cultures and prompt broad-spectrum antibiotics, because a hyposplenic patient can deteriorate within hours.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: EXAM PEARL: Why is exchange (not simple) transfusion used for stroke/ACS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back:
• Acute stroke and severe ACS need rapid HbS% reduction, so exchange transfusion is used
  • simple top-up transfusion covers symptomatic anaemia, aplastic crisis, sequestration and pre-operative optimisation.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What is the pathophysiology of a vaso-occlusive (painful) crisis in SCD?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Hypoxia/dehydration/cold/infection → HbS polymerisation → RBC sickling → microvascular occlusion → ischaemia/infarction → severe pain. Most common crisis type.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What is the acute chest syndrome (ACS) in SCD and why is it dangerous?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back:
New infiltrate on CXR plus at least one of fever, chest pain, tachypnoea, wheeze, cough or hypoxia in SCD — fat embolism, infection, or in-situ sickling in the pulmonary vasculature. Can be rapidly fatal. Treat:
  • oxygen titrated to SpO₂ >95%
  • analgesia
  • antibiotics with atypical cover
  • incentive spirometry
  • and transfusion — simple top-up if Hb is falling, urgent exchange if severe or deteriorating.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What is the role of hydroxycarbamide (formerly hydroxyurea) in SCD?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Increases HbF (foetal haemoglobin) production → dilutes HbS → reduces sickling. Decreases crisis frequency by ~50%. First-line disease-modifying therapy in SCD.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What vaccinations does a patient with sickle cell disease need (functional asplenia)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back:
• Pneumococcal — the conjugate vaccine as per the national schedule, plus a booster every 5 years
  • Haemophilus influenzae type b
  • meningococcal ACWY and B
  • annual influenza.
Plus lifelong phenoxymethylpenicillin (erythromycin if penicillin-allergic) from 3 months of age.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the key electrophoresis finding that distinguishes SCD from sickle cell trait?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back:
• HbSS: HbS 80–95%, HbA absent (HbS + HbF only)
  • Trait (HbAS): HbA ~55–60%, HbS ~40% — HbA is always present.
Sickle cell disease also includes the compound heterozygotes: HbSC (roughly equal HbS and HbC, absent HbA, milder) and HbSβ-thalassaemia (HbSβ⁰ behaves like HbSS; HbSβ⁺ is milder). Trait patients are carriers — asymptomatic under normal conditions, with partial protection against falciparum malaria.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: How quickly must analgesia be offered to a patient presenting to hospital with an acute painful sickle cell episode, and how often is pain then reassessed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Offer analgesia within 30 minutes of presentation (NICE). The Royal College of Emergency Medicine tightens the emergency-department target to within 15 minutes. Reassess the effectiveness of pain relief every 30 minutes until pain is controlled, then at least 4-hourly, using an age-appropriate pain scoring tool. Follow the patient's individualised care plan where one exists — many patients have a personal analgesia regimen agreed with their haemoglobinopathy team.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: Which opioid does NICE explicitly say not to use in an acute painful sickle cell episode, and why?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Pethidine. Its metabolite norpethidine accumulates in renal impairment — which is common in sickle cell disease — and is proconvulsant, so it can cause seizures. Morphine titrated to effect (oral, IV or SC, with PCA if repeated boluses are needed) is the strong opioid of choice.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: Besides a strong opioid, what analgesia does NICE recommend for every patient with an acute painful sickle cell episode?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Regular paracetamol AND an NSAID, by a suitable route, unless contraindicated — these adjuncts are recommended positively for all patients alongside the opioid (NICE). They are not optional add-ons, though NSAIDs are avoided where there is renal impairment or another contraindication.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What monitoring and co-prescribing accompany opioid analgesia in an acute painful sickle cell episode?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Monitor pain score, sedation score, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and blood pressure hourly for the first 6 hours, then at least 4-hourly once stable, with naloxone immediately available wherever the opioid is given. Co-prescribe a regular laxative, plus an antiemetic and an antihistamine/antipruritic as required — opioid constipation, nausea and itch are predictable and should be pre-empted.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What was the APPG report 'No One's Listening', and what did it find?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: An inquiry by the All-Party Parliamentary Group on Sickle Cell and Thalassaemia with the Sickle Cell Society into avoidable deaths and failures of care for sickle cell patients in secondary care. It found routine failure to meet the national standard on timely pain relief in A&E and on general wards, patients disbelieved about their own pain and mislabelled as drug-seeking, low awareness of sickle cell among non-specialist staff, and concluded that these negative attitudes are underpinned by racism, compounded by chronic under-staffing of specialist services.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: Who is screened with transcranial Doppler (TCD) in sickle cell disease, and how often?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Children with HbSS or HbS-beta-zero thalassaemia — the highest stroke-risk genotypes — are screened annually from age 2 until at least age 16. TCD measures blood flow velocity in the middle cerebral and distal internal carotid arteries; a high velocity signals a narrowed, high-flow vessel at risk of infarction.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What does an abnormal (high-velocity) transcranial Doppler trigger in a child with sickle cell disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: A chronic transfusion programme maintaining HbS below 30%. This dramatically reduces the risk of overt stroke in children with abnormal TCD velocities — which is why TCD screening is worth doing at all.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: A child with sickle cell disease develops an acute focal neurological deficit. How does management differ from the standard stroke pathway?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: It is a haemoglobinopathy emergency: urgent imaging plus an immediate call to the specialist haemoglobinopathy team, and treatment is urgent exchange transfusion to drop HbS rapidly — not the standard thrombolysis pathway used for atherothrombotic stroke. Secondary prevention is then an ongoing transfusion programme, because the recurrence risk without it is very high.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What is silent cerebral infarction in sickle cell disease and why does it matter?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Infarcts visible on MRI with no focal neurological deficit — the commonest form of brain injury in sickle cell disease, and easily missed because nothing dramatic happens. They are associated with falling cognitive performance, school difficulty and a raised risk of later overt stroke, so declining school performance in a child with sickle cell disease is a reason to consider MRI.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: Who should be offered hydroxycarbamide in sickle cell disease (BSH)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Patients with HbSS or HbS-beta-zero thalassaemia who have recurrent vaso-occlusive crises or evidence of end-organ damage. The classic thresholds are three or more crises a year requiring hospital admission, or crises that interfere with daily life, schooling or work. It is also used for recurrent acute chest syndrome and severe symptomatic anaemia. In children with HbSS or HbS-beta-zero thalassaemia it is offered from around 9 months of age irrespective of clinical severity. It is then titrated up to the maximum tolerated dose — up to about 35 mg/kg/day — rather than left at a low fixed dose, because underdosing is a common reason a patient appears not to respond.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What is the blood monitoring schedule for hydroxycarbamide in sickle cell disease, and when do you stop it?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: FBC and reticulocyte count 2 weeks after starting and 2 weeks after every dose increment, then at least every 8–12 weeks for the duration of treatment. Stop treatment if the neutrophil count falls to 1.0 × 10⁹/L or below, and restart at a lower dose once it recovers.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What is the practical marker of adherence and response to hydroxycarbamide?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: A rising MCV. If the MCV has not moved on treatment, suspect the tablets are not being taken before concluding the drug has failed.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What are the adverse effects of hydroxycarbamide?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back:
• Myelosuppression — neutropenia and thrombocytopenia, which is dose-limiting and the reason for the FBC schedule
  • skin and nail hyperpigmentation
  • drug-induced leg ulcers (confusingly, sickle cell disease itself also causes leg ulcers)
  • plus nausea, alopecia and rash.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What must be counselled about hydroxycarbamide and pregnancy?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: It is teratogenic and also reduces sperm counts. It should be stopped at least 3 months before a planned conception, in both women and men, and contraception should be discussed when the drug is started rather than when a pregnancy test turns positive. An unplanned pregnancy on treatment means stopping the drug and urgent referral to a joint obstetric–haematology service.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What is the difference between stuttering and major priapism in sickle cell disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back:
• Stuttering priapism is recurrent, self-limiting episodes lasting under 4 hours, often waking the patient from sleep — a warning sign that predicts major episodes
  • Major (acute ischaemic) priapism is a painful rigid erection lasting more than 4 hours; the corpora cavernosa are hard while the glans and corpus spongiosum are typically soft.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What are the conservative first steps for an early priapic episode in sickle cell disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back:
• Hydration (oral or IV)
  • prompt analgesia
  • a warm bath or shower
  • emptying the bladder
  • and gentle exercise such as walking.
These are for the early episode only and must never be used to run the clock past 4 hours. Patients are taught to attend at 2–3 hours rather than waiting overnight.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: How is major (acute ischaemic) priapism lasting more than 4 hours in sickle cell disease treated?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: It is a urological emergency. Treatment is corporal aspiration, with or without irrigation, followed by intracavernosal injection of the alpha-agonist phenylephrine, which contracts cavernosal smooth muscle and restores venous outflow — given in small diluted aliquots at intervals up to a stated maximum, with blood pressure and pulse monitoring for hypertension and reflex bradycardia (use the dose in your local urology or haemoglobinopathy protocol / the BNF). If aspiration and injection fail, a surgical shunt is next.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What irrigation fluid must never be used for priapism in sickle cell disease, and why?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Cold saline. Cooling precipitates further sickling and can trigger a generalised painful crisis, so any irrigation must use body-temperature or warmed fluid.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: Where does exchange transfusion fit in the management of priapism in sickle cell disease, and what happens if treatment is delayed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Exchange transfusion is adjunctive only: it may be considered alongside urological treatment but must never delay corporal aspiration and intracavernosal phenylephrine — choosing exchange transfusion instead of immediate urological intervention is a classic exam trap. Beyond roughly 24 hours, ischaemia gives way to corporal fibrosis and permanent erectile dysfunction that no later intervention reverses, which is why patients are educated to present early.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What is the decisive fork in thalassaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Which globin chain, and how many genes are affected? Alpha is graded by number of defective alleles (1→4); beta by trait vs non-transfusion-dependent vs transfusion-dependent. Everything — severity, presentation, transfusion-dependence — falls out of gene dosage.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: How does the Anaemia note cross-reference thalassaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Thalassaemia is a key microcytic cause.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What type of condition is thalassaemia and how is it inherited?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: A haemoglobinopathy — autosomal recessive — with reduced or absent globin chain production.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: Which chromosomes carry the alpha and beta globin defects?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Alpha (chromosome 16) or beta (chromosome 11).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What is the disease mechanism of thalassaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Reduced production of one chain → excess of the paired chain → unstable precipitates → ineffective erythropoiesis + haemolysis → fragile RBCs → splenomegaly. It is the imbalance that causes disease.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What is the mechanism specific to beta-thalassaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Chromosome 11 mutation → reduced/absent beta chain → excess alpha chains precipitate → haemolysis + ineffective erythropoiesis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: Beta-thalassaemia trait (carrier): genotype, symptoms, Hb, and key features?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back:
• Genotype: heterozygous (β/β⁺ or β/β⁰)
  • Symptoms: asymptomatic
  • Hb: mildly low or normal
  • Key features: low MCV, low MCH; disproportionate microcytosis; normal ferritin.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: Non-transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia: genotype, symptoms, Hb, and key features?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back:
• Genotype: two abnormal beta alleles of milder combined effect (β⁺/β⁺, β⁰/β⁺, or β⁰/β⁰ with HbF-raising modifiers); also HbE/β-thalassaemia
  • Symptoms: moderate anaemia
  • Hb: 70–100 g/L
  • Key features: splenomegaly, bone deformities, leg ulcers, gallstones.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: Transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia (major): genotype, symptoms, Hb, and key features?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back:
• Genotype: usually homozygous (β⁰/β⁰), though β⁰/β⁺ and β⁺/β⁺ can also be transfusion-dependent
  • Symptoms: severe — presents at 3–6 months, when the HbF→HbA switch unmasks the beta-chain defect
  • Hb: severely low
  • Key features: failure to thrive, recurrent infection, hepatosplenomegaly, bony changes.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What is the highest-yield trait vs IDA discriminator in thalassaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: In thalassaemia trait, ferritin and iron stores are normal, and the microcytosis is disproportionate to the degree of anaemia. IDA has low ferritin, raised TIBC, low iron. HbA2 >3.5% on electrophoresis confirms beta-thalassaemia trait.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What bony abnormalities occur in thalassaemia and why?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Chronic anaemia drives compensatory erythroid hyperplasia. Extramedullary haemopoiesis → hepatosplenomegaly. Expansion of the medullary cavity → raised fracture risk, enlarged maxilla, frontal/parietal bossing, and the 'hair-on-end' skull X-ray appearance.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What causes the bony deformities and hepatosplenomegaly in thalassaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Extramedullary haemopoiesis → hepatosplenomegaly; marrow expansion → raised fracture risk, enlarged maxilla, frontal/parietal bossing.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What is the classic skull X-ray finding in thalassaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: 'Hair-on-end' appearance.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What is the genetic basis of alpha-thalassaemia, and what forms the unstable tetramers?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Chromosome 16; 4 alpha-globin genes. Severity is determined by the number of defective alleles. Excess gamma chains (fetal) or beta chains form unstable tetramers (HbH, Hb Barts).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: Alpha-thalassaemia with 1 allele affected: name and clinical picture?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Minima (silent carrier) — asymptomatic; normal MCV.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: Alpha-thalassaemia with 2 alleles affected: name and clinical picture?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Trait — asymptomatic; mild low MCV.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: Alpha-thalassaemia with 3 alleles affected: name and clinical picture?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: HbH disease — mild–severe haemolytic anaemia; jaundice, gallstones, splenomegaly, leg ulcers, osteopenia, ± aplastic crises.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: Alpha-thalassaemia with 4 alleles affected: name and clinical picture?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Hb Barts — hydrops fetalis; usually fatal in utero or soon after birth, with survival only after intrauterine transfusion followed by lifelong transfusion support. Carries significant maternal risk, including severe pre-eclampsia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: Why does alpha-thalassaemia trait need genetic testing to diagnose?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Alpha thalassaemia trait often has a normal Hb electrophoresis — diagnosis requires genetic testing (or HPLC showing Hb Barts in neonates).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What does the FBC + film show in thalassaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Hypochromic microcytic anaemia with target cells. In major/intermedia there are also raised reticulocytes (modest for the degree of anaemia — erythropoiesis is ineffective) and nucleated RBCs in the periphery. In trait the reticulocyte count is normal and there are no nucleated RBCs.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What does Hb electrophoresis / HPLC show in beta major vs beta trait?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back:
• Beta major: raised HbF, absent/reduced HbA
  • Beta trait: raised HbA2 (>3.5%).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What do ferritin / iron studies show in thalassaemia trait, and why does it matter?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Normal in trait — which distinguishes it from IDA.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: Which investigation is required for alpha-thalassaemia, and why?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Genetic testing — because the electrophoresis may be normal.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What antenatal and ongoing monitoring is offered in thalassaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Antenatal: a haemoglobinopathy screen (FBC + HPLC, with the Family Origin Questionnaire) offered to all pregnant women, ideally by 10 weeks; test the partner if she is a carrier. Newborn bloodspot screening picks up the sickle cell disorders and beta-thalassaemia major, but NOT beta-thalassaemia trait. Ongoing: serum ferritin with T2* MRI for transfusional iron overload.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: How is transfusion-dependent (major) thalassaemia managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back:
• Regular transfusions every 3–4 weeks to keep the pre-transfusion Hb at 95–105 g/L (suppresses ineffective erythropoiesis, prevents bony deformity), using extended red cell typing before the first transfusion and Rh- and Kell-matched units lifelong to avoid alloimmunisation (BSH)
  • lifelong folic acid
  • splenectomy for hypersplenism (vaccinate first: pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib and annual influenza, plus prophylactic penicillin V)
  • and — potentially curative — allogeneic stem cell transplant or CRISPR gene therapy (exagamglogene autotemcel / Casgevy).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: Why are regular transfusions given in thalassaemia major?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: To keep the pre-transfusion Hb at 95–105 g/L — this suppresses ineffective erythropoiesis and prevents bony deformity. The units are Rh- and Kell-matched on extended typing, because alloimmunisation in a lifelong transfusion programme makes every future crossmatch harder.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What must be done before splenectomy in thalassaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Vaccinate first (pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib, and annual influenza), ideally at least two weeks beforehand, and give lifelong prophylactic penicillin V. And know the corollary: fever in an asplenic patient is an emergency — blood cultures and prompt broad-spectrum antibiotics, because prophylactic penicillin does not exclude pneumococcal sepsis (BSH).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What are the potentially curative options in thalassaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Allogeneic stem cell transplant, and — newer — CRISPR gene therapy: exagamglogene autotemcel (Casgevy), approved in the UK (MHRA) for transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: How is trait / mild thalassaemia managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: No treatment required outside pregnancy — but in pregnancy give high-dose folic acid 5 mg, from preconception through the first trimester. Genetic counselling, including formal carrier testing of the partner before any risk is excluded. Avoid iron unless deficiency is confirmed on iron studies.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: Why is iron overload the central long-term problem in thalassaemia, and which organs are affected?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back:
Iron accumulates from two sources — repeated transfusion, and increased gut absorption (ineffective erythropoiesis suppresses hepcidin), so non-transfusion-dependent patients overload too. It deposits in organs:
  • heart → cardiomyopathy/cardiac failure (leading cause of death)
  • liver → cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma
  • pituitary → growth failure, infertility
  • thyroid/parathyroid → hypothyroidism, hypoparathyroidism
  • pancreas → diabetes mellitus
  • gonads → hypogonadism, delayed puberty.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What is the leading cause of death in thalassaemia major, and how is iron overload treated?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Cardiac iron overload (cardiomyopathy/cardiac failure) is the leading cause of death. Iron chelation: subcutaneous desferrioxamine or oral deferasirox/deferiprone. Deferiprone causes agranulocytosis — check the neutrophil count before starting and weekly on treatment, stop the drug if neutrophils fall below 1.5 × 10⁹/L, and tell the patient to stop it and get an urgent FBC the same day for fever, sore throat or flu-like symptoms [BNF]; it is the most effective chelator at removing cardiac iron. Monitor serum ferritin PLUS cardiac and hepatic T2* MRI — cardiac T2* is what predicts the cardiomyopathy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: EXAM PEARL: How do you tell thalassaemia trait from IDA, and what confirms beta trait?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Disproportionate microcytosis + normal ferritin → think thalassaemia trait, not IDA. HbA2 >3.5% confirms beta-thalassaemia trait on electrophoresis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: EXAM PEARL: What do Hb Barts (4 alleles) and HbH (3 alleles) represent?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back:
• Hb Barts (4 alleles) = hydrops fetalis — usually fatal in utero or soon after birth; survival only with intrauterine transfusion and then lifelong transfusion support
  • HbH (3 alleles) = symptomatic but survivable haemolytic anaemia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: EXAM PEARL: How does electrophoresis differ between alpha and beta trait?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back:
• Alpha thalassaemia trait — electrophoresis can be normal; needs genetic testing
  • Beta trait — electrophoresis shows raised HbA2.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What is the Hb electrophoresis finding in beta-thalassaemia major?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back:
• HbA absent (no beta chains)
  • HbF markedly elevated as the main oxygen carrier
  • HbA2 variable and not diagnostic.
Severe microcytic anaemia presenting at 3–6 months as the HbF→HbA switch unmasks the defect, and transfusion-dependent thereafter.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What is beta-thalassaemia intermedia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Intermediate severity — two beta-globin gene mutations but less severe than major. Can maintain Hb 70–100 g/L without regular transfusion. Requires transfusion only periodically (e.g. during infection, pregnancy, or growth spurts).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What skull radiograph finding is seen in severe beta-thalassaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: 'Hair-on-end' (crew-cut) skull — cortical thinning with vertical striations from marrow expansion trying to compensate for anaemia. Also: 'chipmunk facies' from maxillary hypertrophy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What is the management of beta-thalassaemia major?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back:
• Regular transfusions every 3–4 weeks, target pre-transfusion Hb 95–105 g/L
  • iron chelation (desferrioxamine SC or deferasirox/deferiprone oral)
  • and — potentially curative — HLA-matched allogeneic SCT or CRISPR gene therapy (exagamglogene autotemcel / Casgevy, approved in the UK (MHRA)).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What is Hb H disease and how does it present?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: 3 deleted alpha-globin genes → Hb H (β4 tetramers) — moderately severe haemolytic anaemia. Splenomegaly, Hb ~70–100 g/L, intermittent transfusion. Hb electrophoresis shows HbH.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: EXAM PEARL: How does thalassaemia trait differ from iron deficiency on FBC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back:
Both: microcytic hypochromic anaemia.
  • Thalassaemia trait: normal/high red cell count (RCC), NORMAL ferritin, high HbA2 on electrophoresis in BETA trait (alpha trait: normal electrophoresis)
  • Iron deficiency: low/normal RCC, LOW ferritin, normal HbA2.
Mentzer index: <13 = thalassaemia; >13 = iron deficiency.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What is multiple myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: A malignant clonal proliferation of bone marrow plasma cells → monoclonal paraprotein (usually IgG > IgA).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What is the single dividing line between myeloma and its precursor states?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: End-organ damage: MGUS and smouldering myeloma lack CRAB; myeloma has it. That discriminator is how the spectrum is usually examined — but the myeloma-defining biomarkers (clonal plasma cells ≥60%, involved:uninvolved free light chain ratio ≥100, >1 focal lesion on MRI) diagnose myeloma and mandate treatment even with no CRAB feature.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: MGUS: defining feature and presence of end-organ (CRAB) damage?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Incidental paraprotein, <10% plasma cells. No CRAB — monitor annually.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: Smouldering myeloma: defining feature and presence of end-organ (CRAB) damage?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Higher paraprotein / 10–60% plasma cells. No CRAB — premalignant; higher progression risk. Monitor every 3 months for the first 5 years, then by stability [NICE].

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: Multiple myeloma: defining feature and presence of end-organ (CRAB) damage?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Paraprotein + clonal plasma cells. Yes — CRAB present.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What is Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia and how does it present?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: An IgM-secreting lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma — a distinct entity, NOT a subtype of myeloma. Presents with hyperviscosity, lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly rather than lytic bone disease; hypercalcaemia and lytic lesions are characteristically absent.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What are the risk factors for myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back:
• Older age
  • male
  • Black African ethnicity
  • family history
  • obesity.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What does the 'C' in CRAB stand for, with features and mechanism?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back:
HyperCalcaemia →
  • constipation
  • nausea
  • confusion
  • polyuria
  • thirst ('bones, groans, moans, stones').
Mechanism: osteoclastic bone resorption driven by myeloma cytokines.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What does the 'R' in CRAB stand for, with mechanism?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Renal failure. Mechanism: light-chain cast nephropathy, hypercalcaemia, hyperuricaemia, amyloid, dehydration, nephrotoxic drugs.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What does the 'A' in CRAB stand for, with mechanism?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Anaemia (normocytic normochromic) ± pancytopenia. Mechanism: marrow infiltration crowds out normal haematopoiesis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What does the 'B' in CRAB stand for, with sites and mechanism?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back:
Bone pain / lytic lesions —
  • skull
  • spine
  • ribs
  • pelvis
  • long bones.
Mechanism: RANKL-driven osteoclast activation (with osteoprotegerin suppressed), plus IL-1/TNF-α and DKK-1 inhibition of osteoblasts → resorption without repair.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What are the features of the paraprotein / hyperviscosity branch in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back:
• Blurred vision, headache
  • bleeding/bruising (impaired platelet function)
  • infections — immunoparesis (reduced normal polyclonal Ig)
  • peripheral neuropathy
  • heart failure (hyperviscosity).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: Why do myeloma patients get recurrent infections?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Immunoparesis — reduced normal polyclonal Ig.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What emergency presentation must not be delayed in a myeloma patient with back pain + new neurological signs?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Spinal cord compression — back pain + new neurological signs in a myeloma patient = dexamethasone 16 mg with PPI cover on clinical suspicion, plus whole-spine MRI as soon as possible and always within 24 hours [NICE]. Do not delay the steroid for the scan.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: Besides spinal cord compression, what other emergency presentations occur in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back:
• Acute hypercalcaemia
  • renal failure
  • hyperviscosity crisis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What is the two-step investigation pathway in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Initial screen → if suspicious, send BLIP → confirm with bone marrow biopsy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What does the initial screen show in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back:
• FBC: low Hb, ± pancytopenia
  • raised ESR, raised plasma viscosity
  • raised calcium, raised creatinine
  • raised total protein, low albumin
  • urine dipstick negative for Bence-Jones (dipstick detects albumin, not light chains).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: Why is the urine dipstick negative for Bence-Jones protein in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: The dipstick detects albumin, not light chains — so you must send urine electrophoresis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What does the 'B' in the BLIP diagnostic panel stand for?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Urine electrophoresis for Bence-Jones protein (urinary light chains).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What does the 'L' in the BLIP diagnostic panel stand for?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Serum-free light-chain assay.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What does the 'I' in the BLIP diagnostic panel stand for?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Serum immunoglobulins (paraprotein type).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What does the 'P' in the BLIP diagnostic panel stand for?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Serum protein electrophoresis — monoclonal band.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What confirms the diagnosis on bone marrow biopsy in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Clonal plasma cells ≥10% (or plasmacytoma). This is mandatory. Combined with a myeloma-defining event — a CRAB feature, or one of the biomarkers (clonal plasma cells ≥60%, free light chain ratio ≥100, >1 focal lesion on MRI) — it is diagnostic of myeloma.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What is the imaging preference order in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back:
• 1. Whole-body MRI — first-line
  • 2. Whole-body low-dose CT
  • 3. Skeletal survey (plain X-ray).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What are the classic imaging signs in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back:
• Punched-out lytic lesions
  • raindrop skull
  • vertebral collapse.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What is the standard first-line anti-myeloma therapy?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: The bortezomib + thalidomide + dexamethasone (VTD) triplet is the backbone; current practice adds daratumumab (anti-CD38) — the "Dara-VTd" quadruplet is now standard first-line for transplant-eligible patients, followed by autologous SCT.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What anti-myeloma therapy is used in fit patients, and what is the disease course?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Autologous stem cell transplant in fit patients. Relapsing-remitting course; managed by haem-onc MDT.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: How is bone disease managed in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back:
Bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid) — suppress osteoclasts, reduce fractures; offered to EVERYONE with myeloma, not only those with lytic lesions, with dental assessment considered and renal function checked before the first dose (osteonecrosis of the jaw) — though dental assessment must not delay urgent myeloma treatment. Zoledronic acid is dose-reduced in moderate renal impairment and avoided below a creatinine clearance of about 30 mL/min; denosumab if bisphosphonates are unsuitable, but correct any hypocalcaemia first, co-prescribe calcium and vitamin D and monitor the calcium — severe hypocalcaemia is commonest in exactly this renal-impaired group [MHRA].
  • Radiotherapy for localised bone pain
  • orthopaedic stabilisation for pathological fracture
  • vertebroplasty/kyphoplasty for vertebral collapse.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What is the role of bisphosphonates (zoledronate) in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: They suppress osteoclasts and reduce fractures.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: VTE PROPHYLAXIS EXAM TRAP: Why must aspirin or LMWH be co-prescribed with thalidomide?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Thalidomide is prothrombotic → must co-prescribe thromboprophylaxis (aspirin at standard risk, LMWH/DOAC at higher risk). The same applies to LENALIDOMIDE — it is a class effect of the immunomodulatory drugs, and is amplified by dexamethasone, so it applies to lenalidomide maintenance too. A classic MCQ distractor.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What supportive care is given in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Hypercalcaemia: stop thiazides and any calcium/vitamin D supplements, then IV fluids, then a bisphosphonate once rehydrated (loop diuretics are not first-line). Transfusion for symptomatic anaemia; infection prophylaxis + vaccinations — and treat any fever in a patient on anti-myeloma treatment as neutropenic sepsis: IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, without waiting for the neutrophil count [NICE]. Renal: avoid NSAIDs/nephrotoxins, dialysis if needed — but the DEFINITIVE treatment of myeloma AKI is urgent anti-myeloma therapy, not supportive care alone.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What are the complications on the marrow / bone branch in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back:
• Anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia
  • recurrent infections (immunoparesis)
  • pathological fractures
  • spinal cord compression
  • hypercalcaemia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What are the complications on the paraprotein branch in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back:
• Renal failure (cast nephropathy)
  • hyperviscosity syndrome
  • AL amyloid → cardiac, renal, peripheral neuropathy
  • treatment-related neuropathy (bortezomib, thalidomide).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: EXAM PEARL: What is CRAB and why does it matter?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: CRAB is the diagnostic tetrad. Its presence separates myeloma from MGUS/smouldering — the single most important discriminator in exams. The exception to know: the myeloma-defining biomarkers (clonal plasma cells ≥60%, free light chain ratio ≥100, >1 focal MRI lesion) diagnose myeloma and mandate treatment even without CRAB.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: EXAM PEARL: When should you screen for myeloma in an older patient with bone symptoms?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Over-60 + persistent back pain or unexplained fracture → screen for myeloma: FBC, calcium and plasma viscosity/ESR, with serum protein electrophoresis and serum free light chains. If those are consistent with myeloma, arrange very urgent electrophoresis and a Bence-Jones urine test within 48 hours and refer on a suspected cancer pathway [NICE]. Do not attribute it to mechanical or osteoporotic causes without checking.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the classic radiology of myeloma, and what is the preferred first-line imaging?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Raindrop skull + punched-out lytic lesions = classic radiology. Whole-body MRI is now first-line imaging (more sensitive than skeletal survey).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: EXAM PEARL: What is Bence-Jones protein, and why is the urine dipstick misleading?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Bence-Jones protein = urinary light chains. The urine dipstick is negative because it detects albumin, not light chains — must send urine electrophoresis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the thalidomide VTE trap?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Thalidomide OR lenalidomide → VTE — always co-prescribe thromboprophylaxis (aspirin at standard risk, LMWH/DOAC at higher risk). A guaranteed MCQ trap.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: EXAM PEARL: How does Waldenström's differ from myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Waldenström's = IgM variant; hyperviscosity not bone disease. Anaemia is normocytic normochromic; ESR and plasma viscosity raised.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the CRAB criteria for myeloma and what does each letter stand for?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back:
• C — hypercalcaemia (corrected calcium >2.75 mmol/L)
  • R — renal impairment (creatinine >177 µmol/L or creatinine clearance <40 mL/min)
  • A — anaemia (Hb <100 g/L, or >20 g/L below the lower limit of normal)
  • B — one or more OSTEOLYTIC bone lesions (osteoporosis alone is not a CRAB criterion).
One or more = symptomatic myeloma requiring treatment. Treatment is also indicated with no CRAB feature if a myeloma-defining biomarker is present: clonal plasma cells ≥60%, involved:uninvolved free light chain ratio ≥100, or >1 focal lesion on MRI.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What is the definitive treatment of myeloma-induced AKI (cast nephropathy)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Urgent anti-myeloma therapy to switch off light-chain production - a bortezomib-based regimen is started without waiting for renal recovery. Fluids and dialysis only buy time; the kidney keeps being injured until the marrow stops making light chains.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: Which procedure is explicitly NOT recommended for myeloma-induced acute renal disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Plasma exchange. Stripping light chains out of the plasma does nothing about the marrow that keeps producing them, and trials showed no renal benefit.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: Plasma exchange is not used for myeloma kidney - so what IS its role in a paraprotein disorder?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Symptomatic hyperviscosity. Same disease, different problem: hyperviscosity is treated by removing paraprotein; cast nephropathy is treated by stopping light-chain production.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: List the immediate supportive measures in myeloma-induced AKI, alongside starting anti-myeloma therapy.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back:
• Aggressive IV rehydration
  • treat the hypercalcaemia
  • stop ACE inhibitors/ARBs and NSAIDs
  • avoid iodinated contrast
  • dialysis only for standard AKI indications, as a bridge while treatment takes effect.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: Why is hypercalcaemia treated as part of the renal rescue in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: It is both a cause and an amplifier of the AKI - it causes volume depletion and vasoconstriction and worsens cast formation, so correcting it is part of treating the kidney, not a separate issue.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: Is renal recovery possible in myeloma cast nephropathy?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Yes - including coming off dialysis - if light-chain production is switched off quickly. Recovery is time-dependent, so new renal impairment in myeloma is treated as an emergency.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What determines whether a myeloma patient is transplant-eligible?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Fitness: performance status, comorbidity (cardiac, respiratory, renal) and frailty, decided by the MDT. There is no hard age cut-off - eligibility is fitness, not a birthday.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: Is autologous stem cell transplant curative in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: No. It deepens and prolongs the first remission, but relapse is expected. Each relapse triggers the next line of therapy, with remissions typically getting shorter.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: Which marker is used to track response to treatment in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: The paraprotein on serum protein electrophoresis, measured serially - its level tracks disease burden. A falling paraprotein means the patient is responding; a plateau means maximum response from that line.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: Which marker is followed instead of the paraprotein in light-chain-only myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Serum free light chains - used where there is no measurable serum paraprotein, and they also change faster than electrophoresis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: How often should someone who has completed myeloma treatment be monitored?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: At least every 3 months - paraprotein (or serum free light chains) with FBC, U&E and calcium.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What does a rising paraprotein in a myeloma patient in remission mean, and what do you do?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back:
It is the first sign of relapse and usually rises before symptoms return.
  • Repeat it
  • reassess the patient for new end-organ damage
  • and refer back to the haem-onc MDT for the next line of therapy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: How does the monitoring interval for treated myeloma differ from MGUS, and why?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Treated myeloma: at least every 3 months, watching for relapse of an incurable disease. MGUS: annually, watching for progression.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: Who is offered zoledronic acid in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Everyone with myeloma, to prevent bone disease - not only patients who already have lytic lesions.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What must be considered before the first bisphosphonate dose in myeloma, and why?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Immediate referral for dental assessment and treatment, to reduce the risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw. Renal function should also be checked before dosing.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What is used for myeloma bone protection when bisphosphonates are unsuitable?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Denosumab.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What defines Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) — hallmark cell, markers, age, spread, cure rate?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back:
Classical HL:
  • Reed-Sternberg cells present (owl-eye nuclei), CD15+, CD30+ and NOT CD20 (the separate entity nodular lymphocyte-predominant HL is the mirror image - CD20+, CD30-)
  • bimodal age 20s & 60s
  • contiguous nodal spread
  • ~85% cure rate.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What defines Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) — hallmark cell, origin, age, spread, cure rate?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back:
• No Reed-Sternberg cells
  • B-cell or T-cell origin
  • peak age >60
  • non-contiguous, extranodal spread
  • variable cure rate (10–90%).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: HL vs NHL: what is the hallmark cell of each?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Hodgkin: Reed-Sternberg (owl-eye nuclei). Non-Hodgkin: lymphocytes (B or T).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: HL vs NHL: how does the age distribution differ?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Hodgkin: bimodal (20s & 60s). Non-Hodgkin: any age, peak >60.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: HL vs NHL: how does the pattern of spread differ?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Hodgkin: contiguous nodal. Non-Hodgkin: non-contiguous, extranodal.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: HL vs NHL: how do B symptoms and mediastinal mass compare?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: B symptoms: common in Hodgkin, less common in Non-Hodgkin. Mediastinal mass: common in Hodgkin, less common in Non-Hodgkin — the exceptions are primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma (a DLBCL variant, typically a young woman, may cause SVC obstruction) and T-lymphoblastic lymphoma (typically a teenage boy).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: HL vs NHL: what is the EBV association of each?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Hodgkin: yes (mixed cellularity). Non-Hodgkin: Burkitt's — but only the ENDEMIC African form is reliably EBV-driven; sporadic Burkitt (the usual UK form) and HIV-associated Burkitt are generally EBV-negative.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: HL vs NHL: how do cure rates compare?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Hodgkin: ~85%. Non-Hodgkin: variable (10–90%).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What are the risk factors for Hodgkin lymphoma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back:
• EBV (especially mixed cellularity subtype)
  • HIV
  • immunosuppression.
Note HIV raises non-Hodgkin lymphoma risk far more than Hodgkin risk (DLBCL, Burkitt, primary CNS lymphoma).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: How does Hodgkin lymphoma present?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back:
• Painless cervical lymphadenopathy
  • mediastinal mass on CXR
  • B symptoms (fever >38°C, drenching night sweats, >10% weight loss in 6 months)
  • buzzword: alcohol-induced nodal pain — classic for HL, but present in only a few per cent of patients, so its absence means nothing.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What is the classic buzzword for Hodgkin lymphoma, and how much weight should it carry?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Alcohol-induced nodal pain — the classic HL buzzword and effectively diagnostic in an exam stem, but present in only a few per cent of real patients, so its absence means nothing.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What are the B symptoms in lymphoma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back:
• Fever >38°C
  • drenching night sweats
  • >10% weight loss in 6 months.
But do not read every fever as a B symptom: in a patient on chemotherapy, fever is neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise — IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, without waiting for the neutrophil count (NICE).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What investigations are used in Hodgkin lymphoma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back:
• Excision (whole-node) biopsy — NOT fine-needle aspiration, which cannot show nodal architecture
  • core biopsy if the node is deep or inaccessible → Reed-Sternberg cells (CD15+, CD30+, CD20−, owl-eye nuclei — this profile defines classical HL; NLPHL is the mirror image, CD20+ CD30−)
  • PET-CT for staging
  • FBC: eosinophilia, lymphopenia in advanced disease
  • ESR: disease activity marker.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What is the first-line chemotherapy regimen for Hodgkin lymphoma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: ABVD ± radiotherapy: Adriamycin (doxorubicin), Bleomycin, Vinblastine, Dacarbazine — still standard for EARLY-stage disease. For ADVANCED-stage HL, brentuximab vedotin + AVD is now recommended for untreated stage 3–4 CD30-positive disease (NICE); nivolumab + AVD has outperformed it in trials but is not yet recommended for NHS use. Any fever during treatment is neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What does ABVD stand for in Hodgkin lymphoma management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back:
• Adriamycin (doxorubicin)
  • Bleomycin
  • Vinblastine
  • Dacarbazine.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What is the key toxicity of bleomycin in ABVD?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Pulmonary fibrosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What is the key toxicity of adriamycin (doxorubicin) in ABVD?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Cardiomyopathy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What is the key toxicity of vinblastine in ABVD?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Peripheral neuropathy, constipation.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What are the general features of Non-Hodgkin lymphoma and its standard chemotherapy?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back:
More common than HL; most are B-cell origin. R-CHOP (Rituximab + Cyclophosphamide + Hydroxydaunorubicin/doxorubicin + Oncovin/vincristine + Prednisolone) is standard for DLBCL and most aggressive B-cell NHL — but not for every NHL:
  • indolent disease is often observed
  • gastric MALT is treated by H. pylori eradication
  • and Burkitt needs an intensive short-course regimen with CNS prophylaxis, not R-CHOP.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What does R-CHOP stand for in NHL management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back:
• Rituximab
  • Cyclophosphamide
  • Hydroxydaunorubicin/doxorubicin
  • Oncovin/vincristine
  • Prednisolone.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: DLBCL: key features and translocation/marker?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Diffuse Large B-Cell — most common NHL, aggressive, potentially curable. t(14;18) in some; BCL-2.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: Follicular lymphoma: key features and translocation/marker?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Indolent, incurable but manageable; 'waxing and waning' lymph nodes. t(14;18); BCL-2 overexpression.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: Burkitt's lymphoma: key features and translocation/marker?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back:
• Highly aggressive
  • 'starry sky' histology
  • jaw mass (African endemic).
It is a medical emergency — the fastest-doubling human tumour, with the highest tumour lysis risk of any lymphoma, and it needs an intensive short-course regimen with CNS prophylaxis, NOT R-CHOP. EBV association: endemic (African) form is EBV-driven (+ malaria co-factor); sporadic and HIV-associated forms are usually EBV-negative. t(8;14); MYC.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: MALT lymphoma: key features and management point?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Gastric; associated with H. pylori — treat H. pylori first, then confirm eradication and re-scope to confirm histological regression. Radiotherapy where eradication fails, the disease progresses, or it is H. pylori-negative — eradication alone cures only about two-thirds of early disease.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: Mantle cell lymphoma: key features and translocation/marker?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Aggressive, poor prognosis. t(11;14); cyclin D1.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What is tumour lysis syndrome and its biochemical picture?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Massive cell death after chemo → raised K⁺, raised phosphate, low Ca²⁺, raised uric acid → renal failure, arrhythmia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: How is tumour lysis syndrome prevented?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: IV fluids plus allopurinol (standard risk) or rasburicase (high risk — bulky/high-grade disease such as Burkitt, high LDH, renal impairment) before chemotherapy. Check G6PD status before giving rasburicase: it is CONTRAINDICATED in G6PD deficiency (severe haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia) and is not given alongside allopurinol. Monitor U&Es, calcium, phosphate and urate before treatment and repeatedly through the first days in high-risk patients — and do not correct an asymptomatic hypocalcaemia while the phosphate is high, because calcium-phosphate deposition worsens the kidney injury (BSH).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: Ann Arbor staging: what are stages I and II?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: I: single nodal region. II: ≥2 nodal regions, same side of diaphragm.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: Ann Arbor staging: what are stages III and IV?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: III: nodal regions on both sides of the diaphragm. IV: diffuse or disseminated involvement of one or more extralymphatic organs (liver, bone marrow, lung), with or without nodal disease — note that limited extranodal extension contiguous with an involved node is stage E, not stage IV.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What do the A and B suffixes mean in Ann Arbor staging?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: A = no B symptoms. B = B symptoms present (fever >38°C, drenching night sweats, >10% weight loss in 6 months).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the marker profile of Reed-Sternberg cells?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: RS cells are CD15+ and CD30+ — NOT CD20.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: EXAM PEARL: What symptom is the classic buzzword for Hodgkin lymphoma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Alcohol-induced nodal pain — effectively diagnostic in an exam stem, but present in only a few per cent of real patients, so its absence means nothing.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: EXAM PEARL: What are the key chemotherapy toxicities to remember (bleomycin, doxorubicin)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Bleomycin → pulmonary fibrosis; doxorubicin → cardiomyopathy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: EXAM PEARL: What are the translocations for Burkitt's and follicular lymphoma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Burkitt's = t(8;14) MYC; follicular = t(14;18) BCL-2.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: EXAM PEARL: How does H. pylori eradication relate to MALT lymphoma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: H. pylori eradication can cure early gastric MALT lymphoma.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the tumour lysis biochemistry and how is it prevented?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Tumour lysis: raised K, raised PO₄, low Ca, raised uric acid — hydration plus allopurinol at standard risk, or rasburicase at high risk (Burkitt, high LDH, renal impairment). Never both together (BSH).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What is the Ann Arbor staging system for lymphoma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back:
• Stage I: single nodal region
  • Stage II: ≥2 regions same side of diaphragm
  • Stage III: both sides of diaphragm
  • Stage IV: diffuse or disseminated extralymphatic involvement (liver, marrow, lung).
