Add A (no B symptoms) or B (fever >38°C, night sweats, weight loss >10%). E = limited contiguous extranodal extension (not stage IV); S = splenic involvement (not stage IV either).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What are the B symptoms in lymphoma and their significance?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Fever >38°C, drenching night sweats, weight loss >10% in 6 months — indicate systemic disease (stage B), worse prognosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What is the International Prognostic Index (IPI) for DLBCL?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back:
5 factors:
  • age >60
  • stage III/IV
  • raised LDH
  • ECOG performance status ≥2
  • >1 extranodal site.
Each = 1 point: 0–1 low risk; 4–5 high risk.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: EXAM PEARL: What differentiates Hodgkin from non-Hodgkin lymphoma clinically?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: HL: young adults, contiguous spread, mediastinal mass, Reed-Sternberg cells, highly curable (>80%). NHL: older, non-contiguous, extranodal common, diverse subtypes, variable prognosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What are the four histological subtypes of CLASSICAL Hodgkin lymphoma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back:
• Nodular sclerosis (commonest)
  • mixed cellularity
  • lymphocyte-rich
  • and lymphocyte-depleted.
Nodular lymphocyte-predominant HL (NLPHL) is a separate entity, not a fifth classical subtype.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: Which is the commonest subtype of classical Hodgkin lymphoma, and what is the typical picture?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Nodular sclerosis. Typically a young adult, often a woman, presenting with a mediastinal mass; the node is divided into nodules by fibrous bands.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: Which classical Hodgkin lymphoma subtype is most strongly EBV-associated, and who gets it?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Mixed cellularity. It tends to affect older patients and those who are immunosuppressed or HIV-positive.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: Contrast lymphocyte-rich and lymphocyte-depleted classical Hodgkin lymphoma.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Lymphocyte-rich: uncommon, abundant background lymphocytes with few Reed-Sternberg cells, generally favourable. Lymphocyte-depleted: the rarest, sparse lymphocytes with many RS cells, seen in older and HIV-positive patients, and the most aggressive.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What is nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma (NLPHL), and what is its malignant cell?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: A separate entity from classical HL. The malignant cell is the 'popcorn' (LP) cell — a polylobated nucleus like a popped kernel — not a classical Reed-Sternberg cell. It is indolent, usually early-stage, relapses late, and being CD20+ it responds to rituximab.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: Does the rule 'CD15+, CD30+, NOT CD20' apply to every Hodgkin lymphoma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: No — it defines CLASSICAL Hodgkin lymphoma only. NLPHL is the mirror image: CD20+, CD30 negative, CD15 negative (and CD45+).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What is the classic microscopic appearance of the Reed-Sternberg cell?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: A large binucleate cell whose two mirror-image lobes each carry a huge eosinophilic nucleolus — the 'owl-eye' appearance. It may also be multinucleate.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What is the end-of-treatment PET for, and how do you read a residual mass?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: It confirms a complete metabolic response after the final cycle. A residual mass on CT is common and does NOT by itself mean residual lymphoma — PET separates active disease from inert fibrous tissue. A positive end-of-treatment scan should be biopsied before declaring refractory disease, since infection and inflammation are also FDG-avid.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: How is radiotherapy used alongside chemotherapy in Hodgkin lymphoma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Limited (early) stage disease is often treated with combined-modality therapy: chemotherapy followed by involved-field (or involved-site) radiotherapy to the originally involved nodes. The end-of-treatment PET helps decide who needs consolidation radiotherapy to a residual site.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: When do you watch and wait in follicular lymphoma, and what triggers treatment?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back:
Watch and wait for asymptomatic, low-bulk disease — immediate chemotherapy does not improve overall survival, so the patient is observed with regular review. Treat when there is a reason:
  • B symptoms or other symptomatic disease
  • bulky nodal masses
  • compression of or threat to an organ
  • marrow failure from infiltration
  • or steady progression.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What is the first-line treatment of follicular lymphoma that needs treating?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Rituximab (anti-CD20) plus a chemotherapy backbone, followed by rituximab maintenance. Maintenance prolongs progression-free survival, though a benefit in overall survival has not been shown. FL remains indolent but not curable with standard therapy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: How do you suspect, and how do you confirm, transformation of follicular lymphoma to DLBCL?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Suspect it when one node suddenly grows rapidly out of keeping with the rest, the LDH rises, or new B symptoms appear. Confirm by re-biopsy, targeting the most FDG-avid site on PET-CT. Transformed disease is then treated as an aggressive lymphoma, not as FL.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What second malignancies follow treatment for Hodgkin lymphoma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back:
Secondary AML and MDS from alkylating agents and topoisomerase-II inhibitors — these appear relatively early, within the first decade. Solid tumours arising within the radiotherapy field appear much later and the risk keeps rising for decades:
  • lung (compounded by smoking)
  • thyroid
  • breast
  • stomach and sarcoma.
Breast cancer after mediastinal radiotherapy in women treated young is the classic example, and warrants a dedicated early breast-screening programme.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What are the non-malignant late effects of Hodgkin lymphoma treatment, and what baseline test is needed before anthracycline?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back:
• Cardiovascular disease (doxorubicin cardiomyopathy plus radiotherapy-accelerated coronary, valve and pericardial disease) — a leading cause of late death
  • pulmonary toxicity from bleomycin
  • hypothyroidism after neck or mediastinal radiotherapy (check TFTs annually for life)
  • infertility
  • persistent fatigue
  • infection risk after splenic irradiation or splenectomy.
Arrange a baseline echocardiogram with LVEF before the first anthracycline dose.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: When must fertility be discussed in a patient starting treatment for lymphoma, and what is offered?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Before the first cycle of chemotherapy — once treatment has started the opportunity is largely gone. Offer sperm banking to men, and oocyte or embryo cryopreservation (ovarian tissue cryopreservation in selected cases) to women, with urgent referral to reproductive medicine so preservation runs alongside rather than delaying treatment. Alkylating-agent-heavy regimens are far more gonadotoxic than ABVD.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What is leukaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: A malignancy of haematopoietic stem cells → marrow replaced by clonal cells → other lineages suppressed (anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What is the two-axis classification of leukaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Speed (Acute/Chronic) × Lineage (Myeloid/Lymphoid).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: How do lymphoma and leukaemia differ in what they affect (cross-reference)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Lymphoma affects nodes; leukaemia affects marrow/blood.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: In the 2×2 master grid, what defines acute myeloid leukaemia (AML)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back:
Acute (blasts) + myeloid.
  • >75y
  • commonest acute leukaemia
  • Auer rods
  • raised risk after MDS/myeloproliferative disease.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: In the 2×2 master grid, what defines acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back:
Acute (blasts) + lymphoid.
  • Children (<5) & >45y
  • Down's syndrome
  • CNS spread
  • commonest childhood cancer.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: In the 2×2 master grid, what defines chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back:
Chronic (mature) + myeloid.
  • ~65y
  • Philadelphia t(9;22)/BCR-ABL
  • massive splenomegaly
  • 3 phases.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: In the 2×2 master grid, what defines chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back:
Chronic (mature) + lymphoid.
  • >55y
  • commonest leukaemia overall
  • smudge cells
  • Richter's transformation.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What is the age mnemonic for the four leukaemias?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back:
• ALL <5 & >45
  • CLL >55
  • CML ~65
  • AML >75
(rises across the alphabet).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What are the four key buzzword associations in leukaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back:
• Auer rods → AML
  • Philadelphia t(9;22)/BCR-ABL → CML
  • smudge cells → CLL
  • Down's syndrome & CNS spread → ALL.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What is the general aetiology of leukaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back:
Genetic change → clonal population. Triggers:
  • benzene
  • alkylating agents (→ secondary AML)
  • radiation
  • HTLV-1
  • Down's syndrome (10–20× risk; both ALL and AML).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What does t(9;22) Philadelphia → BCR-ABL signify and how is it targeted?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Present in >95% CML, and some ALL → target with imatinib (TKI).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What does t(15;17) → PML-RARα signify and how is it targeted?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: APML (AML subtype) → blocks differentiation → target with ATRA.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What is the biochemical picture of tumour lysis syndrome?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Chemo lyses cells → raised urate, raised K⁺, raised phosphate, low Ca²⁺ → AKI (urate crystals).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: How is laboratory tumour lysis syndrome defined?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: ≥2 abnormalities within 3 days pre / 7 days post chemo.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: How is tumour lysis syndrome prevented, and what is the key distinction between the two agents?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibitor — prevents urate formation) OR rasburicase (urate oxidase — breaks down existing urate to allantoin) + IV hydration. Never give both together. Check G6PD status before rasburicase — it is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency (severe oxidative haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia); use allopurinol and hydration instead (BSH). Key distinction: allopurinol works upstream/preventatively; rasburicase works on already-formed urate.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: Why are allopurinol and rasburicase not given together?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Allopurinol blocks xanthine oxidase and so reduces the urate substrate that rasburicase needs to act on — giving them together blunts rasburicase's effect while adding nothing. Choose one: rasburicase for high-risk patients (bulky ALL, very high WCC, established hyperuricaemia), allopurinol for lower-risk prophylaxis. Allopurinol can follow after a rasburicase course, but they are not run concurrently. (Rasburicase is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency.)

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: How does acute leukaemia present (marrow failure)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back:
• Anaemia (low RBC)
  • bleeding/petechiae (low platelets/thrombocytopenia)
  • infection (low neutrophils/neutropenia)
  • ± lymphadenopathy/hepatosplenomegaly.
Then act on the result: blasts on the film, a new pancytopenia, or a WCC >100 is a same-day haematology referral, not a count to repeat next week — and any fever in a neutropenic patient is neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise, IV antibiotics within 1 hour, before the neutrophil count is back.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What are the differentials for a non-blanching rash (relevant to acute leukaemia)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back:
• Leukaemia
  • meningococcaemia
  • ITP
  • HSP
  • vasculitis
  • NAI.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What investigations are used in acute leukaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back:
• FBC: low Hb, low platelets, WCC raised or low
  • bone marrow aspirate + film = definitive
  • Auer rods = AML (pathognomonic)
  • immunophenotyping for lineage
  • LP in ALL (CNS risk)
  • MRD by flow cytometry guides relapse risk and de-escalation.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What is the definitive investigation in acute leukaemia, and what confirms AML on it?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Bone marrow aspirate + film is definitive; Auer rods are pathognomonic for AML.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What does MRD by flow cytometry guide in acute leukaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Relapse risk and de-escalation.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: AML: age, hallmark, risk factor, and chemo?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back:
• Age predominantly older adults (median ~70y)
  • hallmark Auer rods
  • raised risk after MDS or myeloproliferative disease
  • chemo cytarabine + an anthracycline (the "7+3" regimen) but only for patients FIT for intensive induction — patients unfit for intensive chemotherapy receive lower-intensity therapy such as venetoclax + azacitidine instead.
It is fitness, not age, that decides. Allogeneic transplant for intermediate/high-risk cytogenetics.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What is the APML subtype of AML, its association, and treatment?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: APML (median ~40y, younger than other AML): t(15;17)/PML-RARα, presents with DIC and life-threatening haemorrhage. Start ATRA IMMEDIATELY on clinical suspicion — before genetic confirmation — with aggressive blood-product support. ATRA IMPROVES the coagulopathy and drives differentiation; it is cytotoxic chemotherapy (blast lysis) that worsens the DIC, not ATRA. ATRA + arsenic trioxide makes APML the most curable AML subtype. Watch for differentiation syndrome (fever, dyspnoea, hypoxia, oedema, weight gain, pulmonary infiltrates) → dexamethasone, and hold ATRA if severe.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: ALL: age, associations, CNS management, and significance?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back:
• Age children (<5y) and >45y
  • associations Down's syndrome and ionising radiation
  • the CNS is a SANCTUARY site, so intrathecal methotrexate is given as prophylaxis to ALL patients (with a diagnostic LP), not only those with proven CNS disease
  • highest tumour lysis risk of the four leukaemias at induction
  • commonest childhood cancer.
(EBV is linked to Burkitt/mature B-ALL, not typical ALL.)

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What is the ALL chemotherapy and maintenance?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back:
• Vincristine
  • dexamethasone
  • asparaginase
  • daunorubicin
  • 2-year maintenance.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: How is Philadelphia+ ALL and B-ALL managed beyond standard chemo?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Philadelphia+ ALL: add TKI (imatinib). B-ALL monoclonals: rituximab (anti-CD20), blinatumomab (CD19/CD3).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: CML key facts: genetics, age, and the three phases?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back:
• Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) → BCR-ABL in >95%
  • age ~65, middle-aged
  • three phases: Chronic (~5 years IF UNTREATED, often incidental raised WCC — on a TKI most patients remain in chronic phase indefinitely) → Accelerated → Blast crisis (≥20% blasts in blood or marrow by WHO criteria, usually transforms to AML, often fatal).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: How does CML present?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back:
• Insidious onset: fever, weight loss, sweats
  • massive splenomegaly
  • blood film: leucocytosis with myeloid precursors, basophilia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: How is CML managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Imatinib (TKI — blocks BCR-ABL) first-line; 2nd-generation TKIs (dasatinib, nilotinib) are alternative first-line options, and ponatinib is used for the resistant T315I mutation. Allogeneic SCT for TKI-resistant or advanced-phase disease; interferon is now reserved for pregnancy, not for advanced disease.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: CLL key facts: frequency, age/cells, blood film, and immunophenotype?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back:
• Commonest leukaemia overall
  • elderly patients (>55y)
  • clonal mature B-cells
  • indolent but incurable
  • blood film smudge/smear cells
  • immunophenotype CD5, CD19, CD20, CD23.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What is the immunophenotype of CLL?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back:
• CD5
  • CD19
  • CD20
  • CD23.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: How does CLL present and what are its key complications?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back:
• Often asymptomatic — incidental lymphocytosis on routine bloods
  • later marrow failure features, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly
  • AIHA (warm antibody)
  • Richter's transformation → high-grade lymphoma (DLBCL).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What is Richter's transformation in CLL?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Transformation to a high-grade lymphoma (DLBCL).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: How is CLL managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back:
• Watch-and-wait (early/asymptomatic disease)
  • symptomatic/progressive: FCR (fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, rituximab) — now largely second-line
  • modern first-line: BTK inhibitors (ibrutinib/acalabrutinib) or venetoclax ± obinutuzumab.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What is the modern first-line treatment for CLL?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: BTK inhibitors (ibrutinib/acalabrutinib) or venetoclax ± obinutuzumab. Venetoclax is started on a weekly dose ramp-up with hydration, urate-lowering cover and tumour lysis bloods around each dose increase — the tumour lysis rule is not confined to cytotoxic chemotherapy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: EXAM PEARL: How does the 2×2 capture the whole leukaemia topic?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Acute = blasts/marrow failure/emergency; chronic = mature/insidious/incidental.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise the four buzzword associations.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back:
• Auer rods → AML
  • Philadelphia/BCR-ABL → CML
  • smudge cells → CLL
  • Down's & CNS → ALL.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: EXAM PEARL: What do imatinib and ATRA target?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Imatinib (TKI) targets BCR-ABL in CML/Ph+ ALL; ATRA targets PML-RARα in APML.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the classic APML vignette?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: APML → DIC (can worsen on chemo) — the classic vignette; cross-reference the DIC note.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: EXAM PEARL: What two transformations/complications are linked to CLL?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: CLL → Richter's transformation (DLBCL) and AIHA.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: EXAM PEARL: Contrast allopurinol and rasburicase, and state the two 'commonest' facts.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: TLS: allopurinol (prevents urate) vs rasburicase (breaks down urate) — never both, and check G6PD before rasburicase. ALL = commonest childhood cancer; CLL = commonest leukaemia overall.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: In acute myeloid leukaemia, what actually decides between intensive and non-intensive treatment?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Fitness, not age alone: performance status (ECOG), comorbidity and organ reserve (cardiac, renal, hepatic) and frailty. AML is predominantly a disease of older adults (median age at diagnosis around 70), so many patients diagnosed with it are not candidates for intensive induction. A fit 75-year-old may be treated intensively; an unfit 60-year-old may not.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What is '7+3' induction in AML?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: The standard intensive induction regimen: 7 days of continuous-infusion cytarabine plus 3 days of an anthracycline (daunorubicin or idarubicin). It is offered only to patients fit for intensive chemotherapy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: A patient fit for intensive AML therapy achieves remission after 7+3. What comes next, and what decides whether they are transplanted?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Consolidation chemotherapy, with or without allogeneic stem cell transplant. The transplant decision is driven by cytogenetic/molecular risk group: favourable risk goes to consolidation chemotherapy alone, while intermediate or adverse risk is considered for allogeneic SCT in first remission (donor and fitness permitting).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: Where does best supportive care fit in AML?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: For the frailest patients it is a legitimate, actively chosen pathway rather than a failure to treat: transfusion support, antimicrobials and hydroxycarbamide for white-count control, with early involvement of palliative care.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What is the five-year survival of ALL in adults, and why is it so much worse than in children?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Roughly 40-50% in adults. Adults have more adverse cytogenetics (Philadelphia-positive disease is commoner) and tolerate intensive protocols less well. Childhood ALL outcomes and the full prognostic factor lists are covered in the Paediatric Cancers note.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: How does prognosis in AML vary, and what drives it?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: AML has the worst outcome of the four leukaemias overall, and survival falls steeply with age. Long-term survival is a realistic aim in fit younger adults given intensive induction, but is uncommon in the older, unfit majority treated non-intensively. The drivers are fitness for intensive therapy and cytogenetic risk group; secondary AML (post-MDS or post-alkylating agent) does worse.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What is the outlook for a patient with chronic-phase CML on a tyrosine kinase inhibitor?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Near-normal life expectancy: around 85% ten-year survival on imatinib. Progression to blast crisis is now uncommon, and the modern clinical question is how long to stay on therapy (and whether treatment-free remission is possible) rather than whether the patient will survive.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What is the natural history and outlook of CLL?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Indolent but incurable. Many older patients die with CLL rather than of it, and early-stage disease may never require treatment. Infection is the leading cause of CLL-related death.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: How is CLL diagnosed, and does it need a bone marrow?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: On peripheral-blood flow cytometry alone: a clonal mature B-cell lymphocytosis of at least 5 x 10^9/L with the CLL phenotype (CD5, CD19, CD20, CD23). No bone marrow is needed. The rule that 'bone marrow aspirate is definitive' applies to the acute leukaemias, not to CLL.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: Why do patients with CLL get recurrent bacterial infections?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: The malignant clone is a useless B-cell clone: it expands while normal antibody production collapses, producing progressive hypogammaglobulinaemia. This is a secondary immunodeficiency that deepens with advancing disease and is deepened further by treatment.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: Which organisms typically infect patients with CLL, and how important is infection?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Low IgG means failed opsonisation, so encapsulated organisms dominate: Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae, causing recurrent pneumonia, sinusitis and otitis. Infection accounts for roughly half of all CLL-related deaths - more than Richter's transformation and more than marrow failure.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What vaccination advice applies to a patient with CLL?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Give annual influenza vaccination and pneumococcal vaccination - antibody responses are blunted but the vaccines are still worthwhile. Live vaccines are contraindicated because these patients are immunocompromised.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: When is immunoglobulin replacement considered in CLL?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: For recurrent or severe bacterial infection despite prophylactic antibiotics, in a patient with a low IgG. It reduces the frequency of infection rather than prolonging survival, so it is a reserved therapy and not routine.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What lymphocyte doubling time is an indication to treat CLL?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: A lymphocyte doubling time of less than 6 months (or otherwise rapidly progressive lymphocytosis). It is the rate of change, not the absolute count, that matters.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: Is a very high lymphocyte count on its own an indication to treat CLL, and why is early asymptomatic disease not treated?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: No - a high count alone is never an indication. Early-stage asymptomatic CLL is not treated because early treatment confers no survival benefit; it only brings forward toxicity and immunosuppression. Watch-and-wait means clinical review plus an FBC, and is an active evidence-based decision.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What are myeloproliferative disorders (MPDs)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Uncontrolled clonal proliferation of a single myeloid stem cell line — cells are still mature (contrast acute leukaemia, where blasts fail to differentiate).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What is the unifying genetics of MPDs and what can they all transform to?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: In the BCR-ABL-negative MPNs (PV, ET, MF): JAK2, CALR or MPL driver mutations → constitutive JAK-STAT signalling. CML is the BCR-ABL-positive MPN. All can transform to AML.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What are the three classical types of MPD and their proliferating lines?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back:
• PV — erythroid line raised
  • ET — megakaryocyte line raised
  • primary myelofibrosis — HSC → marrow fibrosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: How does CML relate to the MPDs (cross-reference)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: CML is the 4th classical MPD but uses BCR-ABL, not JAK2 — the key discriminator.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What is the exam SBA fork in approaching polycythaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: 'Is this even true polycythaemia?'

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: Absolute polycythaemia: what defines it, and what are the primary and secondary subtypes with EPO levels?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Absolute = true raised red cell mass. Primary = PV (JAK2 mutation, marrow-driven; EPO LOW). Secondary = chronic hypoxia (lung disease, high altitude, R→L shunt, heavy smoking) or EPO-secreting tumour (renal, hepatic, cerebellar); EPO HIGH.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: Relative/apparent polycythaemia: what defines it and its two causes?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back:
Normal red cell mass with low plasma volume.
  • Gaisböck syndrome — middle-aged obese men, smoking, HTN, alcohol (EPO normal)
  • dehydration — simple volume depletion (EPO normal).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What is the key discriminator that separates dangerous clonal polycythaemia from reactive causes?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: EPO is LOW in PV (marrow autonomy suppresses EPO) but HIGH in secondary polycythaemia — this single value separates the dangerous clonal disease from reactive causes.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: MPD discriminator: what is the proliferating line in PV vs ET vs MF?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back:
• PV: raised RBC (± plt, neut)
  • ET: raised platelets
  • MF: marrow fibrosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: MPD discriminator: what proportion are JAK2-positive in PV vs ET vs MF?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back:
• PV ~95%
  • ET ~50%
  • MF ~50%.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: MPD discriminator: what is the hallmark of PV vs ET vs MF?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back:
• PV: aquagenic pruritus, ruddy plethora, raised Hct
  • ET: thrombosis ± bleeding
  • MF: massive splenomegaly.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: MPD discriminator: what is the blood film clue in PV vs ET vs MF?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back:
• PV: raised haematocrit
  • ET: abnormal large platelets
  • MF: teardrop poikilocytes, leucoerythroblastic.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: MPD discriminator: what does the bone marrow show in PV vs ET vs MF?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back:
• PV: hypercellular
  • ET: raised megakaryocytes
  • MF: dry tap → trephine.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: MPD discriminator: what is the 1st-line treatment in PV vs ET vs MF?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back:
• PV: venesection (PCV <0.45) + aspirin
  • ET: aspirin; cytoreduction only if high-risk
  • MF: supportive; a JAK1/2 inhibitor (ruxolitinib, or fedratinib/momelotinib); allogeneic BMT (only cure).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What are the features of polycythaemia vera (PV)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back:
• Aquagenic pruritus after contact with water, classically a warm bath or shower (the hallmark)
  • conjunctival plethora, ruddy complexion, hypertension, splenomegaly
  • hyperviscosity → thrombosis (stroke, DVT, Budd-Chiari) — symptomatic hyperviscosity needs urgent venesection
  • haemorrhage (abnormal platelet function)
  • headache, visual disturbance, gout, angina.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What is the hallmark feature of polycythaemia vera?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Aquagenic pruritus after contact with water, classically a warm bath or shower — a classic clue present in about 40% of PV. Suggestive, not diagnostic: check the haematocrit.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What are the investigation findings in polycythaemia vera?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back:
• Raised haematocrit (diagnostic thresholds Hct >0.52 men, >0.48 women — not the same as the <0.45 venesection target)
  • JAK2 V617F+ with a raised Hct = confirmed, and if V617F-negative test JAK2 exon 12
  • low ESR (high viscosity paradox)
  • low EPO (separates from secondary polycythaemia).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What confirms a diagnosis of polycythaemia vera?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: JAK2+ with a raised haematocrit.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: How is polycythaemia vera managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back:
• Venesection (PCV <0.45) — first-line; the resulting iron deficiency is therapeutic, so do NOT give iron
  • Aspirin 75 mg od (antithrombotic) — but withhold at platelets >1000–1500 x10^9/L until acquired von Willebrand syndrome is excluded, and cytoreduce first
  • Cytoreduction if high-risk (age >=65 or prior thrombosis) with hydroxycarbamide first-line, or interferon alfa in younger patients — pegylated interferon alfa-2a is the agent used in pregnancy, whereas ropeginterferon alfa-2b is not recommended in pregnancy (busulfan is leukaemogenic — elderly/palliative only)
  • Ruxolitinib (JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor) if hydroxycarbamide-resistant or intolerant.
Anagrelide is an ET agent, not a PV one. Hydroxycarbamide and busulfan are teratogenic.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What is the first-line management of polycythaemia vera?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Venesection (PCV <0.45).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What is the pathophysiology of myelofibrosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Stem cell proliferation → abnormal megakaryocytes release TGF-beta (and PDGF) → fibroblast activation → marrow fibrosis. Can arise de novo (primary) or evolve from PV/ET (post-PV / post-ET myelofibrosis).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What are the features of myelofibrosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back:
• Anaemia (fatigue — commonest symptom)
  • bleeding
  • hypermetabolic: weight loss, night sweats
  • massive hepatosplenomegaly → portal hypertension (extramedullary haemopoiesis).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What is the commonest symptom of myelofibrosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Fatigue (from anaemia).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What causes the massive hepatosplenomegaly in myelofibrosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Extramedullary haemopoiesis → massive hepatosplenomegaly → portal hypertension.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What are the investigation findings in myelofibrosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back:
• Anaemia
  • WCC/platelets high early, fall late
  • film: leucoerythroblastic + teardrop poikilocytes
  • raised urate, raised LDH
  • dry tap → trephine biopsy (the classic pairing).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What is the classic blood film + biopsy pairing in myelofibrosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Leucoerythroblastic + teardrop poikilocytes on film, with a dry tap → trephine biopsy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: How is myelofibrosis managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back:
• Transfusions
  • allopurinol
  • and a JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor — ruxolitinib (shrinks the spleen, eases constitutional symptoms); fedratinib and momelotinib are alternatives (momelotinib where anaemia is prominent).
Allogeneic BMT = only cure.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What are the features of essential thrombocythaemia (ET)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Isolated raised platelets with a normal or near-normal Hb and a normal or mildly raised WCC (a mild leucocytosis is common and is itself a thrombosis risk factor). Platelets abnormal in size/function → thrombosis > bleeding. Diagnosis of exclusion — rule out reactive thrombocytosis (infection, iron deficiency, malignancy) first.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: Why is essential thrombocythaemia a diagnosis of exclusion?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: You must rule out reactive thrombocytosis (infection, iron deficiency, malignancy) first.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: How is essential thrombocythaemia managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Aspirin in all patients unless contraindicated — but at platelets >1000–1500 x10^9/L check von Willebrand factor activity first (acquired von Willebrand syndrome causes bleeding). Cytoreduction only if high-risk — age >60, platelets >1500 x10^9/L, or previous thrombosis or haemorrhage (BSH): hydroxycarbamide first-line, anagrelide second-line, interferon alfa in pregnancy (busulfan elderly/palliative only). On hydroxycarbamide monitor the FBC (weekly at first, then about 3-monthly) with renal function and LFTs; painful leg ulcers mean stopping the drug, and long-term use raises non-melanoma skin cancer risk — advise sun protection and skin self-examination (BNF). Hydroxycarbamide and busulfan are teratogenic.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: EXAM PEARL: What does aquagenic pruritus after a hot bath indicate?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Check the haematocrit for PV — it is a classic clue (~40% of PV) but is suggestive rather than diagnostic, and also occurs in other MPNs and in Hodgkin lymphoma.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: EXAM PEARL: How does EPO distinguish PV from secondary polycythaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: EPO is low in PV (marrow autonomy); EPO is high in secondary polycythaemia — the key discriminator.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the signature pairing for myelofibrosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Teardrop poikilocytes + dry tap = myelofibrosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise the JAK2 positivity rates and the CML discriminator.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: JAK2: ~95% PV, ~50% ET/MF. CML uses BCR-ABL — not JAK2.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: EXAM PEARL: What are the treatment backbones for PV and ET?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Venesection + aspirin = PV backbone; aspirin alone = ET backbone.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise the transformation/end-stage and key category points across MPDs.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: All MPDs can transform to AML; myelofibrosis can be the end-stage of PV/ET. ET = diagnosis of exclusion; Gaisböck = relative (apparent) polycythaemia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What is the JAK2 V617F mutation and which MPDs carry it?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back:
Point mutation in Janus kinase 2 → constitutive cytokine signalling.
  • PV: ~95% V617F (a further ~3% carry JAK2 exon 12, so ~98% are JAK2-mutated)
  • ET: ~50% (50–60%)
  • MF: ~50% (50–60%).
Absent in CML (which has BCR-ABL instead).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What is myelofibrosis and its classic blood film finding?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: MPD → progressive marrow fibrosis (reticulin/collagen) → extramedullary haematopoiesis (splenomegaly). Film: leukoerythroblastic picture + teardrop poikilocytes (dacrocytes) — classic 'tear drop cells'.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What is the treatment target in polycythaemia vera (venesection target)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Target haematocrit <0.45 in all patients, male and female. Aspirin 75 mg daily for all PV unless contraindicated — but check von Willebrand factor activity first at platelets >1000–1500 x10^9/L. Hydroxycarbamide for high-risk cytoreduction (age >=65 or prior thrombosis) (BSH).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the Budd-Chiari syndrome association with MPDs?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: JAK2 V617F mutation causes thrombophilia → Budd-Chiari (hepatic vein thrombosis) and portal vein thrombosis. Test for JAK2 in any young patient with unprovoked mesenteric or hepatic vein thrombosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What is the defining paradox of myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Hypercellular marrow + peripheral pancytopenia — the clonal cells proliferate but die by premature apoptosis before reaching the blood (marrow is full; periphery is empty).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What is MDS (definition)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: A group of acquired clonal bone marrow disorders → ineffective haematopoiesis → progressive marrow failure.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: Where does MDS sit on the disease spectrum?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Cytopenias → MDS → AML. MDS is the pre-leukaemic middle ground.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What is the key blast cut-off separating MDS from AML?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back:
• <20% blasts = MDS
  • ≥20% blasts = AML.
The AML-defining genetic abnormalities override the count: t(15;17)/PML::RARA, t(8;21), inv(16) and NPM1 mutation are AML at any blast %, and missing t(15;17) means missing APL, an emergency needing immediate ATRA.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: How does MDS contrast with MPN (cross-reference)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: MPN (myeloproliferative neoplasm) = over-production of mature cells; MDS = ineffective production with dysplasia — same myeloid origin, opposite output. Overlap MDS/MPN entities such as CMML show both.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What are the risk factors for MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back:
• Elderly — median onset >70 years, mostly primary/idiopathic
  • therapy-related — prior chemotherapy (alkylating agents) or radiotherapy (key secondary cause)
  • benzene exposure (environmental).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What is the key secondary (therapy-related) cause of MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Prior chemotherapy (alkylating agents) or radiotherapy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: How does MDS typically present?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Often incidental — asymptomatic abnormal FBC. Symptoms arise from one or more cytopenias; anaemia is the commonest and is often the only one, with full pancytopenia in a minority at diagnosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What are the clinical features of MDS by cytopenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back:
• Anaemia → fatigue, pallor, shortness of breath
  • neutropenia → recurrent/severe infections
  • thrombocytopenia → purpura, bleeding.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What does the FBC and blood film show in MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back:
• One or more cytopenias (anaemia commonest)
  • often macrocytic anaemia (raised MCV — the classic film clue)
  • blood film: dysplastic cells, blasts <20%
  • pseudo-Pelger–Huët cells (acquired bilobed/hypolobated neutrophils) and hypogranular neutrophils — named dysplasia findings, examinable.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What is the classic film clue for the anaemia in MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Macrocytic anaemia (raised MCV).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What are the named, examinable dysplasia findings on the MDS blood film?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Pseudo-Pelger–Huët cells (acquired bilobed "pince-nez" neutrophils — the inherited Pelger–Huët anomaly is a benign mimic) and hypogranular neutrophils.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What is the definitive investigation in MDS, and what does it confirm?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back:
Bone marrow aspirate + biopsy = confirms
  • hypercellular marrow
  • dysplastic lines
  • and blast %.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What drives prognosis in MDS, and give an example?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Cytogenetics drive prognosis — isolated del(5q) = good prognosis; complex karyotype and monosomy 7/del(7q) = poor prognosis. (Isolated del(5q) is also the lenalidomide-responsive subtype.)

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What score guides treatment intensity in MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: IPSS-R (Revised International Prognostic Scoring System).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: How is low-risk MDS managed (supportive)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back:
• Watchful waiting — active monitoring, not discharge: regular FBC surveillance, with a repeat marrow if counts fall, transfusion need rises or blasts climb
  • Transfusions — RBC for symptomatic anaemia on a restrictive threshold, one unit at a time with reassessment, and an individualised threshold and target for patients on a regular programme (NICE)
  • EPO/ESA in selected patients (lower-risk, low transfusion burden, low serum EPO) — do not over-correct, avoid exceeding Hb 120 g/L (MHRA)
  • Luspatercept for transfusion-dependent anaemia with ring sideroblasts/SF3B1 after ESA failure — licensed, but not the subject of a positive NICE recommendation
  • Infection management — neutropenic sepsis is an emergency needing IV antibiotics within 1 hour
  • Iron chelation for transfusion overload.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: Why is iron chelation used in MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: For transfusional overload (cross-ref haemochromatosis/thalassaemia). Started in lower-risk patients with a long expected survival, typically once ferritin exceeds ~1000 µg/L or about 20 units have been transfused, with ferritin monitored on treatment (BSH).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What is the targeted treatment for the 5q- subtype of MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Lenalidomide (a thalidomide analogue — the targeted exam fact). Teratogenic: the UK Pregnancy Prevention Programme applies; it also causes marked early neutropenia/thrombocytopenia needing close FBC monitoring.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: How is high-risk MDS (or younger/fit patients) managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Hypomethylating agents (azacitidine) for those not eligible for transplant, intensive chemo; allogeneic stem cell transplant = only cure (reserved for fit patients — selection is by fitness and comorbidity, not a fixed age limit).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What is the only cure for MDS, and why is it limited?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Allogeneic stem cell transplant — reserved for younger/fit patients given the elderly demographic.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: MDS discriminator — marrow cellularity in aplastic anaemia vs MDS vs AML?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Aplastic anaemia: hypocellular. MDS: usually hypercellular (normocellular in some; ~10–15% is hypoplastic MDS, which overlaps with aplastic anaemia). AML: hypercellular.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: MDS discriminator — blood picture in aplastic anaemia vs MDS vs AML?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Aplastic anaemia: pancytopenia. MDS: >=1 cytopenia (anaemia commonest, often the only one); pancytopenia in a proportion. AML: blasts dominate.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: MDS discriminator — blast % in aplastic anaemia vs MDS vs AML?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Aplastic anaemia: not increased. MDS: <20%. AML: ≥20%.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: MDS discriminator — dysplasia in aplastic anaemia vs MDS vs AML?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Aplastic anaemia: no dysplasia. MDS: dysplasia in >=1 lineage. AML: dysplasia may be present (AML with myelodysplasia-related changes) — it is the blast count >=20% that defines AML, not the dysplasia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: MDS discriminator — trajectory of MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: MDS may transform to AML (~30% overall; risk driven by IPSS-R). Most lower-risk patients die of the complications of cytopenias — infection and bleeding — rather than of leukaemia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: EXAM PEARL: State the MDS paradox.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Hypercellular marrow + peripheral pancytopenia = MDS (premature intramedullary apoptosis).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the blast cut-off separating MDS from AML, and what overrides it?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: <20% blasts = MDS; ≥20% = AML — the general cut-off. The AML-defining genetic abnormalities override the count: t(15;17)/PML::RARA, t(8;21), inv(16) and NPM1 mutation are AML at any blast %, and missing t(15;17) means missing APL, an emergency needing immediate ATRA.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: EXAM PEARL: In which demographic/context is MDS classic?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: MDS is pre-leukaemic — classic in the elderly or post-chemo/radiotherapy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: EXAM PEARL: What are the dysplasia clues on the film?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Macrocytic anaemia; pseudo-Pelger–Huët / hypogranular neutrophils = dysplasia clues on film.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: EXAM PEARL: What targeted treatment matches the 5q- syndrome?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Isolated del(5q) → lenalidomide (teratogenic — UK Pregnancy Prevention Programme applies).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: EXAM PEARL: How does MDS differ from aplastic anaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: vs aplastic anaemia: same cytopenias, but aplastic anaemia has a hypocellular marrow with no dysplasia. Cellularity usually separates them, but ~10–15% of MDS is hypoplastic and overlaps — the definitive discriminators are dysplasia, excess blasts and clonal cytogenetics.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What is the significance of the 5q- syndrome subtype of MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back:
Del(5q) —
  • good prognosis
  • macrocytic anaemia with a preserved or raised platelet count
  • older women
  • lenalidomide-responsive.
Hallmark: hypolobulated ('non-lobulated') megakaryocytes on biopsy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What are the WHO subtypes of MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back:
• MDS with single lineage dysplasia (MDS-SLD)
  • MDS with multilineage dysplasia (MDS-MLD)
  • MDS with excess blasts 1 (MDS-EB1, 5–9% marrow blasts)
  • MDS with excess blasts 2 (MDS-EB2, 10–19%)
  • MDS with ring sideroblasts (MDS-RS)
  • MDS with isolated del(5q).
The current WHO classification renames these MDS-IB1/MDS-IB2, MDS-SF3B1, MDS-LB and MDS-5q, and renames the group itself "myelodysplastic neoplasms" — the abbreviation MDS is unchanged, and "syndromes" remains in wide UK clinical use.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What are the haematological features suggesting MDS transformation to AML?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back:
• Rising blast count approaching 20%
  • worsening pancytopenia
  • acquisition of new cytogenetic abnormalities
  • increasing transfusion requirements.
These prompt urgent haematology review and a repeat bone marrow to re-score risk — they are not something to observe further.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What does ring sideroblasts in MDS indicate and what gene is mutated?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Ring sideroblasts (iron-laden mitochondria around nucleus) indicate MDS-RS subtype. SF3B1 mutation drives this — associated with better prognosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: How does azacitidine work in MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Hypomethylating agent — incorporates into DNA, inhibits DNA methyltransferase → re-expresses silenced tumour suppressor genes → promotes differentiation and apoptosis of dysplastic clones.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What is the role of erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) in MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: EPO or darbepoetin for symptomatic anaemia in lower-risk MDS with serum EPO <500 IU/L and a low transfusion burden; response is best when EPO <200 IU/L and unlikely above 500. Reduces transfusion requirements in ~40–50% of patients.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What is the IPSS-R (revised IPSS) and why is it used over the original IPSS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Revised IPSS — incorporates 5 cytogenetic risk groups, more granular Hb/platelet/neutrophil thresholds. Better stratifies into very low/low/intermediate/high/very high risk for treatment decisions.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: When is allogeneic SCT considered in MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Higher-risk MDS (IPSS-R intermediate with adverse features / high / very high) with a suitable donor. Selection is by fitness and comorbidity rather than a fixed age limit — reduced-intensity conditioning allows transplant in selected patients into their early 70s. Only curative option.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: EXAM PEARL: What three things distinguish MDS from aplastic anaemia definitively?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: MDS: usually hypercellular (dysplastic) marrow, dysplasia in ≥1 lineage, and clonal cytogenetic abnormalities (blasts <20%; low-grade subtypes have <5%). AA: hypocellular marrow, no dysplasia, no excess blasts, usually normal cytogenetics — a clonal abnormality or PNH clone does not exclude AA but raises concern for clonal evolution to MDS.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What are ring sideroblasts, and how do they relate to MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Erythroblasts with iron-laden mitochondria forming a ring around the nucleus (seen on Prussian-blue stain). They define the MDS with ring sideroblasts (MDS-RS) subtype, often SF3B1-mutated, whose transfusion-dependent anaemia may respond to luspatercept.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Von Willebrand disease: how common is it, inheritance, defect, and bleeding type?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
• Commonest inherited bleeding disorder
  • mostly autosomal dominant
  • deficiency/dysfunction of VWF
  • bleeding type is mucocutaneous.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Haemophilia A & B: inheritance, factor deficiencies, and bleeding type?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
• X-linked recessive — almost exclusively males
  • A = factor VIII deficiency
  • B = factor IX (Christmas disease)
  • Bleeding type is deep (haemarthroses, muscle).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What are the two jobs of VWF, and why does this explain haemophilia-like features in severe VWD?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
VWF has two jobs:
  • (1) platelet adhesion/aggregation at the vessel wall
  • (2) carrier and stabiliser of factor VIII
That dual role explains why severe VWD can produce haemophilia-like features (low VIII, raised APTT).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What is the core pathophysiology of von Willebrand disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: VWF deficiency → defective platelet function + secondary factor VIII deficiency.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: VWD Type 1: defect and key notes?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
Partial reduction in VWF quantity.
  • ~80% of cases
  • mildest
  • autosomal dominant.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: VWD Type 2: defect and key notes?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
Qualitative / abnormal VWF. Mostly autosomal dominant — 2N is recessive. Subtypes:
  • 2A (loss of high-molecular-weight multimers)
  • 2B (increased platelet binding, with thrombocytopenia — desmopressin contraindicated)
  • 2M (reduced platelet binding, multimers normal)
  • 2N (defective factor VIII binding — low VIII with normal VWF antigen, so it mimics mild haemophilia A but affects both sexes).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: VWD Type 3: defect and key notes?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Total absence of VWF. Autosomal recessive; severe — mimics haemophilia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What are the mucocutaneous clinical features of VWD?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
• Gum bleeding on brushing, epistaxis
  • menorrhagia (often the presenting complaint)
  • prolonged bleeding after dental/surgical procedures
  • easy bruising
  • positive family history (AD).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What is often the presenting complaint of VWD?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Menorrhagia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What are the investigation findings in VWD?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
• Prolonged PFA-100 closure time (the skin bleeding time is obsolete in UK practice, and a normal PFA does not exclude VWD)
  • APTT normal or raised (raised if VIII secondarily low)
  • PT normal
  • platelets normal except in type 2B, where they are low
  • low VWF antigen + activity
  • moderately low factor VIII
The diagnosis is made on the VWF panel — antigen plus a ristocetin-based activity assay (VWF:RCo/GPIbM).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What is the specific diagnostic test for VWD?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Reduced VWF activity on a ristocetin-based assay (VWF:RCo or GPIbM) alongside VWF antigen — the VWF panel is what makes the diagnosis. Ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation (RIPA) is a subtyping test, and in type 2B low-dose RIPA is INCREASED, not reduced.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: How is acute bleeding / pre-procedure VWD managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
• Desmopressin (DDAVP) — releases endogenous VWF; first-line for minor bleeding and procedural cover in type 1
  • VWF concentrate (± factor VIII) — for type 2/3 or severe bleeds
  • Tranexamic acid — antifibrinolytic for minor/mucosal bleeding, but not for haematuria: it stabilises clot in the renal tract and can obstruct the ureter [BNF].

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: How is menorrhagia managed in VWD?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
Not a fixed ladder.
  • A levonorgestrel intrauterine system is the first treatment to consider where it is suitable [NICE]
  • tranexamic acid and combined hormonal contraception or a cyclical progestogen are the alternatives, and are often used alongside it
  • NSAIDs such as mefenamic acid — standard for heavy periods in the general population — are AVOIDED in a bleeding disorder because they add a platelet defect
Hysterectomy is a last resort, and the plan is agreed with the haemophilia centre.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Haemophilia A: factor deficiency, inheritance/carrier pattern, frequency, and desmopressin use?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
• Factor VIII deficiency
  • X-linked recessive (males affected, females usually carriers — but carriers can have factor levels in the mild haemophilia range and do bleed, especially menorrhagia and postpartum, so they need their own levels checked)
  • the most common of the two
  • desmopressin useful in mild disease.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Haemophilia B: factor deficiency, alternative name, comparison to A, and desmopressin use?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
• Factor IX deficiency
  • X-linked recessive
  • clinically identical to A
'Christmas disease' — named after Stephen Christmas, the first patient described. Desmopressin is not effective.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Why is haemophilia B called 'Christmas disease'?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: It is named after Stephen Christmas, the first patient described.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Haemophilia severity grading: severe — factor level and bleeding pattern?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Severe: factor level <1% — spontaneous bleeds (haemarthroses, muscle haematomas from infancy).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Haemophilia severity grading: moderate — factor level and bleeding pattern?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Moderate: factor level 1–5% — bleeds with minor trauma.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Haemophilia severity grading: mild — factor level and bleeding pattern?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Mild: factor level 5–40% — bleeds only with significant trauma or surgery.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What are the deep-bleeding clinical features of haemophilia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
• Haemarthroses — the hallmark (knees, ankles, elbows)
  • muscle haematomas
  • prolonged post-surgical/traumatic bleeding
  • haematuria, GI bleeding
  • retroperitoneal haematoma
  • intracranial haemorrhage (severe disease).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What is the hallmark clinical feature of haemophilia, and which joints?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Haemarthroses — knees, ankles, elbows.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What are the investigation findings in haemophilia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
• Raised APTT
  • PT, TT, PFA closure time, platelets, VWF — all normal
  • low factor VIII (A) or low factor IX (B) confirms diagnosis
  • Bethesda assay detects inhibitor antibodies.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What does the Bethesda assay detect in haemophilia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Inhibitor antibodies.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: How is haemophilia managed with factor replacement?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
• IV factor VIII or IX concentrate — on demand or prophylaxis
  • Severe disease: prophylaxis from early childhood to protect joints — factor VIII roughly 3×/week or alternate days, factor IX around twice weekly because of its longer half-life
  • Desmopressin — mild haemophilia A only (releases stored VIII); ineffective in B
  • Tranexamic acid — adjunct for mucosal bleeding, but not for haematuria: it stabilises clot in the renal tract and can obstruct the ureter [BNF].

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: In severe haemophilia, how is prophylaxis given and why?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
Prophylaxis from early childhood to protect joints:
  • recombinant factor VIII roughly 3× weekly or alternate days
  • recombinant factor IX around twice weekly (factor IX has the longer half-life).
Extended half-life products and subcutaneous emicizumab allow less frequent dosing.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What are the complications and modern therapy considerations in haemophilia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
• Inhibitor antibodies — develop against infused factor, so treatment fails
  • Emicizumab (Hemlibra) — a bispecific antibody mimicking factor VIII; standard prophylaxis in haemophilia A including inhibitor patients
  • Chronic arthropathy from repeated haemarthroses
  • Historically HIV/HCV from plasma-derived products.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What is emicizumab (Hemlibra) and its role?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: A bispecific antibody mimicking factor VIII; now standard prophylaxis in haemophilia A, including inhibitor patients. But it is prophylaxis only: a breakthrough bleed still needs factor, or a bypassing agent if there is an inhibitor. It does nothing in haemophilia B, which lacks factor IX rather than VIII.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Discriminator table — inheritance of VWD vs Haemophilia A/B vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
• VWD: autosomal dominant (mostly)
  • Haemophilia A/B: X-linked recessive
  • DIC: acquired.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Discriminator table — bleeding type of VWD vs Haemophilia A/B vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
• VWD: mucocutaneous
  • Haemophilia A/B: deep (joints/muscle)
  • DIC: mixed.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Discriminator table — platelet function (PFA closure time) in VWD vs Haemophilia A/B vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
• VWD: prolonged
  • Haemophilia A/B: normal
  • DIC: prolonged.
(The skin bleeding time this row used to quote is obsolete in UK practice.)

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Discriminator table — APTT in VWD vs Haemophilia A/B vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
• VWD: normal or raised
  • Haemophilia A/B: markedly raised
  • DIC: markedly raised.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Discriminator table — PT in VWD vs Haemophilia A/B vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
• VWD: normal
  • Haemophilia A/B: normal
  • DIC: raised.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Discriminator table — platelets in VWD vs Haemophilia A/B vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
• VWD: normal — EXCEPT type 2B, where the abnormal VWF binds platelets and causes thrombocytopenia
  • Haemophilia A/B: normal
  • DIC: low.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Discriminator table — factor VIII in VWD vs Haemophilia A/B vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
• VWD: moderately low
  • Haemophilia A/B: markedly low (A only)
  • DIC: low.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Discriminator table — VWF / ristocetin in VWD vs Haemophilia A/B vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
• VWD: abnormal
  • Haemophilia A/B: normal
  • DIC: not applicable.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: EXAM PEARL: How does the bleeding pattern tell you the level of the defect?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
• Mucocutaneous → VWF/platelet problem
  • haemarthrosis → coagulation factor (haemophilia).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: EXAM PEARL: What does an isolated raised APTT with everything else normal suggest?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Think haemophilia (or mild VWD). PT normal = intrinsic pathway only.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: EXAM PEARL: In which conditions does desmopressin work, and where does it NOT work?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
• Desmopressin works in haemophilia A (mild) and VWD type 1
  • It does NOT work in haemophilia B — there is no stored IX to release.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the one fact explaining the VWD/haemophilia overlap?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: VWF carries factor VIII — type 3 VWD → very low VIII → mimics haemophilia A.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the inheritance/carrier pattern of haemophilia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: X-linked recessive → haemophilia in males, carrier mothers. Daughters of affected males are obligate carriers.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What is the role of gene therapy in haemophilia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
A single-dose AAV vector delivers the clotting-factor gene.
  • For haemophilia B, etranacogene dezaparvovec is approved for NHS use under a managed-access arrangement and is given at a small number of specialist centres [NICE]
  • The haemophilia A product, valoctocogene roxaparvovec, has been withdrawn from the market by its manufacturer for commercial reasons and is no longer available.
Gene therapy is not a permanent cure — expression wanes over years, and transaminitis needing steroid cover is common. Emicizumab (a factor VIII-mimicking bispecific antibody) and factor prophylaxis remain the mainstay.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: In which type of von Willebrand disease must desmopressin NOT be used, and why?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Type 2B. The abnormal von Willebrand factor already binds platelets too avidly; releasing more of it worsens the thrombocytopenia. This is the clinically important meaning of the '2B' subtype. Its mimic is platelet-type (pseudo-)VWD, where the gain-of-function defect is in the platelet receptor GPIbα rather than in VWF — an identical picture, but treated with platelet transfusion rather than VWF concentrate.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Why is desmopressin ineffective in type 3 von Willebrand disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Because desmopressin works by releasing stored endogenous VWF, and in type 3 there is essentially none to release. It is the same logic that makes desmopressin useless in haemophilia B, where there is no stored factor IX.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What adverse effect of desmopressin must patients be warned about, and how is it managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Hyponatraemia, which has caused seizures - particularly in young children. Desmopressin is an ADH analogue, so patients must restrict fluid intake around dosing and have sodium monitored.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What is tachyphylaxis in the context of desmopressin?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Stored VWF and factor VIII are depleted by each dose, so repeated doses produce progressively smaller responses. It limits how often desmopressin can be relied on.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Why is a desmopressin trial or test dose performed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: To establish whether this particular patient actually responds, with paired factor levels before and after. Response cannot be assumed from the subtype alone.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: A known haemophiliac attends after a head injury. What is done first?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Factor replacement, immediately - before imaging and before waiting for specialist advice. The factor goes in and then you investigate. A normal initial neurological examination does not exclude an intracranial bleed.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Which bleed sites in haemophilia are immediately life- or limb-threatening?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
• Intracranial (the leading cause of bleeding death)
  • throat and neck (airway)
  • iliopsoas or retroperitoneal (large silent-volume bleed)
  • compartment syndrome in a limb
  • and gastrointestinal bleeding.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: A haemophiliac presents with groin pain and holds the hip flexed. What should you suspect?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: An iliopsoas bleed. It can accommodate a large volume of blood silently, may cause hypovolaemia, and classically mimics appendicitis or a hip problem. It needs factor replacement and imaging.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: How does the target factor level vary with the type of bleed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: It rises with the seriousness of the bleed - a joint bleed needs a moderate rise, whereas a life-threatening or intracranial bleed needs a level close to normal, maintained for longer.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: How is a haemarthrosis managed in haemophilia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
• Factor replacement first — on suspicion, without waiting for imaging — then rest, ice, compression and elevation, with analgesia and early physiotherapy
  • The joint is NOT routinely aspirated: aspiration risks further bleeding and infection, and is reserved for suspected septic arthritis or an exceptionally tense joint, under factor cover and by the haemophilia team
  • Avoid aspirin and non-selective NSAIDs.
The aim is to prevent recurrence, because repeated bleeds into one joint cause chronic haemophilic arthropathy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What is an inhibitor in haemophilia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: An alloantibody directed against the infused clotting factor, neutralising it. It is the most serious complication of haemophilia treatment, is far commoner in severe haemophilia A than in haemophilia B, and typically develops early - within the first several dozen exposures, so usually in young children.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What is the clinical signature of an inhibitor?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: A dose of factor that used to work stops working - a bleed fails to respond to adequate replacement, and there is no expected rise in the post-infusion factor level.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Which laboratory test flags an inhibitor, and which quantifies it?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
• The mixing study flags it: if the prolonged APTT fails to correct on mixing with normal plasma, an inhibitor is present rather than a factor deficiency
  • Factor VIII inhibitors are time- and temperature-dependent, so the immediate mix may correct and the failure to correct only appears after incubation at 37°C for 1–2 hours
  • The Bethesda assay then quantifies it: at low titre more factor can overwhelm the antibody, while at high titre a bypassing agent (rFVIIa or FEIBA) is needed, with immune tolerance induction used to try to eradicate the inhibitor.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Which analgesics should be avoided in haemophilia, and which are acceptable?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
• Avoid aspirin and non-selective NSAIDs - they add a platelet defect to an existing factor defect
  • Paracetamol and opioids are acceptable.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: How should vaccinations be given to a patient with haemophilia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Vaccination is encouraged, not avoided. Injections are given subcutaneously where possible, or intramuscularly under factor cover, with firm pressure applied afterwards. Routine IM injections without cover should be avoided.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What planning is needed before dental extraction or surgery in a bleeding disorder?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back:
Both are planned in advance with the haemophilia centre.
  • Dental work is often safe with tranexamic acid mouthwash plus desmopressin or factor cover
  • surgery needs a written haemostatic plan setting out what to give, when, and for how many days afterwards.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Where is haemophilia care delivered in the UK?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Through a designated haemophilia comprehensive care centre, providing home therapy, an alert card, physiotherapy and 24-hour specialist advice. Patients and families are usually experts in their own condition and carry a treatment plan that should be followed.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the decisive fork (consumption) in DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Massive coagulation activation consumes platelets and clotting factors faster than they are replaced — giving the paradox of clotting and bleeding simultaneously.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Trace the consumption chain that produces the DIC lab picture.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back:
• Factors used up → PT/APTT/TT prolong
  • fibrinogen consumed → low
  • platelets consumed → thrombocytopenia
  • red cells sheared through intravascular fibrin strands → schistocytes
  • secondary fibrinolysis → raised FDPs/D-dimer.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Is DIC ever a primary condition?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: No — DIC is always secondary; there is no primary DIC.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is DIC (definition)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Widespread intravascular fibrin generation from massive coagulation cascade activation.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the core paradox of DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Too much clotting and too little clotting simultaneously — microvascular thrombosis plus haemorrhage.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the mechanism chain of DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Trigger → tissue factor exposed → coagulation cascade fires → fibrin + platelet consumption → secondary fibrinolysis → FDPs (which themselves worsen bleeding by inhibiting fibrin polymerisation) → haemorrhage + microvascular thrombosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: How do FDPs worsen bleeding in DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: They inhibit fibrin polymerisation.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the unifying mechanism behind all DIC triggers?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back:
Anything that exposes or expresses tissue factor —
  • endothelial damage
  • monocyte TF expression driven by cytokines
  • or direct TF release.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the commonest cause of DIC, and its mechanism?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Sepsis (classically Gram-negative, though Gram-positive sepsis does the same) — cytokine-driven TF expression on monocytes.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Which trauma/tissue destruction causes trigger DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back:
• Burns
  • major surgery
  • crush injury
  • fat embolism.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Which obstetric causes trigger DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back:
• Amniotic fluid embolism
  • HELLP syndrome
  • placental abruption
  • retained products of conception.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Which malignancy causes trigger DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back:
• Advanced solid tumours
  • APML (acute promyelocytic leukaemia) — the classic haematological trigger.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Which transfusion and vascular causes trigger DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back:
• Transfusion reaction: ABO-incompatible transfusion
  • Vascular: aortic aneurysm, haemangioma.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the APML link to DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Acute promyelocytic leukaemia is the classic leukaemia trigger for DIC — promyelocytes release procoagulant granules.
