ATRA rapidly IMPROVES the coagulopathy and should be started on suspicion, before genetic confirmation; it is cytotoxic chemotherapy (blast lysis) that can transiently worsen the DIC.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What are the bleeding (haemorrhagic end) clinical features of DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back:
• Oozing from ≥3 unrelated sites (exam buzzword)
  • venepuncture/cannula sites, IV lines
  • nose, mouth, gums
  • GI bleeding, haematuria
  • wound/surgical site bleeding.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the exam buzzword for the bleeding end of DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Oozing from ≥3 unrelated sites.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What are the thrombosis (thrombotic end) clinical features of DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back:
Microvascular occlusion → end-organ ischaemia
  • AKI (renal cortical necrosis)
  • delirium / reduced GCS (cerebral ischaemia)
  • purpura fulminans (digital/skin necrosis)
  • respiratory failure (ARDS pattern).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is purpura fulminans in DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Digital/skin necrosis — a thrombotic feature.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the range of severity in DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: From subclinical (lab abnormalities only) to complete haemostatic failure.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Investigations — what happens to platelets and PT/APTT/TT in DIC, and why?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back:
• Platelets very low (consumed in microthrombi)
  • PT/APTT/TT all prolonged (clotting factors consumed).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Investigations — what happens to fibrinogen and D-dimer/FDPs in DIC, and why?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back:
• Fibrinogen low (consumed — acute phase reactant, so may be normal early)
  • D-dimer/FDPs markedly raised (secondary fibrinolysis).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Investigations — what does the blood film and FBC show in DIC, and why?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back:
• Blood film: schistocytes (fragmented RBCs — sheared through fibrin strands in vessels)
  • FBC: low Hb, low platelets (haemolysis + consumption).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Why may fibrinogen be normal early in DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: It is an acute phase reactant, so it may be normal early despite being consumed.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Discriminator — PT/APTT and fibrinogen in DIC vs liver disease vs TTP/HUS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back:
• PT/APTT: DIC raised, liver disease raised, TTP/HUS normal
  • Fibrinogen: DIC low, liver disease low (late), TTP/HUS normal.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Discriminator — D-dimer and schistocytes in DIC vs liver disease vs TTP/HUS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back:
• D-dimer: DIC markedly raised, liver disease mildly raised, TTP/HUS normal/mildly raised
  • Schistocytes: DIC yes, liver disease no, TTP/HUS yes.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the key discriminator (Factor VIII) between DIC and liver disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Factor VIII is extrahepatic — normal/high in liver disease, but low in DIC. This is the key discriminator (TTP/HUS: Factor VIII normal).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is Priority 1 in managing DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back:
Treat the underlying cause — this is the only thing that reverses DIC.
  • Antibiotics for sepsis
  • deliver in obstetric cases
  • treat APML
Everything else is supportive.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What supportive blood products are given in DIC, and when?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back:
Only if bleeding, at high bleeding risk, or pre-procedure:
  • platelets → keep >50 ×10⁹/L if bleeding (>20 ×10⁹/L if not bleeding but at high bleeding risk)
  • FFP → replaces all clotting factors, initial dose 15 mL/kg if PT/APTT >1.5× normal
  • cryoprecipitate → replaces fibrinogen (target >1.5 g/L, but >2 g/L in ongoing obstetric haemorrhage)
  • red cells → for anaemia/blood loss.
Treat the patient, not the numbers alone.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What does cryoprecipitate replace in DIC, and the target?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Fibrinogen — target >1.5 g/L, but >2 g/L in ongoing obstetric haemorrhage.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the heparin exam trap in DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Therapeutic-dose anticoagulation is considered only in thrombosis-predominant DIC (e.g. purpura fulminans, dominant microvascular clotting with minimal bleeding), with LMWH generally preferred over unfractionated heparin, and is withheld when bleeding dominates. The trap runs both ways: do not reach for therapeutic heparin reflexively, but do not withhold prophylactic-dose LMWH from a critically ill, non-bleeding patient with DIC either - VTE prophylaxis is still indicated there.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the DIC pentad?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back:
• Low platelets
  • raised PT/APTT
  • low fibrinogen
  • raised D-dimer
  • schistocytes
All five together = DIC until proven otherwise.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: EXAM PEARL: Why does 'DIC is always secondary' matter for management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Because the most important management step is identifying and treating the underlying cause.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise the triggers (sepsis, APML, obstetric).
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back:
• Sepsis = commonest trigger
  • APML = classic leukaemia link
  • Obstetric causes (amniotic fluid embolism, HELLP, abruption) are also high-yield.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: EXAM PEARL: When do you replace products in DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Treat the patient, not the numbers — only replace products (platelets, FFP, cryo) if actively bleeding or pre-procedure.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: EXAM PEARL: How does DIC differ from liver disease and TTP/HUS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back:
• vs liver disease: factor VIII is extrahepatic — normal/high in liver disease, low in DIC
  • vs TTP/HUS: thrombocytopenia + schistocytes but normal coagulation screen.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise the heparin trap in DIC.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Therapeutic-dose anticoagulation: only in thrombosis-predominant DIC (purpura fulminans), LMWH preferred over unfractionated heparin, withheld when bleeding dominates. Prophylactic-dose LMWH is a separate question and is still given for VTE prophylaxis in the critically ill non-bleeding patient.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the laboratory hallmark of DIC — the key 4-test combination?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back:
• ↑PT
  • ↑APTT
  • ↓fibrinogen
  • ↑D-dimer/FDPs
simultaneous coagulation activation AND consumption. Thrombocytopenia present.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the underlying mechanism of DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Systemic thrombin activation → widespread microvascular clotting → consumption of clotting factors and platelets → secondary haemolysis and bleeding.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the paradox of DIC clinically?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Simultaneous thrombosis AND bleeding — patients clot in microvessels (organ failure) but bleed from consumption of factors/platelets.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: EXAM PEARL: What differentiates DIC from liver failure on clotting tests?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Both have ↑PT, ↑APTT, ↓fibrinogen — but DIC has a markedly elevated D-dimer and schistocytes (MAHA), whereas in liver failure the D-dimer is normal or only mildly raised and there are no fragmented cells. Factor VIII (made extrahepatically) is the definitive discriminator: low in DIC, normal or high in liver disease.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: A critically ill patient has laboratory DIC but is not bleeding. What is the anticoagulation decision?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Give prophylactic-dose LMWH for VTE prophylaxis. DIC is a prothrombotic state and these patients sit at high thrombotic risk; a deranged clotting screen on its own is not a reason to withhold thromboprophylaxis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: State the three-step anticoagulation ladder in DIC.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back:
• 1) Not bleeding and critically ill: prophylactic-dose LMWH for VTE prophylaxis
  • 2) Thrombosis predominates: therapeutic-dose anticoagulation
  • 3) Bleeding dominates: hold anticoagulation, support with blood products and press on with treating the trigger.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: When thrombosis predominates in DIC and therapeutic anticoagulation is chosen, which agent is generally preferred?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: LMWH is generally preferred over unfractionated heparin. UFH is reserved for situations where a short half-life and easy reversibility matter — high bleeding risk or severe renal impairment.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Which clinical pictures put a DIC patient on the 'thrombosis predominates' rung of the ladder?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back:
• Purpura fulminans
  • digital or skin necrosis
  • microvascular organ ischaemia (AKI, delirium)
  • and overt venous thromboembolism
— with little or no bleeding.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the classic heparin exam trap in DIC, and what is the trap on the other side?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back:
• The classic trap is reaching for therapeutic heparin in the bleeding DIC patient — therapeutic anticoagulation belongs to the thrombosis-predominant phenotype, and you hold it when bleeding dominates
  • The trap on the other side is withholding prophylactic-dose LMWH from a non-bleeding critically ill patient because the clotting numbers look bad.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Is tranexamic acid part of routine DIC management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: No. It is not routine, and it is harmful in the thrombotic phenotype: blocking fibrinolysis while thrombin generation continues leaves microvascular fibrin undissolved, a recognised route to catastrophic thrombosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the narrow exception in which an antifibrinolytic may be considered in DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Hyperfibrinolysis-predominant DIC in which bleeding persists despite treating the trigger and replacing blood products. This is a specialist decision, not a ward reflex.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Why is 'give tranexamic acid early' correct in traumatic haemorrhage but wrong in DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back:
They are opposite problems.
  • In trauma, early hyperfibrinolysis is destroying clot the patient needs, so blocking it helps — and the same applies in postpartum haemorrhage, which keeps its tranexamic acid even once DIC has developed
  • In DIC outside those two settings the dominant lesion is usually ongoing thrombin generation with microvascular fibrin deposition, so shutting off fibrinolysis removes the only mechanism clearing those microthrombi.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Which group of DIC patients should specifically not receive tranexamic acid?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Patients with acute promyelocytic leukaemia being treated with ATRA — thrombotic events are reported with this combination.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Which tests do you repeat to monitor the response in DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back:
• FBC (platelets and Hb)
  • PT/APTT
  • fibrinogen and D-dimer
— rechecked after blood products are given and as the underlying trigger is treated. How often is driven by how unwell the patient is, not by a fixed timetable.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: In monitoring DIC, what matters more than any single laboratory value?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: The trend across serial samples. A falling platelet count together with a falling fibrinogen is the powerful dynamic clue that consumption is still winning.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Why can a normal fibrinogen early in DIC be misleading?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Fibrinogen is an acute-phase reactant, so it can start high and fall through the normal range while consumption is already well established. The serial trend, not the single value, shows what is happening.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the only real endpoint of DIC treatment?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Control of the precipitant. Blood products and anticoagulation buy time and manage the phenotype; only treating the underlying cause reverses DIC.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: You transfuse products for bleeding DIC and the repeat clotting numbers improve. Is the DIC treated?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: No. Product replacement corrects the measurement, not the process. Unless the trigger is being controlled the consumption continues, so keep repeating FBC, PT/APTT, fibrinogen and D-dimer and keep working on the cause.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is the guiding principle of transfusion strategy?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: A restrictive transfusion strategy (lower thresholds) → better outcomes. Give one unit at a time, then reassess.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is the indication for red cell transfusion?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Anaemia / acute blood loss.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What are the red cell transfusion thresholds and targets in non-ACS vs ACS patients?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• Non-ACS: transfuse if Hb <70, target 70–90 g/L
  • ACS: transfuse if Hb <80, target 80–100 g/L.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What are the key practical facts for red cell transfusion (infusion time, storage, use-by)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• Infuse each unit over 90–120 min
  • stored at 2–6°C in a controlled-temperature blood fridge
  • each unit must be COMPLETED within 4 hours of leaving controlled-temperature storage.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: Which blood group is the universal donor for red cells?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: O negative.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is the indication for FFP?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Clotting factor deficiency (PT/APTT >1.5× normal).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What does FFP contain, who is the universal donor, and what is the caution?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• Contains all clotting factors
  • Universal donor = AB (no anti-A or anti-B)
  • Large volume — avoid in fluid overload.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is the indication for cryoprecipitate?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Low fibrinogen (<1.5 g/L) — DIC, liver failure, massive transfusion.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What does cryoprecipitate contain, and where does the name 'cryo' come from?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• Concentrated fibrinogen
  • factor VIII
  • vWF
  • factor XIII
It is the precipitate of FFP at 4°C — hence 'cryo'.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What are the indications for platelet transfusion?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• Severe thrombocytopenia with bleeding
  • prophylactic if <10×10⁹/L.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: How are platelets stored, why, and what does one adult dose achieve?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• Stored at 20–24°C with continuous gentle agitation, up to 7 days
  • Never refrigerated — chilling activates platelets and causes rapid clearance by the liver, destroying post-transfusion survival
  • Room-temperature storage is also why bacterial contamination is commoner with platelets than any other component
One adult dose raises the count by ~20–30×10⁹/L.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is the indication for PCC (prothrombin complex concentrate)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Emergency warfarin reversal (major bleed, ICH, emergency surgery).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What does PCC contain, how fast does it work, and what must always be co-administered?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• Fastest reversal — within 1h
  • Contains factors II, VII, IX, X
  • Always give with IV vitamin K (factor VII has a short half-life → INR creeps back up).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is the role of CMV-negative blood products and who are they used for?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
CMV is leucocyte-transmitted, and universal leucodepletion makes standard UK components "CMV-safe". CMV-seronegative components are reserved for
  • intrauterine transfusion
  • neonates up to 28 days
  • and elective (non-emergency) transfusion in pregnancy
— NO LONGER routinely for transplant recipients, HIV or other immunocompromised patients.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What do irradiated blood products do, and what do they prevent?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• Donor T-lymphocytes are inactivated by irradiation so they cannot proliferate — they are not removed
  • Prevents TA-GVHD (Transfusion-Associated Graft-versus-Host Disease) — almost always fatal in immunocompromised patients (haematology, stem cell transplant).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: Why is a restrictive transfusion strategy preferred over a liberal one?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
A restrictive strategy (lower threshold) →
  • fewer reactions
  • less fluid overload
  • and better outcomes than liberal.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What are the four steps of warfarin reversal?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• 1. Stop warfarin
  • 2. Vitamin K — IV (works in 4–6h) or oral (24h); always give
  • 3. PCC — for major bleed/ICH/emergency surgery, reversal within 1h, give WITH vitamin K
  • 4. FFP — older alternative; large volume, avoid in fluid overload.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: In warfarin reversal, how quickly does vitamin K work by IV vs oral route?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• IV works in 4–6h
  • oral works in 24h
Always give it.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: Why must vitamin K be given WITH PCC in warfarin reversal?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Factor VII has a short half-life — without vitamin K, new factors won't be synthesised and the INR will rebound.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is the universal first step for every transfusion reaction?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: STOP the transfusion.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: Febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction: cause, features, and management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• Cause: anti-leucocyte antibodies → cytokine release
  • Features: mild = a temperature rise of 1–2°C to below 39°C with no other features
  • Management: STOP and assess; paracetamol; may restart cautiously at a slower rate if mild and the patient is stable
Rigors, a temperature ≥39°C or a rise ≥2°C is a moderate reaction — do not simply restart; exclude bacterial contamination and haemolysis first (BSH).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: Minor allergic transfusion reaction: cause, features, and management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• Cause: reaction to donor plasma proteins
  • Features: urticaria, pruritus — no systemic compromise
  • Management: stop temporarily; antihistamine; can restart.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: Anaphylaxis during transfusion: cause, features, and management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• Cause: allergy to donor plasma proteins — classically severe IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies, though often no antibody is identified
  • Features: hypotension, bronchospasm, angioedema — rapid onset
  • Management: STOP; IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (500 micrograms) into the anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5 min if no response; ABC; high-flow O₂; IV fluids
If severe IgA deficiency is confirmed, flag it and use washed or IgA-deficient components in future.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction: cause, features, and management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• Cause: ABO incompatibility (wrong blood — human error)
  • Features: fever, loin/back pain, hypotension, dark urine — onset within minutes
  • Management: STOP immediately; keep IV access open with 0.9% saline and resuscitate aggressively to maintain urine output; check patient ID + bag label; call for senior/critical care help and TELEPHONE THE TRANSFUSION LABORATORY AT ONCE (another patient may be about to receive the swapped unit); return the unit and giving set with fresh clotted and EDTA samples for DAT, repeat group and crossmatch; monitor for AKI and DIC.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: TRALI: cause, features, and management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• Cause: donor antibodies → neutrophil activation → capillary leak
  • Features: non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema; hypoxia; HYPOtension; fever — within 6h
  • Management: STOP; O₂ + supportive; NO diuretics.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: TACO: cause, features, and management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• Cause: volume overload (too fast / pre-existing HF/renal failure)
  • Features: pulmonary oedema; HYPERtension; raised JVP; orthopnoea — cardiogenic
  • Management: STOP; sit upright; O₂ + IV furosemide; if transfusion must continue afterwards, restart slowly one unit at a time
Largely preventable: do a pre-transfusion TACO risk assessment, especially over 50, under 50 kg, or with heart failure or renal impairment (SHOT).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: TRALI vs TACO: what is the key discriminator?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
Both cause pulmonary oedema during/after transfusion — the key difference is blood pressure (and mechanism):
  • TRALI = HYPOtension
  • TACO = HYPERtension.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: TRALI vs TACO: contrast mechanism and oedema type.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• TRALI: immune-mediated capillary leak, non-cardiogenic oedema
  • TACO: volume overload, cardiogenic oedema.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: TRALI vs TACO: contrast management.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• TRALI: O₂ + supportive, NO diuretics
  • TACO: furosemide + O₂.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: Give the one-line memory hooks for TRALI and TACO.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• TRALI — leaky lungs + low BP → no diuretics
  • TACO — too much fluid + high BP → diurese.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is the maximum storage time and temperature for red cell concentrates?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: 35 days at 2–6°C.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What are the signs of an acute haemolytic transfusion reaction and its mechanism?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• Fever
  • rigors
  • loin pain
  • haemoglobinuria
  • hypotension
— ABO incompatibility → complement activation → intravascular haemolysis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is TACO and how does it differ from TRALI?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• TACO (Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload) — cardiogenic pulmonary oedema; responds to diuretics
  • TRALI (Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury) — non-cardiogenic; anti-leukocyte antibodies; PAOP normal; treat supportively.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is the threshold for transfusing platelets prophylactically in a stable patient?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• <10 × 10⁹/L in stable patients
  • <50 × 10⁹/L pre-procedure
  • <100 × 10⁹/L for CNS/ophthalmic surgery.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is irradiated blood and when is it used?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
Irradiated (gamma or X-ray) to INACTIVATE donor T-lymphocytes so they cannot proliferate — they are not removed — preventing transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease (TA-GvHD), which is almost always fatal. UK indications:
  • Hodgkin lymphoma (lifelong)
  • purine analogues (fludarabine, cladribine, bendamustine) and alemtuzumab/ATG
  • allogeneic and autologous stem cell transplant
  • congenital T-cell immunodeficiency
  • intrauterine and neonatal exchange transfusion
  • granulocytes
  • HLA-matched platelets
  • and any directed donation from a relative
Not needed for a haematological malignancy per se, nor for HIV.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is the indication for CMV-negative blood products?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
Since universal leucodepletion, standard UK components are 'CMV-safe.' CMV-seronegative products are now reserved for
  • intrauterine transfusion
  • neonates (≤28 days)
  • and elective (non-emergency) transfusion in pregnancy
— no longer routinely for transplant recipients or HIV patients.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is the standard dose of FFP and when is it given?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: 15–20 mL/kg (about 4 units in an average adult), given for clinically significant coagulopathy WITH BLEEDING or before an invasive procedure (PT/APTT >1.5× normal) — DIC, liver disease, massive haemorrhage. It is not indicated to correct an abnormal clotting screen in a non-bleeding patient, and it is not first choice for warfarin reversal (PCC is).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the transfusion trigger in a stable, asymptomatic patient without cardiac disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• Hb <70 g/L → transfuse, target 70–90 g/L
  • Hb 70–90 → clinical judgement and symptoms
  • Hb >90 → generally avoid transfusion in a non-ACS patient (NICE).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: EXAM PEARL: What are the four main delayed transfusion complications?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• Delayed haemolytic reaction (days–weeks)
  • iron overload (repeat transfusions)
  • alloimmunisation
  • transfusion-transmitted infection (rare).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What must be covered and documented when consenting a patient for a blood transfusion?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• The indication
  • the expected benefit
  • the alternatives (iron, tranexamic acid, treating the underlying cause)
  • and the risks
— with the discussion documented in the notes. Give the patient the transfusion patient information leaflet. If the patient declines (for example a Jehovah's Witness), record the refusal and any advance decision.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What must appear on a blood component prescription / transfusion chart?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
Each unit prescribed separately, stating:
  • the component
  • the volume or number of units
  • the rate or duration for that unit
  • and any special requirements (irradiated, CMV-negative) so the laboratory can supply them.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: How should a pre-transfusion blood sample be taken and labelled?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• Positive patient identification first — ask the patient to state their name and date of birth, then check it against the wristband
  • Hand-write the tube label at the bedside, next to the patient, before leaving them
Never pre-label the tube and never label it away from the bedside.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is checked in the bedside check, and where is it performed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
At the patient's side, immediately before the unit is connected — never at the fridge or in the corridor. Ask the patient to state their name and date of birth, then match the wristband and the compatibility label on the unit for:
  • surname
  • first name
  • date of birth
  • hospital number
  • donation/unit number
  • component and group
  • expiry date
  • and that any special requirement has been met
Inspect the pack for leaks, clots or discolouration.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is the observation schedule for a blood transfusion?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
Pulse, blood pressure, temperature and respiratory rate:
  • within 60 minutes BEFORE starting each unit
  • 15 minutes AFTER the start of each unit
  • and within 60 minutes AFTER the unit finishes
The patient is also observed visually throughout (BSH).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: Why are observations taken 15 minutes after the start of every unit?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Because the severe early reactions — acute haemolytic (ABO) reaction, bacterial sepsis from a contaminated unit, and anaphylaxis — declare themselves within the first few minutes of the unit running. The check is repeated for every unit, not just the first.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is the 30-minute rule in transfusion?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: A component that has been out of controlled-temperature storage for more than 30 minutes cannot be returned to the blood fridge — it must be transfused or discarded. So collect the unit only when you are ready to start.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is the 4-hour rule in transfusion?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Each unit must be COMPLETED within 4 hours of leaving controlled-temperature storage (JPAC). The limit reflects bacterial proliferation once the pack warms, not the shelf life of the component.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: Which fluids and drugs may be given through a blood administration line, and what giving set is required?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
Only 0.9% sodium chloride may share the line —
  • no drugs
  • no glucose
  • and no calcium-containing fluid such as Hartmann's (calcium overrides the citrate anticoagulant and clots the line)
Use a dedicated blood administration set with an integral 170–200 micrometre filter, changed at least 12-hourly.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: Where should a transfusion be given, and what should the patient be told before going home?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• Somewhere the patient can be directly observed and staff can respond
  • avoid overnight transfusion unless clinically necessary, because reactions get missed
Counsel the patient verbally and in writing to seek urgent help if they become unwell in the next 24 hours — fever, rash, breathlessness or dark urine.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What are the universal immediate steps when a transfusion reaction is suspected?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• STOP the transfusion
  • keep the line open with 0.9% saline through a new giving set
  • assess airway, breathing and circulation
  • RECHECK the patient's identity against the bag label
  • and inform the transfusion laboratory, keeping the unit and its giving set
Only a mild febrile or minor allergic reaction may be cautiously restarted.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is SHOT, and what do its reports consistently identify as the commonest cause of transfusion-related death?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: SHOT (Serious Hazards of Transfusion) is the UK haemovigilance scheme — professionally mandated confidential reporting of transfusion adverse events, adverse reactions and near misses, including wrong blood in tube. Its reports consistently identify TACO as the commonest cause of transfusion-related death, and most serious incidents as avoidable human error rather than component failure.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: Which transfusion reporting is a statutory (legal) requirement in the UK, and under what regulations?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Serious adverse reactions and serious adverse events must be reported to the MHRA via SABRE (Serious Adverse Blood Reactions and Events) under the Blood Safety and Quality Regulations 2005. The same portal is used to submit the SHOT report. The regulations also require the fate of every component to be traceable for 30 years.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: Bacterial contamination of a blood component: which component, what features, and what is the management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• Most often platelets, because they are stored at room temperature
  • High fever, rigors and shock soon after starting the unit
  • Management: STOP the transfusion, take cultures from the patient AND the unit, give broad-spectrum antibiotics and resuscitate.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: Delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction: mechanism, timing, findings and management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• An anamnestic alloantibody response — an antibody from previous transfusion or pregnancy, undetectable at crossmatch, is boosted by re-exposure
  • Falling Hb, jaundice and a positive DAT days to about 2 weeks later, often after discharge
  • Management is supportive, but the antibody must be identified and recorded so future units are crossmatched against it.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: Name the delayed complications of transfusion and roughly when each appears.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back:
• Delayed haemolytic reaction and post-transfusion purpura at days to about 2 weeks (TA-GvHD also about 1–2 weeks)
  • then red cell alloimmunisation, iron overload and transfusion-transmitted infection over weeks to years.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is post-transfusion purpura, and how is it treated?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: A rare delayed reaction: profound thrombocytopenia about 5–12 days after transfusion, classically in a previously pregnant woman who is HPA-1a negative, in whom platelet-specific alloantibodies destroy her own platelets as well as the donor's. Treat with IVIg; further platelet transfusions are largely ineffective.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: How much iron does a unit of red cells contain, and why does that matter?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Roughly 250 mg of iron per unit, and there is no physiological route to excrete it — so regularly transfused patients accumulate iron in the heart, liver and endocrine organs. Monitoring and chelation are covered under Thalassaemia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is red cell alloimmunisation and why does it matter?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Antibodies form against donor red cell antigens the patient lacks (Rh, Kell, Kidd, Duffy). It is usually silent at the time, but it makes future units harder and slower to crossmatch, sets up delayed haemolytic reactions, and risks haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn in girls and women of childbearing age. If an RhD-negative girl or woman of childbearing potential is inadvertently given RhD-positive red cells or platelets, give anti-D immunoglobulin and take specialist transfusion advice.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: How likely is transfusion-transmitted infection in the UK, and why was universal leucodepletion introduced?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Very unlikely — donor selection and testing put the residual risk of HIV or hepatitis C well below one per million donations, so bacterial contamination of a component is the commoner infective hazard. Universal leucodepletion was introduced as a precaution against transmission of variant CJD.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is the clinical significance and timing of neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: A medical emergency — the commonest serious complication of chemotherapy, typically 7–14 days post-cycle (the nadir).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is the definition of neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Neutrophils 0.5 ×10⁹/L or LOWER (≤0.5) in a patient on anticancer treatment PLUS either temp >38°C or other signs/symptoms consistent with clinically significant sepsis. (The diagnosis is a definition, not a judgement call.)

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: Why is neutropenic sepsis described as 'a definition, not a judgement call'?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: If the neutrophil and temperature/sepsis-sign criteria are met in a patient on anticancer treatment, the diagnosis is made — it is not a matter of clinical judgement.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: Why may the signs of neutropenic sepsis be blunted?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Without neutrophils there is less inflammatory response, so fever may be the only sign. The patient may be hypothermic, confused, or hypotensive instead — maintain a low threshold to treat.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is the commonest organism in neutropenic sepsis, and where does it come from?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Staph epidermidis (coagulase-negative Gram-positive) — usually from indwelling lines in cancer patients.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: Why must empirical antibiotic cover in neutropenic sepsis target Gram-negatives including Pseudomonas?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Empirical cover must target Gram-negatives including Pseudomonas — this is why piperacillin-tazobactam (Tazocin) is chosen over narrow Gram-positive cover.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is the key principle of the emergency response in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Antibiotics are NOT delayed for investigations — give Tazocin first, take cultures around it.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: Emergency response Step 1: what is the first action and its timing?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: IV piperacillin-tazobactam (Tazocin) immediately — within 1 hour ('door-to-needle'), before cultures if needed.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: Emergency response Step 2: what cultures and septic screen are taken?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back:
Cultures + septic screen:
  • blood (peripheral and line)
  • FBC
  • CRP
  • U&E
  • LFT
  • clotting
  • lactate
  • CXR
  • urine/sputum/stool.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: Emergency response Step 3: what is done if the patient is still febrile/unwell at 48h?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Escalate: meropenem ± vancomycin (vancomycin if line infection/MRSA suspected).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: Emergency response Step 4: what is done if the patient remains unresponsive at 4–6 days?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Investigate fungal infection → empirical MOULD-ACTIVE antifungal: liposomal amphotericin B, or an echinocandin such as caspofungin. Not conventional amphotericin B deoxycholate (markedly nephrotoxic), and not fluconazole (no Aspergillus cover).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: When is vancomycin added in the escalation of neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: If line infection / MRSA is suspected (added to meropenem at the 48h escalation).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is the de-escalation strategy in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Bedside shorthand: switch to oral antibiotics once apyrexial for 48h, typical total 10–14 days. The NICE criteria: switch IV→oral after 48 hours only if the risk of septic complications has been REASSESSED as low (by a competent professional using a validated scoring system — not apyrexia alone), and stop empiric antibiotics once the SEPSIS HAS RESPONDED, irrespective of the neutrophil count. If a question offers both, the NICE criterion is the safer answer.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is the prophylaxis strategy for anticipated neutropenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Anticipated neutrophils 0.5 or lower → fluoroquinolone prophylaxis (e.g. ciprofloxacin) during the expected period of neutropenia (NICE). G-CSF shortens the duration of neutropenia but is NOT routinely offered to prevent neutropenic sepsis — reserve it for regimens where it is an integral part of the protocol, or where it is needed to maintain dose intensity.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is the role of G-CSF (filgrastim) in neutropenic sepsis prophylaxis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: It shortens the duration of neutropenia in high-risk chemotherapy regimens.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: Which antibiotic is used for fluoroquinolone prophylaxis during the expected nadir?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Ciprofloxacin (a fluoroquinolone), when anticipated neutrophils are 0.5 or lower.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: EXAM PEARL: State the neutropenic sepsis definition succinctly.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Neutrophils 0.5 or LOWER (≤0.5) + temp above 38°C (or other signs of sepsis) on anticancer treatment = neutropenic sepsis — the definition is the diagnosis. A count of exactly 0.5 with a fever counts.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the rule about Tazocin timing?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Tazocin within 1 hour — do NOT wait for cultures, imaging, or the neutrophil count. You treat SUSPECTED neutropenic sepsis; the FBC confirms it afterwards.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: EXAM PEARL: Why may signs be blunted, and what should you beware?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: No neutrophils → muted inflammation; treat on a low threshold — beware hypothermia/confusion as the only signs.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the commonest organism vs what empirical cover targets?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Commonest organism: Staph epidermidis (lines), but empirical cover targets Pseudomonas/Gram-negatives.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the escalation ladder in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Tazocin → meropenem ± vancomycin (48h) → antifungals (4–6 days).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the prophylaxis, and which notes cross-reference it?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Prophylaxis: fluoroquinolone ± G-CSF; cross-ref chemo complications (TLS, marrow failure).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is the definition of neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Neutrophil count 0.5 × 10⁹/L or lower in a patient on anticancer treatment, PLUS either temperature >38°C or other signs/symptoms of clinically significant sepsis (this is the UK/NICE definition; some non-UK definitions also count a neutrophil count expected to fall to ≤0.5 within 48 hours). A medical emergency — IV antibiotics within 1 hour.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is the most common source of infection in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Most episodes have no source identified. The commonest presumed PORTAL OF ENTRY is gut translocation across chemotherapy-damaged mucosa (Gram-negatives — E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas), while the commonest single organism ISOLATED from blood cultures is coagulase-negative Staphylococcus (Staph. epidermidis) from an indwelling central line. The two are not in conflict — commonest portal is not the same as commonest isolate. Also lung, skin, urinary tract, perineum.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: Why is fever unreliable in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Neutropenia ablates the inflammatory response — patients may be septic without a high fever, or with minimal localising signs. A temperature above 38°C in neutropenia is always treated as sepsis regardless, and a normal or low temperature does not exclude it.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What initial investigations are performed in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back:
• FBC + differential (confirm neutropenia)
  • blood cultures ×2 (peripheral + central line if present)
  • CXR
  • urine MC&S
  • wound/exit site swabs
  • CRP
  • LFTs
  • U&E
  • lactate.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is the first-line antibiotic in neutropenic sepsis per NICE?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Piperacillin/tazobactam (Tazocin) IV — broad-spectrum covering Gram-negatives including Pseudomonas. Meropenem if ESBL risk, or in NON-SEVERE (delayed, non-anaphylactic) penicillin allergy — meropenem is itself a beta-lactam. In SEVERE/immediate penicillin allergy (anaphylaxis, angioedema) avoid all beta-lactams and use a non-beta-lactam regimen per local policy — typically IV ciprofloxacin plus a glycopeptide (teicoplanin/vancomycin). Allergy status is never a reason to delay the first dose past 1 hour.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: When is vancomycin added in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back:
NOT empirically at presentation, and never merely because a central line is present — NICE explicitly says do not offer empiric glycopeptides to a patient with a central venous access device without a patient-specific or local microbiological indication. Add a glycopeptide (vancomycin/teicoplanin) when there is an actual indication:
  • a clinically infected line (exit-site pus, tunnel or pocket infection)
  • confirmed Gram-positive bacteraemia
  • known MRSA colonisation
  • a skin/soft-tissue source
  • or at the 48-hour escalation in a patient still febrile and unwell.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: When is antifungal therapy added in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Persistent fever after 4–7 days (≈96 hours) of broad-spectrum antibiotics with ongoing neutropenia — add an empirical MOULD-active antifungal (liposomal amphotericin B or an echinocandin such as caspofungin); fluconazole is inadequate as it lacks Aspergillus cover. Consider CT chest for invasive fungal disease.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is G-CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor) in the context of neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: G-CSF (filgrastim) stimulates neutrophil production and shortens the DURATION of neutropenia. Its role is PROPHYLACTIC: primary prophylaxis where the regimen carries >20% febrile neutropenia risk, secondary prophylaxis after an episode. It is NOT routinely recommended for an established episode of febrile neutropenia (occasionally considered in profound, prolonged neutropenia with severe sepsis), and it is NEVER a substitute for, or a reason to delay, IV antibiotics within 1 hour — it does nothing in the first 24–48 hours.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is the Multinational Association for Supportive Care in Cancer (MASCC) score?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Risk stratification tool for febrile neutropenia — identifies low-risk patients suitable for oral antibiotics/early discharge. Maximum 26; ≥21 = low risk, <21 = high risk, admit for IV treatment. It is applied AFTER the first IV dose, never instead of it. CISNE is an alternative score validated specifically in clinically STABLE solid-tumour patients, where MASCC tends to over-classify patients as low risk. Neither score overrides clinical judgement or social circumstances.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: Which chemotherapy regimens carry the highest risk of neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Regimens with >20% febrile neutropenia risk (e.g. BEACOPP for HL, dose-dense AC for breast cancer, FLAG-IDA for AML) — G-CSF prophylaxis recommended.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What organisms cause early vs late neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: The clinically useful pattern is bacterial → fungal, not Gram-negative → Gram-positive. Early: bacterial — Gram-negatives from gut translocation (E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas) AND Gram-positives from lines (coagulase-negative Staph, Staph. aureus, Strep), both from day one. Late (neutropenia beyond ~7 days on broad-spectrum antibiotics): invasive fungal disease — Candida first, then moulds (Aspergillus) — plus resistant Gram-negatives and C. difficile.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is Hickman line-related bacteraemia and how is it managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back:
Coagulase-negative Staphylococci (Staph. epidermidis) colonise central lines. Once line-related bacteraemia is CONFIRMED on culture, treat with a glycopeptide (teicoplanin or vancomycin) — not empirically, and never merely because a line is present. Remove the line for
  • tunnel or pocket infection
  • candidaemia
  • S. aureus bacteraemia
  • or failure to clear the bacteraemia on appropriate therapy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What prophylactic antibiotics are used in prolonged neutropenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Fluoroquinolone prophylaxis (ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin) in patients expected to have neutropenia >7 days (e.g. induction chemotherapy for AML). Aciclovir for HSV/VZV reactivation prophylaxis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What antifungal prophylaxis is used in high-risk patients?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Fluconazole for Candida (haematology inpatients). Posaconazole for Aspergillus (AML induction, SCT — covers mould).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What are the signs of invasive pulmonary Aspergillosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back:
• Fever unresponsive to antibiotics
  • pleuritic chest pain
  • haemoptysis
  • nodular infiltrates on CT ('halo sign' = ground-glass halo around nodule).
Treat with voriconazole IV.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: When should Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis (co-trimoxazole) be given?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back:
During prolonged immunosuppression:
  • ALL treatment
  • high-dose steroids
  • alemtuzumab
  • SCT
  • AIDS-defining CD4 <200.
Co-trimoxazole or dapsone (if sulfa-allergic).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is the 'sepsis six' in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back:
• Oxygen
  • blood cultures (before antibiotics if that takes minutes — never as a gate to the first dose)
  • IV antibiotics (within 1h)
  • IV fluids
  • monitor urine output
  • lactate measurement.
Applied within 1 hour of recognition — as per sepsis protocol, but antibiotics are mandatory in neutropenia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the key time target in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Antibiotics must be given within 1 hour of presentation. Do not delay for investigations. Blood cultures before antibiotics ideally but do not delay antibiotics if cultures cannot be taken promptly.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: At what point in the neutropenic sepsis pathway does risk stratification happen?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: AFTER the first dose of IV antibiotics, never instead of it. Every patient with suspected neutropenic sepsis gets IV empiric antibiotics within 1 hour; only then, once they have been observed and found stable, do you ask whether they need to stay in hospital. There is no patient who is 'too well for the first dose'.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: Which oral antibiotic regimen is used for low-risk ambulatory febrile neutropenia, and why those two drugs?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Oral ciprofloxacin PLUS co-amoxiclav. Ciprofloxacin provides the Gram-negative and Pseudomonal cover; co-amoxiclav adds the Gram-positive (streptococcal/staphylococcal) and anaerobic cover that ciprofloxacin lacks. It follows the first IV dose and a period of observation confirming clinical stability — it does not replace them.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What clinical, social and safety-netting criteria must be met before a low-risk patient is managed on an ambulatory pathway?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back:
• Clinical: haemodynamically stable, no organ dysfunction, no severe focal infection (pneumonia, tunnel infection, perianal sepsis), able to swallow and absorb tablets (no significant mucositis or vomiting), and not already on quinolone prophylaxis
  • Social: a responsible adult at home, a working telephone, transport, and living close enough to return quickly
  • Safety-netting: explicit WRITTEN return advice with the 24-hour acute oncology number — come straight back (do not ring the GP, do not wait and see) if fever returns or rises, rigors, vomiting or unable to keep tablets down, new pain, diarrhoea, breathlessness, drowsiness/confusion, or simply feeling worse.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is NICE's criterion for switching from IV to oral antibiotics in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Switch after 48 hours of treatment in patients whose RISK of developing septic complications has been reassessed as LOW by a healthcare professional competent in managing complications of anticancer treatment, using a validated risk scoring system. Note this is a RISK criterion — not simply 'apyrexial for 48 hours'. A patient can be afebrile and still high risk.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is NICE's rule for stopping empiric antibiotics in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Discontinue empiric antibiotic therapy in patients whose neutropenic sepsis has RESPONDED to treatment, IRRESPECTIVE OF NEUTROPHIL COUNT. Do not keep antibiotics running until the neutrophils recover — count recovery is not the endpoint, resolution of the sepsis is.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What must happen before a patient having empiric antibiotics for neutropenic sepsis is discharged?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Their risk of developing septic complications must be reassessed as LOW by a competent healthcare professional using a validated risk scoring system, with the patient's social and clinical circumstances taken into account, and explicit discussion of the need to return to hospital promptly if a problem develops.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is reassessed daily in an inpatient with neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back:
Both the RESPONSE to treatment and the RISK of septic complications. Practically:
  • temperature, observations/NEWS2, lactate and CRP trend, oxygen requirement, whether a source has declared itself
  • chase cultures at 24-48 h and rationalise antibiotics to the narrowest effective agent
  • neutrophil trajectory (which tells you how long the risk window has left, not when to stop antibiotics)
  • and new problems — line site, mouth, perineum, abdomen, and C. difficile diarrhoea.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What happens to the next chemotherapy cycle after an episode of febrile neutropenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back:
It changes — febrile neutropenia is a dose-limiting toxicity. Three options:
  • (1) DELAY until counts recover to the regimen-specified threshold and the infection has resolved
  • (2) DOSE REDUCTION of the myelosuppressive agent(s)
  • (3) keep the dose and add SECONDARY G-CSF PROPHYLAXIS ('secondary' = after an episode has occurred; 'primary' = from cycle 1 in a high baseline-risk regimen).
Choose by intent: in curative-intent, dose-sensitive treatment (lymphoma, germ-cell) preserve DOSE INTENSITY with secondary G-CSF; in palliative treatment, dose reduce or delay.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What does NICE say about removing a central venous access device in suspected neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Do NOT remove central venous access devices as part of the INITIAL EMPIRIC management of suspected neutropenic sepsis. Most episodes are not line-related, the line is the patient's route for chemotherapy, blood products and antibiotics, and re-siting one in a neutropenic thrombocytopenic patient carries its own risk.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: Should a patient with a central line get an empiric glycopeptide just because the line is there?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: No. NICE: do not offer empiric glycopeptide antibiotics (vancomycin, teicoplanin) to patients with a central venous access device unless there are patient-specific or local microbiological indications. The presence of a line is not by itself an indication.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What are the indications for removing a central venous access device in a patient with neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back:
• Tunnel or pocket infection (as opposed to simple exit-site redness, which can often be treated through the line)
  • candidaemia/fungaemia
  • Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia (also Pseudomonas and other difficult organisms by local policy, because of metastatic seeding)
  • and persistent bacteraemia or persistent fever despite appropriate antimicrobial therapy.
Plus septic thrombophlebitis, endocarditis, or instability attributable to the line.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What does NICE say about aminoglycosides in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Do NOT offer an aminoglycoside (e.g. gentamicin, amikacin), either as monotherapy or in dual therapy, for the initial empiric treatment of suspected neutropenic sepsis unless there are patient-specific or local microbiological indications. Beta-lactam monotherapy with piperacillin-tazobactam showed lower mortality, fewer adverse events and fewer superinfections than aminoglycoside-containing combinations.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: How do you establish that a central line is the source in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back:
• Paired blood cultures from a peripheral vein AND from each lumen of the line, clearly labelled
  • differential time to positivity (the line culture flagging positive at least 2 hours before the peripheral culture with the same organism implicates the line)
  • and simply looking — inspect the exit site and palpate the tunnel/port pocket at every review.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis) and who gets it?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Bacterial/fungal invasion of the chemotherapy-damaged bowel wall in profound neutropenia, causing oedema, ischaemia and necrosis. It favours the CAECUM (Greek typhlon = caecum) because of its distensibility and relatively poor blood supply. Seen in profound, prolonged neutropenia — AML induction, allogeneic transplant conditioning, taxane-containing regimens — typically in the nadir window.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is the classic presentation of neutropenic enterocolitis, and why is it a finals trap?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Fever + right iliac fossa pain + diarrhoea in a profoundly neutropenic patient, with distension, nausea and vomiting. The reflex answer is appendicitis — that is the trap. RIF pain in a neutropenic patient is typhlitis until proven otherwise. Signs are muted: peritonism may be minimal or absent even with a perforation, because there are no neutrophils to produce peritonitis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What does CT show in neutropenic enterocolitis, and what else do you send?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast is the investigation of choice: circumferential CAECAL WALL THICKENING, pericaecal fat stranding and fluid, mucosal enhancement, and sometimes pneumatosis intestinalis or free gas indicating perforation. Also send stool for C. difficile and culture, plus blood cultures, FBC, clotting and lactate.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: How is neutropenic enterocolitis managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back:
MEDICALLY:
  • bowel rest (nil by mouth)
  • IV fluids and electrolyte correction
  • NG decompression if there is ileus
  • broad-spectrum antibiotics with Gram-negative AND anaerobic cover (piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem; add metronidazole if the chosen regimen lacks anaerobic cover)
  • consider antifungal cover
  • correct coagulopathy and transfuse platelets
  • stop the offending chemotherapy
  • consider G-CSF
  • and review with serial examination and repeat imaging.
Involve surgery early for an opinion, not automatically for an operation.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: When is surgery indicated in neutropenic enterocolitis, and why not operate sooner?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Surgery is reserved for perforation, full-thickness necrosis, uncontrolled GI haemorrhage despite correction of coagulopathy and platelets, or deterioration despite maximal medical therapy. Laparotomy in a patient with no neutrophils, low platelets and friable oedematous bowel carries very high mortality — the wound will not heal and an anastomosis will not hold. Most cases settle as the neutrophil count recovers; count recovery is the treatment. Operate for a hole or dead bowel, not for pain.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: Why can a neutropenic patient deteriorate abruptly, and when do you involve critical care?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Blunted inflammatory signs mean they can look deceptively well and then decompensate suddenly — treat hypotension, tachycardia, rising lactate, oliguria or new confusion as shock, not as tiredness. Sepsis Six within the hour, then reassess. Septic shock (hypotension persisting despite adequate fluid resuscitation, requiring vasopressors, with a raised lactate) warrants EARLY critical care referral, alongside acute oncology/haematology and an explicit ceiling-of-care discussion with the patient and treating oncologist.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: Which examinations and interventions should be avoided in a neutropenic patient, and how does perianal sepsis present?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: No PR (digital rectal) examination and no rectal thermometers; no suppositories or enemas; avoid unnecessary IM injections — mucosal trauma in a neutropenic, often thrombocytopenic, patient can seed bacteraemia and precipitate perianal sepsis. Use tympanic, oral or axillary temperature and INSPECT the perineum visually instead. Perianal sepsis presents WITHOUT pus: no neutrophils means no fluctuant abscess to feel, so pain and induration alone are enough to act on.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What is malaria, and how is it transmitted?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: A protozoan Plasmodium infection via the female Anopheles mosquito. The returning-traveller fever — suspect in anyone with fever who lives in or has travelled to an endemic area.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What is the decisive fork in malaria (falciparum)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Falciparum — most severe, no dormant stage, RBC sequestration → complications (cerebral, AKI, DIC) → admit every case: oral artemether-lumefantrine if uncomplicated, IV artesunate if any severity feature.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What is the decisive fork in malaria (vivax/ovale)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Vivax/ovale — usually milder but relapsing — hypnozoites in liver → need primaquine for radical cure (after G6PD testing). Vivax can still cause severe disease (ARDS, severe anaemia, splenic rupture), so assess severity whatever the species.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What are the protective host factors in malaria (cross-ref sickle cell)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back:
• Sickle-cell trait
  • G6PD deficiency
  • thalassaemia
  • HLA-B53
  • Duffy-negative (specifically blocks vivax).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: Which protective host factor specifically blocks vivax?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Duffy-negative status.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: Life cycle: what happens after the mosquito injects sporozoites?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Mosquito injects sporozoites → liver (hepatocytes) → merozoites.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: Life cycle: what is unique to vivax/ovale in the liver stage?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Some hepatocytes form dormant hypnozoites → relapse weeks/months/years later.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: Life cycle: what happens once merozoites enter RBCs?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Hepatocyte ruptures → merozoites enter RBCs → replicate → rupture every 48h (72h for P. malariae; 24h for P. knowlesi) → haemolysis + pyrogen release → cyclical fever → more merozoites.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: Life cycle: what is the falciparum-specific RBC behaviour?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Infected RBCs adhere to small-vessel endothelium → sequestration/occlusion → cerebral malaria, AKI, etc.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: Species comparison — severity of falciparum vs vivax/ovale vs malariae?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Falciparum: most severe. Vivax/ovale: usually milder, but vivax can still cause severe disease (ARDS, severe anaemia, splenic rupture). Malariae: mild, chronic.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: Species comparison — liver dormancy in falciparum vs vivax/ovale vs malariae?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Falciparum: none. Vivax/ovale: hypnozoites → relapse. Malariae: none.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: Species comparison — fever pattern in falciparum vs vivax/ovale vs malariae?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Falciparum: irregular/continuous. Vivax/ovale: tertian (48h). Malariae: quartan (72h).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: Species comparison — incubation in falciparum vs vivax/ovale vs malariae?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Falciparum: usually 7–14 days (minimum ~6); most present within a month of return, but presentation up to 6 months later occurs — a late presentation does NOT exclude falciparum. Vivax/ovale: 12–18 days, but first presentation may be 6–12 months or more later (long-latency strains/hypnozoites). Malariae: 18 days–6 weeks, may be longer.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: Species comparison — key risk in falciparum vs vivax/ovale vs malariae?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Falciparum: sequestration → complications. Vivax/ovale: relapse. Malariae: nephrotic syndrome (chronic).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What are the symptoms and signs of malaria?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back:
Symptoms:
  • fever
  • rigors
  • profuse sweating
  • malaise
  • myalgia
  • headache
  • vomiting.
Signs:
  • pallor (anaemia)
  • hepatosplenomegaly
  • jaundice (haemolysis → bilirubin).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What are the falciparum complications (severe branch)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back:
• Cerebral malaria (seizures, coma)
  • AKI
  • 'blackwater fever' (massive intravascular haemolysis → haemoglobinuria, which may precipitate AKI)
  • pulmonary oedema/ARDS
  • DIC
  • severe haemolytic anaemia
  • hypoglycaemia
  • multi-organ failure.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What is 'blackwater fever' in falciparum malaria?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Massive intravascular haemolysis → haemoglobinuria (dark "coca-cola" urine), which may then precipitate AKI. Classically associated with quinine and with G6PD deficiency.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: Why is hypoglycaemia a classic trap in falciparum malaria?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: It is both a complication of the disease AND a quinine side-effect (a classic trap).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What is the gold-standard investigation in malaria, and what do thick vs thin films show?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Blood films. Thick film — detects/screens for parasites (sensitivity). Thin film — identifies species + parasitaemia % (quantification).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: How many blood films are taken to exclude malaria, and why?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Three films to exclude — repeat at 12-24h and again 24h later (48h cycle). One negative film never excludes malaria.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What additional investigations are used in malaria?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Rapid antigen tests (RDTs) — an adjunct to the film, never a replacement: a negative RDT does not exclude malaria, and antigen can stay positive for weeks after cure so it cannot judge response. Parasitaemia >2% in a non-immune patient = severe/complicated malaria, mandating parenteral treatment. FBC (anaemia, thrombocytopenia), LFTs, glucose, clotting (DIC screen).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What parasitaemia mandates parenteral treatment, and what counts as hyperparasitaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: >2% in a non-immune patient = severe/complicated malaria, mandating parenteral artesunate. >10% = hyperparasitaemia, a severity criterion in its own right.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: How is uncomplicated FALCIPARUM malaria (oral) managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back:
• Artemether-lumefantrine (Riamet) — first-line
  • atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone)
  • quinine + doxycycline (clindamycin instead of doxycycline in pregnancy and children).
Non-falciparum: chloroquine (an ACT where chloroquine-resistant vivax is likely — Indonesia, Papua New Guinea), then primaquine for vivax/ovale radical cure after G6PD testing.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What is the first-line oral treatment for uncomplicated falciparum malaria?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Artemether-lumefantrine (Riamet).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: How is severe/complicated malaria managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: IV artesunate = treatment of choice (over IV quinine); admit all falciparum (risk of rapid deterioration), and manage severe malaria in a high-dependency or intensive care setting with regular glucose monitoring and cautious fluids. Malaria is notifiable — notify on suspicion. Follow with a FULL ORAL COURSE once the patient can swallow and has had at least 24 h of parenteral treatment (artemether-lumefantrine, or quinine + doxycycline/clindamycin) — artesunate alone risks recrudescence. If IV artesunate is not immediately available, start IV quinine rather than delay, and switch when it arrives. Check FBC weekly for ~4 weeks (post-artesunate delayed haemolysis) and warn the patient to return if pale, breathless, jaundiced or passing dark urine. Routine exchange transfusion is no longer recommended.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What is the treatment of choice in severe malaria, and when is exchange transfusion used?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: IV artesunate (over IV quinine) is the treatment of choice. Routine exchange transfusion for high parasitaemia is no longer recommended — artesunate clears parasites fast enough that no benefit has been shown (UKHSA).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: How is relapse prevented in vivax/ovale malaria?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Primaquine — clears liver hypnozoites (this is RADICAL CURE; the same drug given post-exposure to an asymptomatic traveller is terminal prophylaxis). Check G6PD status first — primaquine causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: Why must G6PD status be checked before primaquine?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Primaquine causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What is the malaria prophylaxis strategy?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Bite avoidance: nets, DEET, covering up; chemoprophylaxis per region: Malarone / doxycycline / mefloquine. No regimen is fully protective — breakthrough malaria occurs, so a history of taking prophylaxis NEVER excludes malaria; still send films. Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy and in children under 12. Pregnant women should be advised not to travel to a malarious area; if travel is unavoidable, mefloquine may be used — including the first trimester where falciparum risk is high — or chloroquine + proguanil (with folic acid 5 mg) by region (UKHSA).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: EXAM PEARL: Why is falciparum 'the killer'?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: No relapse, but sequestration → cerebral malaria/AKI/DIC; admit all.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: EXAM PEARL: How is vivax/ovale relapse handled?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Relapse from hypnozoites → primaquine (check G6PD first — haemolysis risk).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the thick vs thin film rule and the exclusion sequence?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Thick film = detect; thin film = speciate + quantify; 3 negatives over 3 days to exclude.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: EXAM PEARL: What is first-line in severe malaria?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: IV artesunate = first-line in severe malaria (not IV quinine).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise the fever patterns and malariae's chronic risk.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Tertian (48h) vivax/ovale; quartan (72h) malariae; malariae → nephrotic syndrome.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise the protective host factors, and the current position on exchange transfusion.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Protective: sickle trait, G6PD deficiency, thalassaemia, Duffy-negative (vivax) — cross-ref sickle cell. Note: routine exchange transfusion for high parasitaemia is no longer recommended (UKHSA); IV artesunate is the treatment for severe malaria.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What defines severe/complicated falciparum malaria (UK criteria)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back:
P. falciparum malaria PLUS any one of:
  • impaired consciousness or seizures (cerebral malaria)
  • acidosis (pH <7.3) or lactate >4
  • hypoglycaemia <2.2 mmol/L
  • renal impairment/oliguria
  • pulmonary oedema/ARDS
  • Hb <=8 g/dL
  • shock
  • spontaneous bleeding/DIC
  • haemoglobinuria (in the absence of G6PD deficiency)
  • parasitaemia >2% in a non-immune patient (>10% = hyperparasitaemia).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: How is falciparum malaria treated in pregnancy?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: SEVERE malaria — IV artesunate in ANY trimester, including the first: do not delay or downgrade to quinine, as maternal and fetal mortality far outweigh the theoretical embryotoxicity. UNCOMPLICATED malaria — 1st trimester: oral quinine + clindamycin (7 days); 2nd/3rd trimester: artemether-lumefantrine. Primaquine AND doxycycline are contraindicated throughout pregnancy. Malaria in pregnancy is always admitted.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What prophylaxis is recommended for travel to mefloquine-resistant areas (e.g. Thai-Cambodian border)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Doxycycline or Malarone (atovaquone-proguanil) — mefloquine resistance common in South-East Asian borders.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: Why is malaria in pregnancy particularly dangerous?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Placental sequestration of P. falciparum → low birth weight, maternal anaemia, hypoglycaemia, miscarriage, premature labour, maternal death. Pregnant women are about 3x more likely to develop SEVERE disease if infected (primigravidae most at risk).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the key 'returning traveller' clinical question?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: ANY fever in a returned traveller from an endemic area is malaria until proven otherwise. Take immediate blood films ×3 over 3 days. Do not wait for the classic fever pattern before testing.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What is tafenoquine, and how does it compare with primaquine for vivax radical cure?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: A single-dose alternative to primaquine for radical cure of vivax malaria (clears liver hypnozoites). Like primaquine it causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency, so quantitative G6PD testing is required first — and its long half-life makes that screening essential.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What must be monitored after IV artesunate for severe malaria?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Post-artesunate delayed haemolysis — typically 1-3 weeks after treatment, i.e. after discharge. Check FBC weekly for ~4 weeks, and warn the patient to return if pale, breathless, jaundiced or passing dark urine. A falling Hb with raised LDH and bilirubin and low haptoglobin is haemolysis, and some patients need transfusion.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is the decisive fork in thrombocytopenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Reduced production vs increased destruction. Is the marrow failing to make platelets, or are they made but consumed/destroyed?

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What are the reduced-production (marrow fails) causes of thrombocytopenia, and the typical picture?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• B12/folate deficiency
  • liver failure (reduced thrombopoietin)
  • leukaemia, MDS
