  • drugs (valproate, methotrexate, isotretinoin — marrow suppression; antihistamines and PPIs are reported causes but act by an idiosyncratic/immune mechanism rather than marrow suppression)
  • alcohol
Usually comes with other cytopenias + abnormal marrow. Note sepsis is a destruction/consumption cause, not a production one.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What are the increased-destruction causes of thrombocytopenia, and the typical picture?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• ITP — immune (anti-GPIIb/IIIa)
  • TTP — microangiopathic (ADAMTS13 low)
  • HIT — immune (anti-PF4/heparin)
  • HUS — microangiopathic (Shiga toxin)
  • DIC — consumptive
  • sepsis — consumptive/immune, often via DIC
  • drug-induced immune (hapten-type: quinine, vancomycin, sulfonamides)
Isolated low platelet count; normal/active marrow.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What bleeding pattern does thrombocytopenia cause (cross-ref Haemophilia/VWD)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
Mucocutaneous / platelet-type bleeding —
  • petechiae
  • purpura
  • epistaxis
  • gum bleeding
  • menorrhagia.
(Deep joint/muscle bleeding = factor deficiency.)

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: Clinical features by count: what is the risk with a mild fall (100–150)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Often asymptomatic / incidental.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: Clinical features by count: what is the risk with platelets <50?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• Easy bruising
  • prolonged bleeding
  • epistaxis
  • gum bleeding
  • menorrhagia
  • haematuria.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: Clinical features by count: what is the risk with platelets <10?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: High risk of spontaneous bleeding — ICH, GI bleed.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: ITP: what is the mechanism and demographics?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
Anti-GPIIb/IIIa antibodies (usually IgG) → platelet destruction.
  • Children: acute, post-viral, self-limiting
  • Adults: chronic, women; can be 2° to SLE, CLL, HIV
Isolated thrombocytopenia — clotting normal.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What investigations are used in ITP?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• Isolated thrombocytopenia with a normal film — ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion, and antiplatelet antibody testing is not routinely recommended (poor sensitivity and specificity)
  • Screen for secondary causes (HIV, hepatitis C)
  • Bone marrow (raised megakaryocytes) is not routine in typical ITP — reserve for atypical features or older adults (to exclude leukaemia/MDS before immunosuppression).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: When is a bone marrow indicated in ITP, and what does it show?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Not routine in typical ITP — reserve for atypical features or older adults (to exclude leukaemia/MDS before immunosuppression). When done, it shows raised megakaryocytes.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: How is ITP managed (stepwise)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• 1. Oral prednisolone — 1st line, as a SHORT course (weeks including the taper, not months)
  • 2. IVIG — if urgent (pre-procedure/active bleed); raises count fast
  • 3. TPO-receptor agonists (eltrombopag/romiplostim) or rituximab — preferred 2nd line
  • 4. Splenectomy — now usually deferred (≥12 months) given infection/thrombosis risk; vaccinate first (pneumococcal, Hib, meningococcal, annual influenza) and give lifelong penicillin V afterwards.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is the first-line treatment for ITP, and what is used if urgent?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• Oral prednisolone is first-line
  • IVIG is used if urgent (pre-procedure/active bleed) as it raises the count fast.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is the mechanism of TTP?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: ADAMTS13 deficiency (inherited or autoimmune) → uncleaved vWF multimers → platelet microthrombi in small vessels → consumption (thrombocytopenia) + RBC shearing (MAHA).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What are the causes of TTP?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• Idiopathic, post-infection
  • SLE, HIV, tumours
  • drugs (ciclosporin, OCP, clopidogrel, penicillin, aciclovir).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is the classic pentad of TTP?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• Fever
  • neurological signs
  • thrombocytopenia
  • MAHA (microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia)
  • renal failure.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: How is TTP managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• Plasma exchange — urgent, first-line (replaces ADAMTS13)
  • steroids + rituximab
  • caplacizumab (anti-vWF nanobody, NICE-recommended add-on for acute acquired TTP)
  • NEVER transfuse platelets unless life-threatening bleed — it fuels more thrombosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: Why must platelets not be transfused in TTP?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: It fuels more thrombosis (only transfuse in a life-threatening bleed).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is the mechanism of HIT (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Anti-PF4/heparin antibodies → platelet activation → paradoxical thrombosis AND thrombocytopenia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is the key clinical rule for HIT?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• Platelet fall typically 5–10 days after starting heparin
  • the timing is the diagnostic clue (4T score)
  • it is paradoxical thrombosis, not just bleeding.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: How is HIT managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• Stop ALL heparin immediately — LMWH, unfractionated heparin, line and cannula flushes, and heparin-bonded catheters
  • switch to a non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban or danaparoid are UK-licensed; fondaparinux or a DOAC off-licence), continued even if no thrombosis is found
  • NOT warfarin acutely (protein C depletion → venous limb gangrene; start only after platelet recovery, with overlap)
  • NOT platelet transfusion.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: In HIT, why avoid warfarin acutely and platelet transfusion?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• Warfarin acutely depletes protein C faster than factor II, deepening the prothrombotic state and precipitating venous limb gangrene and skin necrosis
  • Platelets are withheld because they add substrate to an ongoing thrombotic process
Instead switch to a non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban or danaparoid are UK-licensed; fondaparinux or a DOAC off-licence), continued even if no thrombosis is found; start a vitamin K antagonist only once the platelet count has recovered (>=150 x10^9/L), at a low dose, overlapped with the non-heparin agent for at least 5 days.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: Discriminator table — mechanism of ITP vs TTP/HUS vs HIT vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• ITP: anti-GPIIb/IIIa
  • TTP/HUS: ADAMTS13 low / Shiga toxin
  • HIT: anti-PF4/heparin
  • DIC: consumptive.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: Discriminator table — clotting (PT/APTT) in ITP vs TTP/HUS vs HIT vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• ITP: normal
  • TTP/HUS: normal
  • HIT: normal
  • DIC: raised (deranged).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: Discriminator table — blood film in ITP vs TTP/HUS vs HIT vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• ITP: normal
  • TTP/HUS: schistocytes
  • HIT: normal
  • DIC: schistocytes.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: Discriminator table — clinical clue in ITP vs TTP/HUS vs HIT vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• ITP: isolated; post-viral child / adult woman
  • TTP/HUS: pentad (TTP) / renal+kids (HUS)
  • HIT: thrombosis + heparin 5–10d
  • DIC: sick + bleeding + systemic cause.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: Discriminator table — key treatment in ITP vs TTP/HUS vs HIT vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• ITP: steroids / IVIg
  • TTP: plasma exchange — HUS is supportive +/- eculizumab (atypical), NOT plasma exchange
  • HIT: stop all heparin, non-heparin anticoagulant
  • DIC: treat cause.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: EXAM PEARL: How does the production-vs-destruction fork narrow the diagnosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• The fork is reduced production vs increased destruction
  • Thrombocytopenia with normal clotting → immune (ITP/HIT) or microangiopathic (TTP/HUS), not DIC
  • Truly isolated thrombocytopenia with a normal film points to ITP or HIT; add anaemia and schistocytes and you are in TTP/HUS.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise ITP.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• ITP = isolated low platelets, anti-GPIIb/IIIa
  • prednisolone 1st line, IVIG for speed
  • bone marrow only if atypical features / older adult (not routine in typical ITP).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise TTP.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• TTP = ADAMTS13 deficiency, pentad, plasma exchange
  • do not transfuse platelets prophylactically — it fuels further thrombosis
Life-threatening bleeding overrides the rule.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise HIT.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• HIT = paradoxical thrombosis, platelet fall 5–10 days post-heparin
  • stop ALL heparin including flushes, switch to a non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban/danaparoid) — not warfarin acutely (venous limb gangrene), not platelets.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the cleanest single discriminator on clotting?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Clotting is normal in ITP/TTP/HIT; deranged in DIC — the cleanest single discriminator.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: EXAM PEARL: When are schistocytes present vs absent?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• Schistocytes = TTP/HUS/DIC (microangiopathy)
  • absent in ITP/HIT.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is the platelet count threshold below which spontaneous bleeding occurs?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• <20 × 10⁹/L — spontaneous mucocutaneous bleeding becomes likely (petechiae, purpura)
  • <10 × 10⁹/L — risk of severe spontaneous bleeding including intracranial haemorrhage
  • ≥50 × 10⁹/L is generally adequate for most invasive procedures and surgery, with higher targets (≥100) for neurosurgery and posterior eye surgery
— see the Transfusion topic for the full ladder.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is the mechanism of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Autoimmune — anti-platelet IgG antibodies (target GPIIb/IIIa or GPIb/IX) → splenic macrophage phagocytosis of opsonised platelets + reduced megakaryocyte platelet production.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is the treatment of severe acute ITP?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• First-line: prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day as a SHORT course (weeks including the taper, not months) OR IV immunoglobulin (IVIg) 1 g/kg (faster response for bleeding)
  • Second-line: a TPO receptor agonist (eltrombopag or romiplostim) or rituximab
Splenectomy is reserved for refractory chronic disease and usually deferred at least 12 months.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) and its paradox?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
HIT: anti-PF4/heparin antibody complex → platelet activation → paradoxical THROMBOSIS (not just bleeding) + thrombocytopenia (fall >50% or <100 × 10⁹/L).
  • Stop all heparin including flushes
  • switch to a non-heparin anticoagulant — argatroban or danaparoid are UK-licensed, fondaparinux or a DOAC are off-licence
Not warfarin acutely, and not platelets.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) and its pentad?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
ADAMTS13 deficiency (acquired or inherited) → uncleaved vWF multimers → platelet microthrombi. Pentad:
  • thrombocytopenia
  • MAHA (schistocytes)
  • fever
  • neurological changes
  • renal impairment
Treat: urgent plasma exchange + steroids (± rituximab, ± caplacizumab). Never transfuse platelets unless there is life-threatening bleeding.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is the 4T score for HIT?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• Thrombocytopenia (degree of fall)
  • Timing (days after heparin start)
  • Thrombosis (presence)
  • oTher causes (excluded)
Score 0–3 low probability, 4–5 moderate, 6–8 high. Act on moderate/high (stop heparin, anticoagulate).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is the mechanism of platelet destruction in drug-induced thrombocytopenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
Drug acts as hapten binding to platelet surface protein → drug-dependent antibody → immune-mediated platelet destruction. Common drugs:
  • quinine
  • vancomycin
  • abciximab
  • sulfonamides
Treat: stop offending drug.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: EXAM PEARL: What differentiates TTP from HUS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• TTP: predominant neurological features, ADAMTS13 <10% (diagnostic)
  • HUS: predominant renal features, often post-infectious (Shiga toxin from E. coli O157:H7), ADAMTS13 normal
Both: MAHA + thrombocytopenia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: Name the four conditions in which prophylactic platelet transfusion is not routinely given.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• Chronic bone marrow failure
  • autoimmune (immune) thrombocytopenia
  • heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
  • and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
The common thread is that platelets are being destroyed or consumed, so transfused platelets are destroyed too - and in the microangiopathies they feed the process.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: Why are platelets avoided in TTP and HIT specifically?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Both are prothrombotic states driven by platelet consumption. Giving more platelets adds substrate to an ongoing thrombotic process - classically described as fuel on the fire. In TTP the treatment is plasma exchange; in HIT it is stopping heparin and starting an alternative anticoagulant.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: Does the 'do not transfuse platelets' rule apply if the patient is bleeding seriously?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
No. The rule concerns prophylactic transfusion. Serious or life-threatening bleeding changes the calculation in any of the four conditions - you treat the haemorrhage in front of you. In ITP that means the interventions are combined rather than tried in sequence:
  • high-dose IV corticosteroid
  • IVIg
  • platelet transfusion given after the IVIg
  • and tranexamic acid.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: Why is repeated prophylactic platelet transfusion avoided in chronic bone marrow failure?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Because repeated exposure drives alloimmunisation and platelet refractoriness, so transfusions become progressively less effective. They are reserved for bleeding rather than given routinely for a number.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: A newly diagnosed adult with ITP is asymptomatic with only minor bruising. What is the usual approach?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Observation rather than immediate corticosteroids. You are treating bleeding and bleeding risk, not a number on a screen. Treatment is reserved for significant bleeding, a very low count, or an upcoming procedure.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: How long should a course of corticosteroids for ITP last?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: A short course - a matter of weeks including the taper, not months. Prolonged prednisolone causes more harm than the thrombocytopenia does in most patients.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: When is IVIg used in ITP, and how does it work?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: When the platelet count must rise quickly - active bleeding or an urgent procedure. It works largely by saturating splenic Fc receptors so that antibody-coated platelets are not cleared. The effect is temporary, so it buys time rather than providing a durable remission.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What are the three phases of ITP?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• Newly diagnosed (under 3 months)
  • persistent (3 to 12 months)
  • and chronic (beyond 12 months).
The phase influences how aggressively treatment is escalated. Children usually remit spontaneously; adults usually do not.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: Drugs cause thrombocytopenia by two distinct mechanisms. What are they?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• Reduced production through marrow suppression
  • and immune destruction
The immune mechanism is hapten-type: the drug binds a platelet glycoprotein and a drug-dependent antibody destroys the platelet. These are different problems with different culprits and different management.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: Which drugs classically cause immune (hapten-type) thrombocytopenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• Quinine
  • vancomycin
  • abciximab
  • and sulfonamides.
Quinine is the classic, including from tonic water.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: How is drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia treated?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Stop the drug. The count typically recovers over days once the offending agent is withdrawn. Supportive treatment is added if there is bleeding, but the definitive action is withdrawal.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is the commonest cause of a low platelet count in pregnancy?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Gestational thrombocytopenia. It appears in the late second or third trimester, is mild and asymptomatic, occurs with a normal blood pressure and no proteinuria, and resolves after delivery. It needs monitoring rather than treatment.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: Which features suggest that thrombocytopenia in pregnancy is NOT gestational?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back:
• Hypertension and proteinuria
  • a steeply falling count
  • deranged liver enzymes
  • epigastric or right upper quadrant pain
  • haemolysis
  • or schistocytes on the film
These point to pre-eclampsia/HELLP or a thrombotic microangiopathy rather than a benign gestational picture.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is HELLP syndrome and what does it require?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes and Low Platelets, occurring in the second half of pregnancy as a severe manifestation of pre-eclampsia. It is an obstetric emergency and delivery is the definitive treatment.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: How does ITP in pregnancy differ from gestational thrombocytopenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: ITP tends to produce lower counts, may predate the pregnancy, and may come with a bleeding history. It can require steroids or IVIg, and it matters for delivery planning and for the neonate, whose platelet count can also be affected.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: Before acting on an unexpected isolated low platelet count, what must be excluded first?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Pseudothrombocytopenia from EDTA-induced platelet clumping. Check the blood film for clumps or repeat the sample in citrate. The patient is not bleeding and the count is spuriously low.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What is the definition of pancytopenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Reduction in all three cell lines — anaemia + neutropenia/leucopenia + thrombocytopenia. It is a pattern, not a disease — the task is always to find the cause.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What is the decisive fork in pancytopenia, and what decides it?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Hypocellular marrow (production failure) vs cellular marrow (ineffective / destruction / infiltration) — decided by bone marrow biopsy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What are the clinical features of pancytopenia, by cell line?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back:
• Anaemia → fatigue, pallor, SOB
  • neutropenia → infections — neutropenic sepsis is an emergency needing empirical IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, without waiting for cultures, the neutrophil count, or a documented fever (cross-ref Neutropenic Sepsis)
  • thrombocytopenia → bruising, bleeding, petechiae (cross-ref Thrombocytopenia).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Aetiology by marrow fork — primary marrow: what are the hypocellular vs cellular causes?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Hypocellular: aplastic anaemia. Cellular: MDS, acute leukaemia, myelofibrosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Aetiology by marrow fork — infiltration: what are the hypocellular vs cellular causes?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Infiltration is a CELLULAR-marrow cause: myeloma, lymphoma, metastatic carcinoma. The marrow is packed with infiltrate and therefore hypercellular, but depleted of normal haematopoiesis — often with a leucoerythroblastic film. It is not an "empty" marrow.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Aetiology by marrow fork — what is the nutritional cause of pancytopenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: B12/folate deficiency (megaloblastic — ineffective haematopoiesis); a cellular-marrow cause.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Aetiology by marrow fork — which drugs/toxins cause pancytopenia (hypocellular)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Chemotherapy, radiation, chloramphenicol, carbimazole, methotrexate, alcohol — also carbamazepine, phenytoin, sulfasalazine, clozapine, azathioprine and trimethoprim/co-trimoxazole. The first treatment is always to stop the culprit drug and recheck the FBC.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Aetiology by marrow fork — which infections cause pancytopenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Viral (parvovirus B19 — classically pure red cell aplasia, with true pancytopenia mainly in the immunocompromised; EBV, CMV, HIV, hepatitis) and overwhelming sepsis. These sit on either side of the marrow fork: sepsis-associated pancytopenia usually has a normo- or hypercellular marrow, often with haemophagocytosis. In a returning traveller add malaria, visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) and disseminated TB — take a travel history.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Aetiology by marrow fork — what are the destruction/pooling causes of pancytopenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Hypersplenism and SLE/autoimmune (cellular-marrow causes). PNH also sits here by convention, but its complement-mediated haemolysis affects red cells only — when PNH causes true pancytopenia it is through the associated marrow failure / aplastic-anaemia overlap, so the marrow is typically hypo- or normocellular.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Why is pancytopenia called the 'unifying presentation' across haematology?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: MDS, leukaemia, myelofibrosis, myeloma, lymphoma, and B12 deficiency are all structured notes — pancytopenia is the unifying presentation pointing at all of them.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What is the definition of aplastic anaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Hypocellular ('empty') marrow replaced by fat — pancytopenia with no abnormal cells (no blasts, no dysplasia). That is the contrast with leukaemia/MDS at presentation; aplastic anaemia still carries a long-term risk of clonal evolution to MDS/AML and of PNH-clone expansion, so these patients need lifelong monitoring.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What are the causes of aplastic anaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back:
• Idiopathic/autoimmune (commonest)
  • drugs
  • viral (EBV, hepatitis, parvovirus)
  • radiation
  • inherited — Fanconi anaemia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What is the commonest cause of aplastic anaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Idiopathic/autoimmune.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What is the commonest inherited cause of aplastic anaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Fanconi anaemia is the commonest (others: dyskeratosis congenita, Shwachman-Diamond). Suspect an inherited cause in any young patient and confirm with chromosome breakage testing before giving immunosuppression or standard-intensity conditioning.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: How is aplastic anaemia managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Severity first: severe AA = cellularity <25% plus 2 of 3 (neutrophils <0.5, platelets <20, reticulocytes <20 x10^9/L); very severe = neutrophils <0.2. Non-severe AA is managed supportively if transfusion-independent, but transfusion-dependent non-severe disease is treated like severe disease. Supportive: IRRADIATED and leucodepleted transfusions (mandatory once ATG is given and for all transplant candidates, to prevent fatal transfusion-associated GvHD); avoid family-member donations in transplant candidates; infection control. Allogeneic SCT — first-line in patients under ~35-40 with an HLA-matched sibling donor. Immunosuppression where there is no matched sibling or the patient is older: horse (equine) ATG + ciclosporin with eltrombopag — that triple regimen is the standard first-line immunosuppression (BSH), though European approval is still required before routine upfront UK use; eltrombopag is separately established here for refractory disease.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What is the curative treatment for aplastic anaemia in young patients?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Allogeneic stem cell transplant — first-line in patients under ~35-40 with an HLA-matched sibling donor; selection is by donor availability and fitness rather than age alone.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What do FBC + reticulocytes show in the pancytopenia workup?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Confirm all three lines down. Low reticulocytes → production failure.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Blood film clues: what do blasts vs dysplasia/Pelger-Huët cells indicate?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Blasts → leukaemia. Dysplasia / pseudo-Pelger-Huet cells → MDS (the inherited Pelger-Huet anomaly is a benign mimic).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Blood film clues: what do teardrop cells + leucoerythroblastic picture vs hypersegmented neutrophils + macrocytosis indicate?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Teardrop cells + leucoerythroblastic picture → myelofibrosis/infiltration. Hypersegmented neutrophils + macrocytosis → B12/folate deficiency.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Blood film clue: what do schistocytes indicate?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Microangiopathy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What is the role of haematinics (B12 and folate) in the pancytopenia workup?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: B12 and folate — exclude the reversible nutritional cause, but send them in PARALLEL, not in sequence: a new unexplained pancytopenia is itself a same-day haematology referral, and pancytopenia with blasts on the film, or with fever/neutropenia, needs same-day referral without waiting for the result. If both are low or B12 status is uncertain, treat B12 FIRST — folate alone in B12 deficiency can precipitate subacute combined degeneration of the cord.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What is the decisive test in pancytopenia, and what does it assess?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Bone marrow aspirate + trephine. Assesses cellularity (empty vs full); blasts, dysplasia, infiltration, fibrosis; a dry tap suggests myelofibrosis — but also hairy cell leukaemia, marrow infiltration, or a technically failed aspirate, which is exactly why the trephine is mandatory.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: On bone marrow, what does a dry tap indicate?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: It suggests myelofibrosis — but also hairy cell leukaemia, marrow infiltration, or simply a technically failed aspirate. The trephine is what settles it.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What supporting tests are used in the pancytopenia workup?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back:
• LFTs
  • virology (HIV, hepatitis, EBV, CMV, parvovirus)
  • autoantibodies (SLE)
  • LDH (cell turnover marker)
  • high-sensitivity flow cytometry for a PNH clone (FLAER-based, on granulocytes and monocytes — more sensitive than red-cell CD55/CD59, which is confounded by transfusion and haemolysis) — PNH is an aplastic-anaemia overlap.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Discriminator table — aplastic anaemia: marrow cellularity, film clue, blasts, other?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back:
• Hypocellular
  • normal cells — just few
  • no blasts
  • no dysplasia, no splenomegaly.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Discriminator table — MDS: marrow cellularity, film clue, blasts, other?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back:
• Usually hypercellular
  • dysplasia, pseudo-Pelger-Huet
  • blasts <20%
  • macrocytosis
  • risk of → AML.
Note ~10-15% of MDS is hypocellular and overlaps with aplastic anaemia — dysplasia and clonal cytogenetics, not cellularity, are decisive.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Discriminator table — acute leukaemia: marrow cellularity, film clue, blasts, other?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back:
• Hypercellular
  • blasts
  • blasts ≥20%
  • Auer rods (AML).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Discriminator table — myelofibrosis: marrow cellularity, film clue, blasts, other?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back:
• Fibrosed (dry tap)
  • teardrop cells + leucoerythroblastic
  • blasts —
  • massive splenomegaly.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Discriminator table — B12/folate deficiency: marrow cellularity, film clue, blasts, other?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back:
• Hypercellular
  • hypersegmented neutrophils, macro-ovalocytes
  • no blasts
  • raised LDH
  • low B12/folate
  • reversible.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Discriminator table — hypersplenism: marrow cellularity, film clue, blasts, other?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back:
• Normal or hypercellular (compensatory) marrow
  • normal film
  • no blasts
  • splenomegaly
  • peripheral pooling
  • reticulocytes normal or raised.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: EXAM PEARL: Why is pancytopenia never a final answer?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Pancytopenia is a pattern (all 3 lines down), never a final answer — always name the cause.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise the marrow fork with examples.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Hypocellular marrow → aplastic anaemia / drugs / radiation; cellular marrow → MDS, leukaemia, megaloblastic, infiltration.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the decisive investigation, and what are the best first clues?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Bone marrow biopsy is the decisive investigation; blood film + reticulocytes are the best first clues.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: EXAM PEARL: Which reversible cause must always be excluded first?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: B12/folate deficiency — cheap and fully reversible. But send it in parallel with the rest of the workup, not before it: a new unexplained pancytopenia is itself a same-day haematology referral, and blasts on the film or fever with neutropenia make that referral urgent from the bedside. It is not a count to repeat next week. Treat B12 before folate.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the three-way discriminator between aplastic anaemia, MDS, and leukaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Aplastic anaemia = empty marrow, no abnormal cells; MDS = usually full marrow + dysplasia (but ~10-15% is hypocellular and overlaps with AA — dysplasia and cytogenetics are decisive); leukaemia = full marrow + >=20% blasts, or any blast count with an AML-defining genetic abnormality such as t(15;17), t(8;21), inv(16) or NPM1.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: EXAM PEARL: What two emergencies sit inside pancytopenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Neutropenic sepsis (IV antibiotics within 1 hour) and bleeding — an emergency at ANY platelet count. The <10 x10^9/L figure is the prophylactic transfusion threshold in a stable patient, not a definition of severe bleeding (<20 if septic/febrile, <50 before invasive procedures). That ladder applies to reversible marrow failure; in chronic marrow failure such as aplastic anaemia prophylactic platelets are not routinely given — transfuse for bleeding. Cross-ref both notes.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: EXAM PEARL: What clinches a diagnosis of myelofibrosis within the pancytopenia workup?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: A dry tap suggests myelofibrosis, and teardrop cells with massive splenomegaly strongly support it — but the trephine (reticulin/collagen fibrosis) plus JAK2/CALR/MPL testing is what confirms it.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What are the bone marrow findings that distinguish the four main causes of pancytopenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back:
• Aplastic anaemia: hypocellular, fatty
  • MDS: usually hypercellular and dysplastic (~10-15% hypocellular — dysplasia and clonal cytogenetics are what separate it from aplastic anaemia)
  • Leukaemia/infiltration: hypercellular, blasts/abnormal cells
  • B12/folate deficiency: hypercellular, megaloblastic, no dysplasia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What is haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) and how does it cause pancytopenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Uncontrolled macrophage activation → bone marrow macrophages phagocytose haematopoietic cells → pancytopenia + fever + splenomegaly + hyperferritinaemia (often >10,000 µg/L). Can be primary or secondary (infection, malignancy). It is a haematological emergency — discuss urgently with haematology, as untreated HLH is rapidly fatal.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the 'pancytopenia screen' — the key investigations?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back:
• FBC + film (morphology)
  • B12/folate
  • reticulocyte count
  • LFTs (liver failure, alcohol)
  • viral screen (EBV, CMV, HIV, hepatitis, parvovirus)
  • autoantibodies (SLE)
  • LDH
  • flow cytometry for a PNH clone
  • bone marrow aspirate + trephine (definitive).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What is the definition of polycythaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Raised Hb / haematocrit / red cell count. It is a pattern, not a disease — the task is to classify the cause.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What is the two-step decisive fork in polycythaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back:
• 1. True (raised red cell mass) vs relative (low plasma volume)
  • 2. If true → EPO low (primary/PV) vs EPO high (secondary).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: Why does polycythaemia matter clinically?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Raised Hct → hyperviscosity → thrombosis (stroke, MI, DVT/PE) — the complication that makes it worth diagnosing and treating.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: Relative/apparent polycythaemia: what defines it, and what are the two subtypes with EPO levels?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back:
Normal red cell mass, low plasma volume.
  • Dehydration — fluid loss concentrates RBCs (EPO normal)
  • Gaisböck syndrome — middle-aged obese man, smoking, HTN, alcohol (EPO normal).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: True primary polycythaemia: what is the subtype, mechanism, and EPO?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back:
Polycythaemia vera (PV) —
  • raised red cell mass
  • clonal marrow, JAK2 V617F ~95% plus JAK2 exon 12 ~3%
  • EPO LOW/subnormal.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: True secondary polycythaemia: what are the appropriate (hypoxic) causes, and the EPO?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back:
Raised red cell mass, EPO-driven. Appropriate (hypoxic):
  • chronic lung disease
  • high altitude
  • R→L cardiac shunt
  • heavy smoking (CO)
  • OSA.
EPO HIGH.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: True secondary polycythaemia: what are the inappropriate (tumour) causes, and the EPO?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back:
EPO-secreting tumours:
  • renal cell carcinoma
  • hepatocellular
  • cerebellar haemangioblastoma
  • uterine fibroids.
EPO HIGH.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What is the discriminating value in polycythaemia, and what does it separate?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: EPO is LOW/subnormal in PV (autonomous marrow needs no stimulus) but normal or high in secondary polycythaemia. It is the LOW EPO that points to PV — a normal EPO does not exclude a secondary cause, and in COPD, OSA, smoking and testosterone use it is frequently normal rather than raised.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: Where does the full PV detail live (cross-reference)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: In the Myeloproliferative Disorders note; the Polycythaemia note carries a summary.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What are the key features of polycythaemia vera?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back:
• Clonal marrow, JAK2 V617F ~95%
  • low EPO
  • aquagenic pruritus (itch on contact with water at any temperature, classically after a warm bath)
  • ruddy/plethoric complexion, conjunctival plethora
  • splenomegaly, HTN, gout
  • headache, visual disturbance, thrombosis — including at unusual sites (Budd-Chiari, portal and cerebral venous)
  • low ESR (hyperviscosity).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What is aquagenic pruritus in polycythaemia vera?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Itch on contact with water at any temperature, classically after a warm bath or shower. Present in about 40% of PV, so suggestive rather than diagnostic — it also occurs in other MPNs and in Hodgkin lymphoma.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: Why is the ESR low in polycythaemia vera?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Hyperviscosity prevents sedimentation (low ESR).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: How is polycythaemia vera managed (stepwise)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back:
• 1. Venesection — 1st line; target Hct <0.45 in all patients. The resulting iron deficiency is therapeutic — do NOT give iron
  • 2. Aspirin 75 mg od for all unless contraindicated — but withhold if platelets >1000-1500 x10^9/L until acquired von Willebrand disease is excluded — and assess and treat cardiovascular risk factors in every patient (BSH)
  • 3. Cytoreduction if high-risk (age >=65 or prior thrombosis): hydroxycarbamide first-line (teratogenic; monitor FBC and advise sun protection and skin self-examination); interferon alfa preferred in younger patients — pegylated interferon alfa-2a is the interferon used in pregnancy, whereas ropeginterferon alfa-2b is not recommended in pregnancy
  • 4. Ruxolitinib — JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor, for hydroxycarbamide-resistant or intolerant disease.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What is the first-line treatment for polycythaemia vera and its target?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Venesection — first-line; target Hct <0.45.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: Secondary polycythaemia: what does 'appropriate (hypoxic)' mean and which causes fall under it?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back:
EPO correctly raised in response to hypoxia:
  • chronic lung disease (COPD)
  • high altitude
  • cyanotic heart disease (R→L shunt)
  • OSA
  • heavy smoking (carboxyhaemoglobin).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: Secondary polycythaemia: what does 'inappropriate (tumour)' mean and which causes fall under it?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back:
EPO secreted autonomously:
  • renal cell carcinoma (classic)
  • hepatocellular carcinoma
  • cerebellar haemangioblastoma
  • uterine fibroids.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What is the classic inappropriate (tumour) cause of secondary polycythaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Renal cell carcinoma.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: How is secondary polycythaemia managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Treat the underlying cause (O₂/CPAP for hypoxia, resect tumour). Venesection only if symptomatic hyperviscosity.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: Investigations Step 1 — confirm and classify: what is done?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Repeat FBC/Hct (exclude spurious); assess for dehydration (relative polycythaemia) — confirm a persistently raised Hct >0.52 in men, >0.48 in women over about 2 months.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: Investigations Step 2 — what is the first-line confirmatory test in a sustained raised haematocrit?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: JAK2 V617F is the first-line confirmatory test — positive in ~95% of PV, and a positive result with a sustained raised Hct essentially establishes it. If V617F is negative, test JAK2 exon 12 and send serum EPO: a low/subnormal EPO supports PV (a minor criterion), while a normal or high EPO steers towards a secondary cause.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: Investigations — how is PV confirmed on mutation testing?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: JAK2 mutation testing — V617F positive in ~95% of PV; test JAK2 exon 12 if V617F-negative (covers most of the remainder).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: Investigations Step 4 — if secondary is suspected, what tests are done?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back:
• ABG / SpO₂ — hypoxia
  • CXR / lung function — COPD
  • sleep study — OSA
  • abdominal imaging (CT/USS) — renal/hepatic tumour.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What are the supporting findings in PV?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back:
• Low ESR (high viscosity prevents sedimentation)
  • raised urate (high cell turnover)
  • splenomegaly on USS.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: EXAM PEARL: How do you approach polycythaemia as a pattern?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Polycythaemia = a pattern (raised Hb/Hct) → classify: true vs relative, then EPO high vs low.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: EXAM PEARL: How is EPO interpreted in polycythaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: EPO low/subnormal = PV (autonomous marrow). EPO normal or high = secondary (hypoxia, tumour, drugs). It is the low EPO that points to PV — a normal EPO does not exclude a secondary cause.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: EXAM PEARL: What triad means PV until proven otherwise?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: JAK2 + low EPO + aquagenic pruritus = PV until proven otherwise.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: EXAM PEARL: How is relative polycythaemia characterised?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Normal red cell mass, low plasma volume (dehydration, Gaisböck) — Hct raised but red cell mass is normal.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise the secondary causes (appropriate vs inappropriate).
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Appropriate (hypoxic — altitude, COPD, OSA, shunt) vs inappropriate (EPO-secreting tumour — renal cell carcinoma is classic).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the danger in true polycythaemia, and how is PV treated?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Danger: hyperviscosity → thrombosis. Treat PV with venesection (target Hct <0.45) + aspirin.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What is the haematocrit threshold that defines polycythaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Haematocrit >0.52 in males, >0.48 in females — the UK threshold prompting investigation, and distinct from the <0.45 venesection target. Red cell mass >125% of predicted defines absolute polycythaemia, but isotope red cell mass studies are now rarely used in UK practice: classification rests on a sustained haematocrit plus JAK2 and EPO.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What is apparent/relative polycythaemia and how does it differ from true polycythaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Apparent/relative polycythaemia: normal red cell mass with a reduced plasma volume. Causes include dehydration and diuretics, and Gaisböck syndrome specifically (middle-aged obese hypertensive man, smoker, high alcohol intake) — Gaisböck is one subtype, not a synonym for the whole category. Venesection has no role here: the treatment is weight, alcohol, smoking and blood-pressure control, plus review of any diuretic (BSH). True/absolute: increased red cell mass (primary = PV; secondary = raised EPO). Smoking sits in both buckets: plasma-volume contraction and carboxyhaemoglobin-driven true secondary polycythaemia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What are the causes of secondary polycythaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back:
Appropriate (hypoxia-driven):
  • COPD
  • sleep apnoea
  • altitude
  • cyanotic heart disease
  • high-affinity haemoglobin.
Inappropriate (EPO-secreting tumours):
  • renal cell carcinoma
  • hepatocellular carcinoma
  • haemangioblastoma.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What is the role of EPO measurement in polycythaemia workup?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Low EPO = PV (autonomous production suppresses EPO). Normal/high EPO = secondary polycythaemia (EPO-driven). EPO distinguishes primary from secondary.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What is the Chuvash polycythaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Autosomal recessive VHL mutation → constitutively upregulated HIF-1α → increased EPO regardless of oxygen. Rare inherited secondary polycythaemia. Not associated with JAK2.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What thrombotic complications occur in polycythaemia vera?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back:
Arterial:
  • stroke
  • MI
  • peripheral arterial thrombosis.
Venous:
  • DVT
  • PE
  • Budd-Chiari (hepatic vein)
  • portal vein thrombosis
— the unusual venous site thrombosis is a hallmark.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What is the target haematocrit in PV management and why?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: <0.45 in all patients, male and female — there is no sex split for the treatment target. Above this, blood viscosity rises steeply → thrombosis risk. Venesection achieves rapid haematocrit reduction. Contrast the DIAGNOSTIC thresholds: Hct >0.52 in men, >0.48 in women.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What is the role of aspirin in PV?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Low-dose aspirin 75 mg daily for all PV patients (unless contraindicated) — reduces thrombotic events. Paradoxically, extreme thrombocytosis >1000-1500 x10^9/L increases bleeding risk (acquired von Willebrand disease) — WITHHOLD aspirin until vWD is excluded (ristocetin cofactor activity) and cytoreduction has brought the count down, then reintroduce it.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What cytoreductive therapy is used in high-risk PV?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back:
• Hydroxycarbamide (hydroxyurea) — first-line; monitor the FBC and advise sun protection and skin self-examination (long-term use causes painful leg ulcers and non-melanoma skin cancer) (BNF)
  • Interferon alfa — preferred in younger patients; pegylated interferon alfa-2a is the agent used in pregnancy, whereas ropeginterferon alfa-2b is not recommended in pregnancy and requires effective contraception (MHRA)
  • Ruxolitinib — for resistant/intolerant cases.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What is the 'spent phase' of polycythaemia vera?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Late complication — marrow fibrosis progresses (MF-like transformation) → anaemia replaces polycythaemia → splenomegaly ↑ as marrow fails. Leukaemic transformation in ~5–10%.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the WHO diagnostic criteria for PV?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back:
WHO major criteria:
  • (1) Hb >165 g/L in men / >160 g/L in women, or Hct >0.49 men / >0.48 women
  • (2) marrow trilineage hypercellularity with pleomorphic megakaryocytes
  • (3) JAK2 V617F or exon 12 mutation.
Minor: subnormal serum EPO. Diagnosis = all three major, OR major 1 and 2 plus the minor. (In UK practice the threshold prompting investigation is Hct >0.52 men / >0.48 women.)

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: What are oncological emergencies?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Acute, life- or function-threatening complications of cancer or its treatment where early recognition and immediate action change the outcome.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: Name the six major oncological emergencies.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back:
• Neutropenic sepsis
  • malignant spinal cord compression
  • superior vena cava obstruction
  • tumour lysis syndrome
  • leukostasis (hyperleukocytosis)
  • and malignant hypercalcaemia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: How is neutropenic sepsis defined?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: A temperature >38 °C (or other signs of sepsis) with a neutrophil count ≤0.5 ×10⁹/L, typically 7–14 days after chemotherapy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: What is the commonest life-threatening complication of chemotherapy?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Neutropenic sepsis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: What is the immediate management of neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour — first-line piperacillin–tazobactam (Tazocin) — alongside the Sepsis 6, WITHOUT waiting for the blood count or cultures.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: What is the first-line antibiotic in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Piperacillin–tazobactam (Tazocin).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: What causes malignant spinal cord compression (MSCC)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Tumour compressing the spinal cord or cauda equina — usually vertebral metastases.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: Which primary cancers most commonly cause MSCC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back:
• Breast
  • lung
  • prostate
  • myeloma and renal.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: What are the clinical features of MSCC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back:
• Back pain (often the first symptom; worse lying flat, coughing or straining)
  • radicular pain
  • limb weakness
  • a sensory level
  • and bladder/bowel dysfunction (a late sign)
  • UMN signs below the level (LMN if cauda equina).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: What is the late, ominous sign of MSCC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Bladder/bowel dysfunction.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: What is the management of MSCC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Treat on clinical suspicion — do not wait for imaging to start treatment. Dexamethasone 16 mg (loading dose as soon as possible, then 16 mg daily) with PPI cover and daily blood-glucose monitoring, given to a patient with neurological symptoms or signs, before the MRI. If a haematological malignancy is seriously suspected, get urgent senior oncology or haematology advice rather than simply withholding — steroids can obscure the histology, but an established neurological deficit takes priority. Reduce spinal loading until stability is assessed, positioning guided by comfort; urgent whole-spine MRI as soon as possible and within 24 h; definitive treatment is surgical decompression or radiotherapy — involve the MSCC coordinator. The neurological function the patient has when treatment starts is the best predictor of the function they keep.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: New or progressive back pain in a patient with cancer should be treated as what until proven otherwise?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Malignant spinal cord compression (MSCC).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: What causes superior vena cava obstruction (SVCO)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back:
• Lung cancer (especially small-cell)
  • lymphoma
  • thymoma
  • mediastinal metastases
  • and central-line thrombosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: What is the commonest cancer causing SVCO?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Lung cancer, especially small-cell.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: What are the clinical features of SVCO?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Swelling and plethora of the face, neck and arms, distended neck/chest-wall veins, dyspnoea, cough, headache (worse bending forward), Pemberton's sign, and in severe cases stridor/airway compromise.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: What is Pemberton's sign?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Facial congestion/cyanosis on raising the arms — seen in SVC obstruction.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: What is the management of SVCO?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back:
• Sit up, oxygen if hypoxic (titrated to target saturations), dexamethasone
  • CXR then CT chest with contrast — obtain tissue diagnosis before steroids if lymphoma is possible (steroids can render the biopsy non-diagnostic)
  • endovascular stenting for rapid relief
  • radiotherapy/chemotherapy per tumour type (chemo for small-cell & lymphoma)
  • anticoagulate if thrombotic.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: What is tumour lysis syndrome (TLS)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Massive tumour-cell breakdown (usually within days of starting chemotherapy, occasionally spontaneous) that releases intracellular contents and causes acute metabolic derangement → AKI, arrhythmia and seizures.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: What are the biochemical abnormalities of tumour lysis syndrome?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back:
• ↑ Potassium
  • ↑ phosphate
  • ↑ urate
  • and ↓ calcium.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: Why is calcium low in tumour lysis syndrome?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Because it binds the raised phosphate.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: Which patients are at highest risk of tumour lysis syndrome?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back:
• High-grade lymphoma (Burkitt's) and acute leukaemias (ALL/AML)
  • bulky chemosensitive tumours
  • a high white-cell count
  • and pre-existing renal impairment/dehydration.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: How is tumour lysis syndrome prevented and treated?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back:
• IV hydration with close monitoring of U&E, urate, phosphate and calcium (+ cardiac monitoring)
  • allopurinol for prophylaxis in lower- and intermediate-risk patients
  • rasburicase for high-risk/established TLS
  • treat hyperkalaemia and manage AKI (dialysis if needed).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: What is an important contraindication to rasburicase?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: G6PD deficiency — rasburicase causes severe haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia. Check G6PD status before giving it to a high-risk patient; if deficient, manage with IV hydration plus allopurinol and close monitoring instead (BSH).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: What are the mechanisms of malignant hypercalcaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back:
• PTHrP (squamous-cell lung, breast, renal)
  • osteolytic bone metastases (breast, myeloma)
  • and tumour production of 1,25-vitamin D (lymphoma).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: What are the clinical features of hypercalcaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back:
'Stones, bones, groans, moans, thrones' —
  • polyuria/polydipsia and dehydration
  • constipation/abdominal pain
  • confusion/lethargy/low mood
  • bone pain
  • renal stones
  • and a short QT/arrhythmia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: What is the first step in managing malignant hypercalcaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Stop the contributors first — thiazide diuretics, calcium and vitamin D supplements — then aggressive IV fluids (0.9% saline) to rehydrate and promote calcium excretion. An IV bisphosphonate follows once rehydrated, never before.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: After rehydration, what is the next treatment for malignant hypercalcaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: An IV bisphosphonate (e.g. zoledronic acid); denosumab if bisphosphonate-refractory or in renal impairment.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: What are the consequences of untreated tumour lysis syndrome?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Acute kidney injury, arrhythmia and seizures.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: What three things determine a patient's tumour lysis syndrome risk?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back:
• What the tumour is (highly proliferative, chemosensitive haematological cancers lyse fastest)
  • how much of it there is (bulky nodal masses, hepatosplenomegaly, a packed marrow, a high white-cell count and a high LDH)
  • and how well the kidneys are working (pre-existing renal impairment, dehydration or a raised baseline urate all push the patient up a band).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: Which two laboratory values stand in for tumour burden when assessing tumour lysis risk?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: The white-cell count and the LDH — both reflect tumour bulk and cell turnover, so a high WCC with a high LDH at presentation marks bulky, fast-dividing disease and a higher TLS risk.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: How does tumour lysis prophylaxis differ between intermediate-risk and high-risk patients?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Intermediate risk (acute leukaemia or aggressive lymphoma without extreme bulk, modestly raised WCC/LDH, preserved renal function): IV hydration + allopurinol. High risk (Burkitt's or other high-grade lymphoma, ALL/AML with a high WCC, bulky chemosensitive disease, high LDH, or any of these with renal impairment or a raised baseline urate): IV hydration + rasburicase — contraindicated in G6PD deficiency.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: When should tumour lysis risk be assessed and prophylaxis started?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Before the first dose of chemotherapy — not after the first abnormal result. Once TLS is established you are firefighting.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: Why must potassium not be added to the hydration fluid in tumour lysis syndrome?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Because the problem in TLS is too much potassium, not too little — hyperkalaemia is the arrhythmia risk. Hydrate with potassium-free crystalloid and check before hanging any bag containing added K⁺.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: Is urinary alkalinisation recommended in tumour lysis syndrome?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: No. Bicarbonate alkalinisation does make urate more soluble, but it drives calcium-phosphate precipitation in the renal tubules and can worsen the very AKI it is meant to prevent. It is no longer recommended.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: Should the hypocalcaemia of tumour lysis syndrome be corrected?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Only if it is symptomatic. Giving calcium into a high-phosphate circulation risks calcium-phosphate deposition in the kidney and other tissues and worsens the AKI — so asymptomatic hypocalcaemia is left alone and monitored.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: Which features make hypocalcaemia in tumour lysis syndrome 'symptomatic', and what is the treatment aim?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Arrhythmia, seizure or tetany. Calcium is given to treat those symptoms — the aim is symptom control, not a normal calcium number on the chart.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: What does 'close monitoring' actually mean in tumour lysis syndrome?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: A schedule, not a phrase: U&E, calcium, phosphate, urate, LDH and fluid balance measured before treatment and then repeated several times a day through the first days of chemotherapy in high-risk patients — not once on the morning round — stepping down as the numbers stabilise, with continuous cardiac monitoring while the potassium is high.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: When should renal replacement therapy be considered in tumour lysis syndrome?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back:
• Hyperkalaemia refractory to medical treatment
  • oliguric/anuric AKI or fluid overload not responding to fluids and diuresis
  • severe hyperphosphataemia with symptomatic hypocalcaemia
  • or refractory acidosis.
TLS-driven AKI often needs dialysis sooner than other causes, so involve renal/critical care early.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: Why must a urate sample taken after rasburicase be put on ice?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Rasburicase is an enzyme and keeps degrading urate inside the sample bottle — the specimen must go into a pre-chilled tube and be transported on ice, otherwise the laboratory reports a falsely low urate.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: What is leukostasis, and how does it differ from hyperleukocytosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Hyperleukocytosis is the high count alone; leukostasis is that count plus organ symptoms. Large, stiff, adhesive blasts plug the pulmonary and cerebral microcirculation and the tissue behind them becomes ischaemic — so it is a clinical diagnosis made at the bedside, not a number.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: In which leukaemias does leukostasis occur, and what count triggers urgent referral?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Blasts on the film or a WCC >100 warrants same-day haematology referral. It is commonest in AML (especially the monocytic subtypes) and CML in blast crisis, and also occurs in ALL — although lymphoblasts are smaller and less adhesive, so ALL tolerates a higher count before symptoms appear.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: What are the two symptom domains of leukostasis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Pulmonary — dyspnoea, tachypnoea and hypoxia, often out of proportion to an unimpressive early chest film, progressing to respiratory failure. CNS — headache, visual change or blurring, tinnitus, dizziness, confusion, drowsiness and ultimately coma, with engorged retinal veins and haemorrhages on fundoscopy. Intracranial haemorrhage is the feared complication.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: Which urological emergency is a classic presentation of leukostasis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Priapism — an emergency in its own right, and a presenting feature of hyperleukocytosis alongside the pulmonary and CNS syndromes.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: Why is red-cell transfusion deferred in leukostasis, and does the same apply to platelets?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Transfusing red cells before the white count has come down raises whole-blood viscosity and can precipitate or worsen leukostasis, so anaemia is corrected after cytoreduction unless the patient is haemodynamically compromised. Platelets do not meaningfully raise viscosity and should not be withheld.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: How is leukostasis managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back:
• Immediate haematology involvement
  • IV hydration
  • cytoreduction with hydroxycarbamide with or without apheresis in symptomatic patients
  • prompt induction chemotherapy for the underlying leukaemia, which is the definitive treatment — cytoreduction only buys time
  • and concurrent TLS prophylaxis, because cytoreduction lyses exactly the cells that cause tumour lysis syndrome.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: What does a raised LDH tell you in a patient with a new haematological malignancy?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: It is a marker of cell turnover and tumour burden — a high LDH marks bulky, fast-dividing disease, and together with a high white-cell count it moves the patient into a higher tumour lysis risk band, changing prophylaxis from allopurinol to rasburicase.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: Which oncological emergency is the commonest life-threatening METABOLIC complication of cancer, and which is the commonest life-threatening complication of CHEMOTHERAPY?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy is the commonest life-threatening metabolic complication of cancer; neutropenic sepsis is the commonest life-threatening complication of chemotherapy. Read the stem carefully — the two 'commonest' facts are easily swapped.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: Which patients with malignant hypercalcaemia are treated with steroids, and what else must be addressed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Steroids are used for lymphoma-related hypercalcaemia (where the mechanism is tumour production of 1,25-vitamin D). Alongside fluids and a bisphosphonate, treating the underlying malignancy is part of management — the calcium will not stay down while the tumour driving it is untreated.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.front: What is superior vena cava obstruction, and what is its most severe manifestation?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Oncological Eme.back: Obstruction of the SVC impairing venous return from the head, neck and upper limbs — causing facial, neck and arm swelling with distended veins, dyspnoea and headache. Severe disease brings stridor/airway compromise and cerebral oedema.

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: What does serum ferritin measure — and what is its key interpretive pitfall?
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: Ferritin reflects total body iron stores (the best single marker). Pitfall: it is an acute-phase reactant — inflammation, infection, malignancy and liver disease raise it, so a ‘normal’ ferritin can mask iron deficiency. Always interpret alongside CRP.

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: Give the iron-study pattern of iron-deficiency anaemia (ferritin, TIBC, transferrin saturation).
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: ↓ ferritin, ↑ TIBC / transferrin, ↓ transferrin saturation (and ↓ serum iron).

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: Give the iron-study pattern of anaemia of chronic disease.
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: Normal or ↑ ferritin, ↓ TIBC, ↓ transferrin saturation. Ferritin >100 µg/L with a low saturation favours ACD over iron deficiency.

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: Iron-study pattern of hereditary haemochromatosis / iron overload — and how is it confirmed?
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: ↑ ferritin with a high transferrin saturation (>45–50%). Confirm with repeat fasting transferrin saturation + ferritin, then HFE genotype (C282Y/H63D), LFTs and MRI liver for iron quantification.

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: Microcytic anaemia with normal iron studies — likely diagnosis and next test?
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: Thalassaemia trait. Confirm with haemoglobin electrophoresis (↑HbA2 = β-trait; α-trait is electrophoresis-normal → genetic testing) — clue: a raised RBC count with a disproportionately low MCV (Mentzer index <13).

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: Confirmed iron-deficiency anaemia — who needs endoscopy, and when is it the 2-week-wait cancer pathway?
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: All men and post-menopausal women with unexplained IDA need bidirectional endoscopy (OGD + colonoscopy) [BSG]. The suspected-cancer (2WW) pathway is triggered at age ≥60, or younger with a positive FIT / alarm features [NICE]. Pre-menopausal women: treat menstrual loss + iron trial; investigate the GI tract only if ≥50, GI symptoms, FHx bowel cancer, or refractory. Check coeliac serology (tTG + total IgA) in everyone.

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: Why take iron studies fasting in the morning and before starting iron therapy?
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: Serum iron has a diurnal rhythm and rises after iron intake, which falsely elevates the transferrin saturation and misleads interpretation.

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: Define transferrin saturation and give its approximate normal range.
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: Transferrin saturation = serum iron ÷ TIBC × 100 — the % of transferrin carrying iron. Normal ≈ 20–45%.

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: When ferritin is confounded by inflammation, how do you distinguish true iron deficiency from anaemia of chronic disease?
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: Soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR) is raised in true iron deficiency and is unaffected by inflammation; reticulocyte-Hb content also helps. Remember combined IDA + ACD is common (RA, IBD, CKD), so a normal ferritin can still hide deficiency.

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: What ferritin thresholds diagnose iron deficiency — normally, and in inflammation?
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: Ferritin <30 µg/L is diagnostic of iron deficiency in either sex (BSG); <15 is near-diagnostic. In inflammation / CKD / heart failure raise the cut-off to <100 µg/L (or 100–299 with transferrin saturation <20%).

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: Why must you check (and replace) B12 before giving folate?
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: Giving folate alone in unrecognised B12 deficiency can precipitate or worsen subacute combined degeneration of the cord. Correct/replace B12 first.

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: Serum folate vs red-cell folate — which is used, and why?
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: Serum folate is the standard test (reflects recent intake; <7 nmol/L supports deficiency). Red-cell folate reflects ~120-day stores but is no longer routinely recommended — unreliable, and falsely low in B12 deficiency (methylfolate trap).

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: How do the functional markers MMA and homocysteine differ between B12 and folate deficiency?
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: B12 deficiency: MMA and homocysteine both raised. Folate deficiency: homocysteine raised, MMA normal. Useful when B12 is borderline (200–300 ng/L).

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: Which antibodies confirm autoimmune gastritis (pernicious anaemia), and what are their test characteristics?
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: Anti-intrinsic-factor antibody — highly specific but insensitive (~50%), so a negative does not exclude it. Anti-parietal-cell antibody — sensitive but poorly specific (not a decision test). NICE now terms the condition autoimmune gastritis and adds endoscopic surveillance for gastric cancer.

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: What does the blood film show in megaloblastic anaemia?
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: Oval macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils (≥6 nuclear lobes).

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: Describe the neurological syndrome of B12 deficiency.
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: Subacute combined degeneration — dorsal columns (↓ vibration/proprioception, sensory ataxia, +ve Romberg), corticospinal tracts (up-going plantars, brisk knees) and peripheral nerves (absent ankle jerks). Can occur without anaemia and may be irreversible — treat promptly.

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: List the main causes of B12 deficiency.
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: Pernicious anaemia; malabsorption (coeliac, terminal-ileal Crohn's, post-gastrectomy/bariatric surgery); strict vegan diet; drugs (metformin, PPIs); nitrous-oxide misuse (inactivates B12).

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: Macrocytic anaemia with normal B12 and folate — what are the (non-megaloblastic) causes?
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: Alcohol / liver disease, hypothyroidism, myelodysplasia, reticulocytosis (haemolysis/bleeding) and drugs. These are non-megaloblastic macrocytoses.

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: Does a normal serum B12 exclude deficiency?
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: No. Serum (total) B12 is imperfect — falsely low in pregnancy/OCP, falsely raised in liver / myeloproliferative disease / infection. In the indeterminate zone (~180–350 ng/L, NICE) with suggestive symptoms, check MMA (or active B12), or treat on clinical grounds. No test is gold-standard.

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: What does haemoglobin electrophoresis (or HPLC) actually measure, and what is it the key test for?
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: It separates and quantifies the different haemoglobins by charge. It is the key test for the haemoglobinopathies — the thalassaemias (reduced globin-chain production) and structural variants (HbS, HbC, HbE).

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: Give the normal adult haemoglobin fractions.
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: HbA (α₂β₂) ~96–98%, HbA₂ (α₂δ₂) 2–3.5%, HbF (α₂γ₂) <1%.

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: Which electrophoresis finding is the hallmark of β-thalassaemia trait — and what commonly masks it?
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: Raised HbA₂ (>3.5%), often with a mild rise in HbF. Iron deficiency lowers HbA₂ and can mask the trait, so exclude/correct iron deficiency and repeat.

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: Why is haemoglobin electrophoresis normal in α-thalassaemia trait, and how is it confirmed?
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: α-thalassaemia does not raise HbA₂ or HbF, so the electrophoresis looks normal. Suspect it when there is microcytosis with normal iron studies and normal HbA₂; confirm with DNA / genetic analysis.

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: Distinguish sickle-cell trait from sickle-cell anaemia on electrophoresis.
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: Trait (HbAS): HbA predominant with HbS ~30–40% (HbA > HbS), usually no anaemia. Anaemia (HbSS): HbS predominant, no HbA, with raised HbF.

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: What is the limitation of the sickle solubility test compared with electrophoresis?
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: The solubility test confirms HbS is present but cannot distinguish trait from disease (or identify other variants). Always characterise with electrophoresis / HPLC.

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: Why can haemoglobin electrophoresis be misleading after a recent blood transfusion?
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: Transfused donor blood introduces HbA, which dilutes/obscures the patient's own pattern. Wait roughly 3 months (or interpret with caution).

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: What blood-count clues point to a thalassaemia rather than iron deficiency in a microcytic anaemia?
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: A raised red-cell count with a disproportionately low MCV and normal iron studies — the Mentzer index (MCV÷RBC) <13 favours thalassaemia.

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: How does the MCV steer the work-up of an anaemia?
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: Microcytic (MCV <80) → iron studies first (then Hb electrophoresis if iron is normal). Macrocytic (MCV >100) → B12 & folate. Normocytic (80–100) → mixed/early deficiency, anaemia of chronic disease, renal, haemolysis or bleeding.

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: What are the three haematinics, and which test represents each?
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: Iron (ferritin / iron studies), vitamin B12 (serum or active B12) and folate (serum folate).

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: Why can a normal MCV fail to exclude a nutritional deficiency?
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: A combined microcytic (iron) + macrocytic (B12/folate) deficiency can average out to a normal MCV. Clues are a raised RDW and a dimorphic blood film (two red-cell populations) — so check ferritin, B12 and folate.

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: What does the reticulocyte count add to the anaemia work-up?
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: It separates underproduction (low reticulocytes — nutritional deficiency, marrow failure, anaemia of chronic disease) from increased loss/destruction (high reticulocytes — haemolysis or bleeding).

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: Which patient groups warrant sending ferritin, B12 and folate together?
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: Those at risk of combined deficiency or malabsorption — coeliac, IBD, bariatric surgery, pregnancy, the elderly, restricted/vegan diet — and anyone with a dimorphic film or normocytic anaemia of unclear cause.

investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.front: Two rules that govern how haematinics are interpreted and replaced.
investigations__HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & H.back: Interpret ferritin alongside CRP (it is an acute-phase reactant — inflammation raises it and can mask iron deficiency), and always check/replace B12 before folate (folate alone in B12 deficiency risks subacute combined degeneration).
