conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.question: What is offered as antenatal screening in thalassaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.answer: A haemoglobinopathy screen at booking
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.explanation: Antenatal screening is a haemoglobinopathy screen offered at booking — ideally by 10 weeks, so that if she is a carrier the partner can be tested and prenatal diagnosis offered in time.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.question: In transfusion-dependent (major) thalassaemia, to what Hb are regular transfusions targeted, and why?
options: A pre-transfusion Hb of 95–105 g/L — suppresses ineffective erythropoiesis, prevents bony deformity
A pre-transfusion Hb above 70 g/L, matching the general restrictive transfusion threshold
A pre-transfusion Hb above 130 g/L, to normalise the haemoglobin completely
A pre-transfusion Hb above 80 g/L, matching the acute coronary syndrome threshold
A pre-transfusion Hb above 50 g/L, to keep the transfusional iron burden to a minimum
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.answer: A pre-transfusion Hb of 95–105 g/L — suppresses ineffective erythropoiesis, prevents bony deformity
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.explanation: Regular transfusions every 3–4 weeks keep the PRE-transfusion Hb at roughly 95–105 g/L. That suppresses ineffective erythropoiesis, which is what prevents the bony deformity and extramedullary haematopoiesis of an under-transfused patient. The post-transfusion Hb is kept below about 140–150 g/L.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.question: Before splenectomy for hypersplenism in thalassaemia, what must be done?
options: Start oral iron supplementation and continue it for three months after the operation to replenish stores
Vaccinate first (pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib) plus annual influenza + lifelong prophylactic penicillin V
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.answer: Vaccinate first (pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib) plus annual influenza + lifelong prophylactic penicillin V
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.explanation: Before splenectomy, vaccinate (pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib, and annual influenza), ideally at least two weeks beforehand, and give lifelong prophylactic penicillin V. The corollary matters just as much: fever in an asplenic patient is an emergency — cultures and prompt broad-spectrum antibiotics, since prophylactic penicillin does not exclude pneumococcal sepsis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.question: Which of the following is a potentially curative option in thalassaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.answer: Allogeneic stem cell transplant
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.explanation: Allogeneic stem cell transplant is potentially curative — as is the newer CRISPR gene therapy (exagamglogene autotemcel / Casgevy, approved in the UK (MHRA)). Transfusion, splenectomy, chelation and folic acid are supportive, not curative.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.question: How is trait / mild thalassaemia managed?
options: Regular transfusion every 3–4 weeks to keep the pre-transfusion Hb above 100 g/L
No treatment required; genetic counselling; avoid unnecessary iron supplementation
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.answer: No treatment required; genetic counselling; avoid unnecessary iron supplementation
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.explanation: Trait / mild disease needs no treatment outside pregnancy — but in pregnancy give high-dose folic acid 5 mg from preconception through the first trimester. Offer genetic counselling with formal carrier testing of the partner, and avoid iron unless deficiency is confirmed on iron studies.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.question: Why is iron overload the central long-term problem in transfusion-dependent thalassaemia?
options: Iron sequestration in the reticuloendothelial system is what causes the microcytosis and the low MCH
Iron is malabsorbed from the gut
Transfusional iron accumulates in organs (heart, liver, pituitary, thyroid/parathyroid, pancreas, gonads)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.answer: Transfusional iron accumulates in organs (heart, liver, pituitary, thyroid/parathyroid, pancreas, gonads)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.explanation: Transfusional iron accumulates in organs — heart, liver, pituitary, thyroid/parathyroid, pancreas, and gonads — making iron overload the central long-term problem. And in non-transfusion-dependent disease, ineffective erythropoiesis suppresses hepcidin, so gut absorption loads iron too.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.question: What is the leading cause of death in beta-thalassaemia major?
options: Sepsis with an encapsulated organism after functional hyposplenism
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.answer: Cardiac iron overload (cardiomyopathy / cardiac failure)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.explanation: Cardiac iron overload (cardiomyopathy / cardiac failure) is the leading cause of death in beta-thalassaemia major.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.question: How is iron overload treated in thalassaemia?
options: Venesection repeated at regular intervals until the iron stores are fully depleted, with a ferritin and a full blood count checked before each session
Iron chelation — subcutaneous desferrioxamine or oral deferasirox/deferiprone; monitor ferritin and T2* MRI, with weekly neutrophil counts on deferiprone
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.answer: Iron chelation — subcutaneous desferrioxamine or oral deferasirox/deferiprone; monitor ferritin and T2* MRI, with weekly neutrophil counts on deferiprone
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.explanation: Iron overload is treated with iron chelation: subcutaneous desferrioxamine or oral deferasirox/deferiprone, monitoring serum ferritin plus cardiac and hepatic T2* MRI. Deferiprone needs a neutrophil count before starting and weekly thereafter — stop it if neutrophils fall below 1.5 × 10⁹/L, and the patient must stop it and get a same-day FBC for fever or sore throat, because the agranulocytosis can be fatal.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.question: EXAM PEARL: What does HbH (3 alleles) represent compared with Hb Barts (4 alleles)?
options: Both are silent carrier states, detected only on targeted genetic testing of the alpha genes rather than on electrophoresis
HbH = fatal in utero; Hb Barts = an asymptomatic silent carrier
HbH = beta trait; Hb Barts = beta major
HbH = symptomatic but survivable haemolytic anaemia; Hb Barts = hydrops fetalis, usually fatal in utero or soon after birth
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.answer: HbH = symptomatic but survivable haemolytic anaemia; Hb Barts = hydrops fetalis, usually fatal in utero or soon after birth
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.explanation: Hb Barts (4 alleles) = hydrops fetalis, usually fatal in utero or soon after birth — survival is possible only with intrauterine transfusion and then lifelong transfusion support. HbH (3 alleles) = symptomatic but survivable haemolytic anaemia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.question: EXAM PEARL: How does electrophoresis differ between alpha and beta thalassaemia trait?
options: Alpha trait — shows raised HbA2 on electrophoresis; beta trait — a normal electrophoresis
Alpha trait — electrophoresis can be normal (needs genetic testing); beta trait — shows raised HbA2
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.answer: Alpha trait — electrophoresis can be normal (needs genetic testing); beta trait — shows raised HbA2
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.explanation: Alpha thalassaemia trait can have a normal electrophoresis and needs genetic testing; beta trait shows raised HbA2.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.question: A 6-month-old infant from a Mediterranean family presents with pallor, hepatosplenomegaly, and Hb of 42 g/L. Electrophoresis shows no HbA and elevated HbF. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.answer: Beta-thalassaemia major (Cooley's anaemia)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.explanation: Beta-thalassaemia major: homozygous beta-globin gene mutations → absent HbA → severe anaemia presenting at 6 months (when HbF switches to HbA). Hepatosplenomegaly from extramedullary haematopoiesis. Regular transfusions required lifelong.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.question: What is the Mentzer index and how is it used?
options: MCV/RCC: <13 suggests thalassaemia; >13 suggests iron deficiency
Ferritin divided by transferrin saturation, expressed as a ratio
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.answer: MCV/RCC: <13 suggests thalassaemia; >13 suggests iron deficiency
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.explanation: Mentzer index = MCV ÷ red cell count. <13: thalassaemia (many small cells — high RCC for low MCV). >13: iron deficiency (fewer, small cells — low RCC). Useful to distinguish these two common causes of microcytic anaemia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.question: What is the key diagnostic finding on Hb electrophoresis for beta-thalassaemia trait?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.answer: Elevated HbA2 (>3.5%)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.explanation: Beta-thalassaemia trait (carrier): elevated HbA2 (>3.5%) is the diagnostic hallmark — delta-chain compensation for reduced beta-chains. HbA is present (typically ~92–95%), HbF slightly raised. Confirmed by electrophoresis/HPLC.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.question: Why does the microcytic anaemia of beta-thalassaemia trait not respond to oral iron?
options: Thalassaemia causes autoimmune destruction of dietary iron in the duodenum before it can be absorbed
Iron absorption is blocked by intestinal inflammation
Iron is rapidly excreted by kidneys in thalassaemia
The anaemia is from reduced globin chain production, not iron deficiency — iron won't help and may overload
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.answer: The anaemia is from reduced globin chain production, not iron deficiency — iron won't help and may overload
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.explanation: Thalassaemia trait anaemia is from reduced globin chain production (ineffective erythropoiesis), not iron deficiency. Iron supplements are NOT indicated unless iron deficiency is separately confirmed (check ferritin and transferrin saturation) — otherwise they add to iron loading without helping the anaemia. Genuine coexisting iron deficiency does respond to iron, which is why it must be checked for rather than assumed absent.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.question: What is alpha-thalassaemia major (Hb Barts hydrops fetalis)?
options: 3 alpha-globin genes deleted — a moderately severe haemolytic anaemia presenting in childhood
All 4 alpha-globin genes deleted → no HbF → Hb Barts (γ4) tetramers → fatal hydrops fetalis in utero
Normal alpha globin with absent beta chains
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.answer: All 4 alpha-globin genes deleted → no HbF → Hb Barts (γ4) tetramers → fatal hydrops fetalis in utero
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.explanation: Alpha-thalassaemia major (--/--): deletion of all 4 alpha-globin genes → no HbF or HbA can form → Hb Barts (γ4) which is non-functional → fatal hydrops fetalis (in utero cardiac failure). Rarely survives without in utero transfusion.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.question: What is the iron chelation regimen for transfusion-dependent thalassaemia?
options: Dietary iron restriction alone, with no chelating drug given
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.answer: Deferasirox (oral) or desferrioxamine (subcutaneous/IV overnight infusion)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.explanation: Iron chelation prevents end-organ damage from transfusional iron overload. Deferasirox (oral, once daily) is first-line for convenience. Desferrioxamine (SC overnight via pump) is alternative. Monitor serum ferritin and cardiac MRI (T2* MRI is gold standard for cardiac iron).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.question: What are the potentially curative treatments for beta-thalassaemia major?
options: Allogeneic HSCT (HLA-matched), or CRISPR gene therapy (exagamglogene autotemcel / Casgevy, approved in the UK (MHRA))
Regular transfusions continued long-term, which normalise the haemoglobin permanently and cure the disease
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.answer: Allogeneic HSCT (HLA-matched), or CRISPR gene therapy (exagamglogene autotemcel / Casgevy, approved in the UK (MHRA))
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.explanation: Allogeneic HSCT (best in children before significant iron overload, >80% disease-free survival) is potentially curative — and CRISPR gene therapy (exagamglogene autotemcel / Casgevy) is now an alternative approved in the UK (MHRA) for those without a matched donor. The others are supportive/disease-modifying.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.question: A woman from Cyprus has microcytic anaemia with elevated HbA2 (beta-thalassaemia trait). Her partner is also found to be a beta-thalassaemia carrier. What is the relevance for their offspring?
options: No risk as partner is normal
Child has a 100% chance of developing beta-thalassaemia major
Child has 25% chance of beta-thalassaemia major — offer antenatal diagnosis
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.answer: Child has 25% chance of beta-thalassaemia major — offer antenatal diagnosis
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.explanation: Beta-thalassaemia trait is autosomal recessive. If BOTH parents are carriers, each child has a 25% chance of beta-thalassaemia major (homozygous), 50% carrier and 25% unaffected — offer genetic counselling and antenatal diagnosis. (A partner with a normal FBC should still have formal carrier testing — HbA2/electrophoresis — before risk is excluded.)

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.question: Which ethnic groups have the highest prevalence of beta-thalassaemia trait?
options: No ethnic predisposition — the carrier prevalence is essentially the same in every population worldwide
Mediterranean (Greek, Italian, Cypriot), Middle Eastern, South Asian, and African populations
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.answer: Mediterranean (Greek, Italian, Cypriot), Middle Eastern, South Asian, and African populations
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.explanation: Beta-thalassaemia has high prevalence in malaria-endemic regions (protective effect of thalassaemia trait against P. falciparum): Mediterranean, Middle East, Indian subcontinent, Southeast Asia, and some African regions. Antenatal screening targets high-prevalence groups.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the key electrophoresis distinction between beta-thalassaemia trait and iron deficiency?
options: Beta-thal trait: HbA is absent altogether; iron deficiency: HbA is present and normal, with a markedly raised HbF
Beta-thal trait: elevated HbA2 >3.5%; iron deficiency: normal HbA2 (iron deficiency can suppress HbA2 — check ferritin first)
Beta-thal trait: HbF >90%; iron deficiency: HbF normal
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.answer: Beta-thal trait: elevated HbA2 >3.5%; iron deficiency: normal HbA2 (iron deficiency can suppress HbA2 — check ferritin first)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.explanation: Key exam trap: concurrent iron deficiency can suppress HbA2 in beta-thal trait to normal range, falsely normalising it. Always check ferritin first in microcytic anaemia — treat iron deficiency, then repeat electrophoresis to unmask beta-thal trait if HbA2 still borderline.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: What is multiple myeloma?
options: Malignant proliferation of myeloid precursors arrested at an early stage of their maturation
Malignant clonal proliferation of bone marrow plasma cells → monoclonal paraprotein (usually IgG > IgA)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Malignant clonal proliferation of bone marrow plasma cells → monoclonal paraprotein (usually IgG > IgA)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Multiple myeloma is a malignant clonal proliferation of bone marrow plasma cells producing a monoclonal paraprotein, usually IgG > IgA.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: What single feature separates multiple myeloma from MGUS and smouldering myeloma?
options: Bone marrow involvement of any degree
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: End-organ damage (CRAB)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: The dividing line is end-organ damage: MGUS and smouldering myeloma lack CRAB; myeloma has it — the single most important discriminator. The exception is the myeloma-defining biomarkers (clonal plasma cells ≥60%, involved:uninvolved free light chain ratio ≥100, >1 focal lesion on MRI), which diagnose myeloma without any CRAB feature.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: Which description matches MGUS?
options: Paraprotein plus clonal plasma cells with CRAB end-organ damage present
Incidental paraprotein, <10% plasma cells, no CRAB — monitor annually
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Incidental paraprotein, <10% plasma cells, no CRAB — monitor annually
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: MGUS is an incidental paraprotein with <10% plasma cells and no CRAB; monitor annually.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: Which description matches smouldering myeloma?
options: Paraprotein plus clonal plasma cells with CRAB end-organ damage already present
Higher paraprotein / 10–60% plasma cells, no CRAB — premalignant with higher progression risk
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Higher paraprotein / 10–60% plasma cells, no CRAB — premalignant with higher progression risk
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Smouldering myeloma has a higher paraprotein / 10–60% plasma cells and no CRAB; it is premalignant with a higher progression risk.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: How does Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia differ from myeloma?
options: It is the IgG variant, presenting with lytic bone disease rather than with hyperviscosity
It is the IgM variant (lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma) presenting with hyperviscosity, not bone disease
It is a precursor of MGUS
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: It is the IgM variant (lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma) presenting with hyperviscosity, not bone disease
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia is the IgM variant (lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma), presenting with hyperviscosity rather than bone disease — a distinct entity.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: Which is a recognised risk factor for myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Black African ethnicity
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Risk factors for myeloma are older age, male sex, Black African ethnicity, family history, and obesity.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: A myeloma patient has constipation, nausea, confusion, polyuria and thirst. Which CRAB feature is this, and what is the mechanism?
options: Hypercalcaemia — osteoclastic bone resorption driven by myeloma cytokines
Renal failure — light-chain cast nephropathy obstructing the tubules
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Hypercalcaemia — osteoclastic bone resorption driven by myeloma cytokines
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Hypercalcaemia ('bones, groans, moans, stones') is driven by osteoclastic bone resorption from myeloma cytokines, causing constipation, nausea, confusion, polyuria, and thirst.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: Which mechanisms contribute to renal failure in myeloma?
options: Marrow infiltration crowding out normal haematopoiesis in the bone marrow cavity itself
Light-chain cast nephropathy, hypercalcaemia, hyperuricaemia, amyloid, dehydration, nephrotoxic drugs
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Light-chain cast nephropathy, hypercalcaemia, hyperuricaemia, amyloid, dehydration, nephrotoxic drugs
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Renal failure (the R of CRAB) is caused by light-chain cast nephropathy, hypercalcaemia, hyperuricaemia, amyloid, dehydration, and nephrotoxic drugs.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: What type of anaemia occurs in myeloma, and by what mechanism?
options: Microcytic hypochromic anaemia from iron deficiency and chronic occult blood loss
Normocytic normochromic ± pancytopenia — marrow infiltration crowds out normal haematopoiesis
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Normocytic normochromic ± pancytopenia — marrow infiltration crowds out normal haematopoiesis
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Myeloma causes a normocytic normochromic anaemia ± pancytopenia, because marrow infiltration crowds out normal haematopoiesis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: Which mechanism underlies the bone lesions of myeloma?
options: Light-chain cast nephropathy obstructing the distal tubules
RANKL-driven osteoclast activation with osteoblast inhibition → resorption without repair
Direct marrow infiltration displacing normal haematopoietic tissue from the cavity
Hyperviscosity from a high circulating paraprotein concentration
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: RANKL-driven osteoclast activation with osteoblast inhibition → resorption without repair
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Bone pain and lytic lesions (skull, spine, ribs, pelvis, long bones) arise from RANKL-driven osteoclast activation — myeloma cells and stroma upregulate RANKL and suppress osteoprotegerin — while DKK-1 inhibits osteoblasts, so there is resorption without repair. IL-1 and TNF-α are contributory cytokines rather than the dominant mechanism.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: Why do myeloma patients suffer recurrent infections?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Immunoparesis — reduced normal polyclonal Ig
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Recurrent infections occur because of immunoparesis — reduced normal polyclonal immunoglobulins.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: A myeloma patient develops back pain with new neurological signs. What is the action?
options: Dexamethasone 16 mg on suspicion plus urgent whole-spine MRI within 24 hours — do not delay
Start bisphosphonates and review the patient in the outpatient clinic in six weeks
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Dexamethasone 16 mg on suspicion plus urgent whole-spine MRI within 24 hours — do not delay
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Back pain + new neurological signs in a myeloma patient indicates spinal cord compression. Give dexamethasone 16 mg with PPI cover on clinical suspicion — before the scan, not after it — and arrange whole-spine MRI as soon as possible and always within 24 hours [NICE]. Neurological function at the start of treatment is the best predictor of the function retained.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: Which of the following is one of the emergency presentations of myeloma besides spinal cord compression?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Acute hypercalcaemia
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Emergency presentations include spinal cord compression, acute hypercalcaemia, renal failure, and hyperviscosity crisis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: What is the two-step investigation pathway in myeloma?
options: Bone marrow biopsy first, then send the BLIP panel afterwards
Initial screen → if suspicious, send BLIP → confirm with bone marrow biopsy
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Initial screen → if suspicious, send BLIP → confirm with bone marrow biopsy
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: The two-step pathway is: initial screen → if suspicious, send BLIP → confirm with bone marrow biopsy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: A suspected myeloma patient has a negative urine dipstick for protein, yet Bence-Jones protein is suspected. Why is the dipstick misleading?
options: Bence-Jones protein is only found in serum
The dipstick detects albumin, not light chains — send urine electrophoresis
The dipstick only detects light chains, and not albumin at all
Bence-Jones protein does not exist in myeloma
The dipstick is falsely positive in myeloma
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: The dipstick detects albumin, not light chains — send urine electrophoresis
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: The urine dipstick is negative for Bence-Jones protein because it detects albumin, not light chains; you must send urine electrophoresis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: Which initial screen findings fit myeloma?
options: Normal calcium with a low total protein, a normal ESR and an entirely normal plasma viscosity all the way through
Raised Hb; low ESR; low calcium
Low Hb ± pancytopenia; raised ESR and plasma viscosity; raised calcium and creatinine; raised total protein, low albumin
Low total protein with high albumin
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Low Hb ± pancytopenia; raised ESR and plasma viscosity; raised calcium and creatinine; raised total protein, low albumin
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: The initial screen shows low Hb ± pancytopenia, raised ESR and plasma viscosity, raised calcium and creatinine, and raised total protein with low albumin.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: In the BLIP diagnostic panel, what does the 'B' stand for?
options: Urine electrophoresis for Bence-Jones protein (urinary light chains)
Bence-Jones protein measured directly on a serum assay
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Urine electrophoresis for Bence-Jones protein (urinary light chains)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: In BLIP, B = urine electrophoresis for Bence-Jones protein (urinary light chains).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: In the BLIP diagnostic panel, what does the 'P' stand for?
options: Paraprotein-free light chains in the serum
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Serum protein electrophoresis — monoclonal band
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: In BLIP, P = serum protein electrophoresis, which shows a monoclonal band.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: What confirms the diagnosis of myeloma on bone marrow biopsy?
options: Hypersegmented neutrophils on the peripheral blood film, together with an oval macrocytosis and a low reticulocyte count
Clonal plasma cells ≥10% (or plasmacytoma), combined with a myeloma-defining event — a CRAB feature or a myeloma-defining biomarker
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Clonal plasma cells ≥10% (or plasmacytoma), combined with a myeloma-defining event — a CRAB feature or a myeloma-defining biomarker
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Bone marrow biopsy showing clonal plasma cells ≥10% (or plasmacytoma), combined with a myeloma-defining event — a CRAB feature or one of the biomarkers (clonal plasma cells ≥60%, free light chain ratio ≥100, >1 focal lesion on MRI) — is diagnostic of myeloma. The ≥10% marrow criterion is mandatory.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: What is the first-line imaging modality in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Whole-body MRI
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: The imaging preference order is whole-body MRI (first-line), then whole-body low-dose CT if MRI is unsuitable or declined, then skeletal survey (plain X-ray) only if both are unsuitable.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: Which are the classic imaging signs of myeloma?
options: Pepper-pot skull from hyperparathyroidism only, with no lytic lesions
Punched-out lytic lesions, raindrop skull, vertebral collapse
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Punched-out lytic lesions, raindrop skull, vertebral collapse
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Classic imaging signs are punched-out lytic lesions, raindrop skull, and vertebral collapse.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: Which triplet forms the classic bortezomib-based backbone of first-line anti-myeloma therapy?
options: Allogeneic stem cell transplant given upfront
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Bortezomib + thalidomide + dexamethasone (VTD)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: The bortezomib + thalidomide + dexamethasone (VTD) triplet is the classic backbone; current practice adds daratumumab (anti-CD38) as a "Dara-VTd" quadruplet, now standard first-line for transplant-eligible patients.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: Which anti-myeloma treatment is used in fit patients?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Autologous stem cell transplant
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Autologous stem cell transplant is used in fit patients; the disease follows a relapsing-remitting course managed by a haem-onc MDT.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: What is the role of bisphosphonates (zoledronate) in myeloma bone disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Suppress osteoclasts and reduce fractures
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Bisphosphonates (zoledronate) suppress osteoclasts and reduce fractures in myeloma bone disease.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: EXAM TRAP: A patient is started on thalidomide for myeloma. What must be co-prescribed, and why?
options: A bisphosphonate — because thalidomide weakens bone
Aspirin or LMWH — because thalidomide is prothrombotic
An antibiotic — because thalidomide causes infection
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Aspirin or LMWH — because thalidomide is prothrombotic
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Thalidomide is prothrombotic, so aspirin or LMWH must be co-prescribed for VTE prophylaxis — a classic MCQ distractor.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: Which supportive care measure is appropriate for renal protection in myeloma?
options: Routine NSAID use for bone pain
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Avoid NSAIDs/nephrotoxins; dialysis if needed
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Supportive renal care is to avoid NSAIDs/nephrotoxins and provide dialysis if needed; other measures include IV hydration, treating hypercalcaemia, transfusion for symptomatic anaemia, and infection prophylaxis + vaccinations.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: Which complication is on the paraprotein branch of myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Hyperviscosity syndrome
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Paraprotein-branch complications include renal failure (cast nephropathy), hyperviscosity syndrome, AL amyloid (cardiac, renal, peripheral neuropathy), and treatment-related neuropathy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: EXAM PEARL: An over-60 patient presents with persistent back pain and an unexplained fracture. What is the appropriate step?
options: Screen for myeloma with electrophoresis and free light chains — do not attribute it to mechanical or osteoporotic causes
Refer to physiotherapy without any further investigation, and review only if the pain persists beyond three months
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Screen for myeloma with electrophoresis and free light chains — do not attribute it to mechanical or osteoporotic causes
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Over-60 + persistent back pain or unexplained fracture should prompt screening for myeloma: FBC, calcium and plasma viscosity/ESR, plus serum protein electrophoresis and serum free light chains. If those are consistent with myeloma, very urgent electrophoresis and a Bence-Jones urine test within 48 hours, and referral on a suspected cancer pathway [NICE]. Do not attribute it to mechanical or osteoporotic causes without checking.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: EXAM PEARL: What is Bence-Jones protein?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Urinary light chains
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Bence-Jones protein = urinary light chains; the urine dipstick is negative because it detects albumin, not light chains, so urine electrophoresis must be sent.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: EXAM PEARL: Which features characterise Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia?
options: IgG variant with widespread lytic bone lesions, hypercalcaemia and a progressive renal impairment
IgM variant; hyperviscosity not bone disease; normocytic normochromic anaemia; raised ESR and plasma viscosity
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: IgM variant; hyperviscosity not bone disease; normocytic normochromic anaemia; raised ESR and plasma viscosity
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Waldenström's is the IgM variant with hyperviscosity rather than bone disease; the anaemia is normocytic normochromic, with raised ESR and plasma viscosity.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: A 68-year-old woman presents with back pain, fatigue, and renal impairment. Her protein electrophoresis shows a monoclonal band. Serum calcium is 3.1 mmol/L and Hb is 88 g/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Multiple myeloma
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Classic myeloma presentation: CRAB criteria met (hypercalcaemia, renal failure, anaemia) plus monoclonal protein (M-band). Bone pain from lytic lesions is common. Confirm with bone marrow biopsy showing ≥10% plasma cells.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: What is the significance of MGUS (Monoclonal Gammopathy of Undetermined Significance)?
options: 1% per year risk of progression to myeloma — requires monitoring but no treatment
It always progresses to symptomatic myeloma within five years of diagnosis
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: 1% per year risk of progression to myeloma — requires monitoring but no treatment
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: MGUS: M-protein <30 g/L, plasma cells <10%, no CRAB features. Risk of progression to myeloma ~1%/year. Annual monitoring with protein electrophoresis; no treatment indicated. Most patients die of unrelated causes.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: What is the characteristic bone lesion of myeloma on imaging?
options: Punched-out lytic lesions on skull X-ray with no surrounding sclerosis
Pathological fracture of femoral neck with osteoblastic lesions
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Punched-out lytic lesions on skull X-ray with no surrounding sclerosis
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Myeloma produces purely lytic (osteoclast-activating) lesions with no surrounding osteoblastic reaction — hence no uptake on isotope bone scan, which is why bone scintigraphy is not used in myeloma. Skull X-ray shows the 'rain-drop' appearance; the granular 'pepper-pot' skull belongs to hyperparathyroidism. Whole-body MRI is now first-line imaging in UK practice, with whole-body low-dose CT the alternative when MRI is unsuitable; the skeletal survey has been superseded.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: Why does myeloma cause renal failure (myeloma kidney)?
options: Hyperviscosity from the circulating paraprotein reducing renal perfusion
Light chain (Bence Jones protein) deposition in tubules causing cast nephropathy
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Light chain (Bence Jones protein) deposition in tubules causing cast nephropathy
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Free light chains (Bence Jones proteins) are filtered at the glomerulus and precipitate in distal tubules → tubular obstruction (cast nephropathy) → renal failure. Hypercalcaemia and dehydration worsen it. Urine protein electrophoresis detects BJP.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: What is the mechanism of hypercalcaemia in myeloma?
options: PTH-related protein secreted directly by the malignant plasma cells
Plasma cells activate osteoclasts via RANKL → lytic lesions → calcium release
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Plasma cells activate osteoclasts via RANKL → lytic lesions → calcium release
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Myeloma cells activate osteoclasts via RANKL (receptor activator of nuclear factor κB ligand) while inhibiting osteoblasts. This causes lytic lesions with calcium release. Bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid) block osteoclast activity.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: What is the first-line induction therapy for transplant-eligible myeloma?
options: Melphalan given as a single-agent monotherapy, without any stem cell transplant
Daratumumab added to a bortezomib-based triplet (Dara-VTd), followed by autologous SCT
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Daratumumab added to a bortezomib-based triplet (Dara-VTd), followed by autologous SCT
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Transplant-eligible patients receive bortezomib-based induction (VTD/VCD) → autologous SCT → lenalidomide maintenance. Current standard adds daratumumab (anti-CD38) to VTd ("Dara-VTd" quadruplet) for deeper responses. Not curative but prolongs remission.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: What complication of myeloma causes cord compression?
options: Vertebral lytic lesion collapse → pathological fracture → epidural cord compression
Direct plasma cell invasion of the cord
Peripheral neuropathy from light chain deposition in the peripheral nerves
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Vertebral lytic lesion collapse → pathological fracture → epidural cord compression
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Vertebral lytic lesions weaken bone → pathological collapse → epidural cord compression. This is a oncological emergency requiring urgent whole-spine MRI, high-dose dexamethasone, and radiotherapy/surgery. ~5% of myeloma patients.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: What investigation detects Bence Jones proteins in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Urine protein electrophoresis (UPEP)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Bence Jones proteins (free light chains) are NOT detected by standard urine dipstick (which detects albumin). Urine protein electrophoresis specifically identifies them. Serum free light chain (FLC) assay is more sensitive.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: What is smouldering myeloma?
options: Plasma cell leukaemia, defined by circulating clonal plasma cells in the peripheral blood
Myeloma complicated by spinal cord compression from vertebral collapse
Myeloma in which the haemoglobin has fallen below 80 g/L on the full blood count
MGUS that has developed lytic bone lesions on whole-body imaging
M-protein ≥30 g/L and/or clonal plasma cells 10–60%, with no CRAB and no myeloma-defining biomarker
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: M-protein ≥30 g/L and/or clonal plasma cells 10–60%, with no CRAB and no myeloma-defining biomarker
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Smouldering myeloma: higher tumour burden than MGUS (M-protein ≥30 g/L and/or clonal plasma cells 10–60%) but NO end-organ damage and no myeloma-defining biomarker. Risk of progression is about 10% per year for the first 5 years, falling thereafter. UK management is close MONITORING — treatment of high-risk smouldering myeloma is confined to clinical trials and is not standard NHS practice.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the diagnostic triad used to distinguish MGUS from myeloma?
options: MGUS has no M-protein at all, whereas myeloma is defined solely by the presence of one on serum electrophoresis, with no bone marrow criterion required
MGUS: M-protein <30 g/L, clonal plasma cells <10%, no CRAB. Myeloma: clonal plasma cells ≥10% (or a plasmacytoma) PLUS a CRAB feature or a myeloma-defining biomarker
Both require a bone marrow biopsy showing at least 20% clonal plasma cells
MGUS always shows Bence-Jones protein in the urine, whereas myeloma does not
MGUS produces only IgM, whereas myeloma produces only IgG or IgA paraprotein
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: MGUS: M-protein <30 g/L, clonal plasma cells <10%, no CRAB. Myeloma: clonal plasma cells ≥10% (or a plasmacytoma) PLUS a CRAB feature or a myeloma-defining biomarker
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: The key distinction: MGUS = M-band <30 g/L, <10% clonal marrow plasma cells, no end-organ damage. Myeloma = ≥10% clonal marrow plasma cells (or a biopsy-proven plasmacytoma) — this is MANDATORY, a paraprotein level alone will not do — WITH ≥1 CRAB feature or a myeloma-defining biomarker. Smouldering sits between (higher burden, no CRAB).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: A 72-year-old with newly diagnosed myeloma has an oliguric AKI with a creatinine that has trebled in a week and a very high serum free light chain level. He is being rehydrated. Which of the following is NOT indicated?
options: Plasma exchange to remove circulating light chains
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Plasma exchange to remove circulating light chains
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Plasma exchange is not indicated in myeloma-induced acute renal disease. Removing circulating light chains does not stop the marrow producing them, and it does not protect the kidney. Everything else listed is standard: rehydrate, treat the calcium, stop nephrotoxics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs, and above all start anti-myeloma therapy urgently.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: A 68-year-old woman presents with a new AKI and is diagnosed with myeloma with cast nephropathy. Which single step does most to protect her kidneys?
options: Starting haemodialysis regardless of the usual AKI indications
Deferring chemotherapy until renal function has recovered
Awaiting a renal biopsy before any treatment
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Urgently starting anti-myeloma therapy
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Cast nephropathy continues for as long as free light chains are being produced, so the definitive renal treatment is urgent anti-myeloma therapy - it is started without waiting for renal recovery. Deferring chemotherapy until the kidneys recover has it backwards. Dialysis is a bridge used on standard AKI indications, not a substitute.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: What determines whether a patient with myeloma is eligible for autologous stem cell transplant?
options: A strict age cut-off of 65 years
The immunoglobulin class of the paraprotein
Overall fitness - performance status, comorbidity and frailty, assessed by the MDT
Whether the paraprotein fell by more than half during the induction phase
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Overall fitness - performance status, comorbidity and frailty, assessed by the MDT
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Eligibility is about fitness, not a birthday: performance status, cardiac/respiratory/renal comorbidity and frailty determine whether a patient can tolerate high-dose chemotherapy and a transplant. There is no hard age cut-off, and the decision is made by the haem-onc MDT.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: A 64-year-old has completed treatment for myeloma and is in remission. How should she be monitored?
options: At least every 3 months, with paraprotein or serum free light chains plus FBC, U&E and calcium
Six-monthly whole-body imaging alone, with no blood tests taken at any point at all
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: At least every 3 months, with paraprotein or serum free light chains plus FBC, U&E and calcium
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: People who have completed myeloma treatment are monitored at least every 3 months. The paraprotein (or serum free light chains in light-chain-only disease) is the tracking marker, checked with FBC, U&E and calcium. Annual monitoring is the MGUS interval, where the concern is progression rather than relapse.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: A 66-year-old in remission from myeloma is asymptomatic, but his paraprotein has risen at two consecutive clinic visits. What does this mean?
options: An expected artefact of the treatment itself, which can safely be ignored without ever repeating the test
Evidence that he has been cured
A reason to stop all monitoring and discharge him
Relapse - repeat it, reassess for new end-organ damage and refer back to the haem-onc MDT for the next line of therapy
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Relapse - repeat it, reassess for new end-organ damage and refer back to the haem-onc MDT for the next line of therapy
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: A rising paraprotein is usually the first sign of relapse and typically climbs before symptoms return. Myeloma is incurable, so relapse is expected: the response is to repeat the marker, look for new end-organ damage, and take the patient back to the MDT for the next line of therapy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.question: A 70-year-old is newly diagnosed with myeloma. Imaging shows no lytic lesions and his calcium is normal. Regarding bone-protecting treatment, what is correct?
options: Zoledronic acid is offered to prevent bone disease, with dental assessment and treatment considered before the first dose
Bisphosphonates are withheld until lytic lesions appear
Bisphosphonates are only ever used to treat an established hypercalcaemia in myeloma, and never for prevention
Denosumab is first-line for everyone with myeloma
No bone protection is needed unless he fractures
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.answer: Zoledronic acid is offered to prevent bone disease, with dental assessment and treatment considered before the first dose
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.explanation: Zoledronic acid is offered to everyone with myeloma to prevent bone disease - it is not reserved for those who already have lytic lesions. Referral for dental assessment and treatment should be considered before starting, because of the risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw; renal function is also checked, and denosumab is used where bisphosphonates are unsuitable.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: Which hallmark cell defines Hodgkin lymphoma, and what is its appearance?
options: Small mature lymphocytes, either B or T lineage
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Hodgkin lymphoma is defined by Reed-Sternberg cells with owl-eye nuclei.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: What is the marker profile of Reed-Sternberg cells?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Reed-Sternberg cells are CD15+ and CD30+, but NOT CD20.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: How does the age distribution differ between Hodgkin and Non-Hodgkin lymphoma?
options: Hodgkin: bimodal (20s & 60s); Non-Hodgkin: any age, peak >60
Hodgkin: only elderly; Non-Hodgkin: only young
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.answer: Hodgkin: bimodal (20s & 60s); Non-Hodgkin: any age, peak >60
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Hodgkin lymphoma has a bimodal age distribution (20s & 60s); Non-Hodgkin occurs at any age with a peak >60.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: How does the pattern of spread differ between Hodgkin and Non-Hodgkin lymphoma?
options: Hodgkin: haematogenous only; Non-Hodgkin: nodal only
Hodgkin: non-contiguous, extranodal; Non-Hodgkin: contiguous nodal
Hodgkin: contiguous nodal; Non-Hodgkin: non-contiguous, extranodal
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.answer: Hodgkin: contiguous nodal; Non-Hodgkin: non-contiguous, extranodal
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Hodgkin spreads contiguously through nodes; Non-Hodgkin spreads non-contiguously and extranodally.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: Which lymphoma is associated with mixed cellularity EBV, and which NHL subtype is EBV-associated?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: The EBV association is yes (mixed cellularity) for Hodgkin, and Burkitt's for Non-Hodgkin.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: How do cure rates compare between Hodgkin and Non-Hodgkin lymphoma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Hodgkin lymphoma has a ~85% cure rate; Non-Hodgkin has a variable cure rate (10–90%).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: Which of the following is a risk factor for Hodgkin lymphoma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Risk factors for Hodgkin lymphoma are EBV (especially mixed cellularity subtype), HIV, and immunosuppression.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: A young patient reports pain in an enlarged lymph node specifically after drinking alcohol. What is this, and what does it indicate?
options: A B symptom of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, indicating advanced disease
Alcohol-induced nodal pain — the classic buzzword for Hodgkin lymphoma
A sign of tumour lysis syndrome
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.answer: Alcohol-induced nodal pain — the classic buzzword for Hodgkin lymphoma
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Alcohol-induced nodal pain is the classic buzzword for Hodgkin lymphoma — effectively diagnostic in an exam stem. In real practice it occurs in only a few per cent of patients, so its absence tells you nothing and must not reassure you about a persistent node.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: What are the B symptoms in lymphoma?
options: Bone pain, hypercalcaemia and renal failure from marrow infiltration
Fever >38°C, drenching night sweats, >10% weight loss in 6 months
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.answer: Fever >38°C, drenching night sweats, >10% weight loss in 6 months
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: B symptoms are fever >38°C, drenching night sweats, and >10% weight loss in 6 months.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: What investigation confirms Hodgkin lymphoma and what does it show?
options: Bone marrow biopsy → clonal plasma cells ≥10% of the marrow
Excision biopsy → Reed-Sternberg cells (CD15+, CD30+, owl-eye nuclei)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.answer: Excision biopsy → Reed-Sternberg cells (CD15+, CD30+, owl-eye nuclei)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Excision biopsy showing Reed-Sternberg cells (CD15+, CD30+, owl-eye nuclei) confirms Hodgkin lymphoma; PET-CT is used for staging.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: What is used for staging Hodgkin lymphoma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: PET-CT is used for staging in Hodgkin lymphoma; ESR is a disease activity marker.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: What does the ABVD regimen for Hodgkin lymphoma consist of?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: ABVD = Adriamycin (doxorubicin), Bleomycin, Vinblastine, Dacarbazine, ± radiotherapy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: A Hodgkin lymphoma patient on ABVD develops a dry cough and progressive breathlessness with fibrotic changes. Which drug is responsible?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Bleomycin causes pulmonary fibrosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: Which ABVD drug is associated with cardiomyopathy?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Adriamycin (doxorubicin) is associated with cardiomyopathy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: Which ABVD drug causes peripheral neuropathy and constipation?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Vinblastine causes peripheral neuropathy and constipation.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: What is the standard first-line chemotherapy regimen for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, the commonest non-Hodgkin lymphoma?
options: VTD (bortezomib, thalidomide and dexamethasone), followed by an autologous stem cell transplant
CHOP without rituximab in all cases
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: DLBCL, the commonest NHL, is treated with R-CHOP (Rituximab + Cyclophosphamide + Hydroxydaunorubicin/doxorubicin + Oncovin/vincristine + Prednisolone). Note R-CHOP is NOT the treatment for every NHL: indolent follicular disease is often observed, gastric MALT is treated by H. pylori eradication, and Burkitt lymphoma needs an intensive short-course regimen with CNS prophylaxis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: Which is the most common Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and what is its behaviour?
options: Mantle cell — most common, good prognosis
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: DLBCL (Diffuse Large B-Cell) is the most common NHL, aggressive, and potentially curable; t(14;18) in some, BCL-2.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: A patient has indolent lymphoma with 'waxing and waning' lymph nodes. Which subtype and translocation is this?
options: Mantle cell lymphoma — t(11;14), cyclin D1 overexpression
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Follicular lymphoma is indolent, incurable but manageable, with 'waxing and waning' lymph nodes, t(14;18) and BCL-2 overexpression.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: A child in an endemic-malaria region presents with a rapidly growing jaw mass; histology shows a 'starry sky' appearance. Which lymphoma and translocation is this?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Burkitt's lymphoma is highly aggressive with 'starry sky' histology and a jaw mass (African endemic, EBV + endemic malaria); t(8;14), MYC. It carries the highest tumour lysis risk of any lymphoma and is treated with an intensive short-course regimen with CNS prophylaxis, not R-CHOP.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: A patient has gastric MALT lymphoma. What is the key initial management step?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: MALT lymphoma is gastric and associated with H. pylori — treat H. pylori first. Then confirm eradication and re-scope to confirm histological regression; radiotherapy is used where eradication fails, the disease progresses, or the lymphoma is H. pylori-negative.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: Which NHL subtype is characterised by t(11;14) and cyclin D1?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Mantle cell lymphoma is aggressive with a poor prognosis, characterised by t(11;14) and cyclin D1.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: Shortly after starting chemotherapy, a patient develops raised potassium, raised phosphate, low calcium and raised uric acid. What is this, and what are the consequences?
options: Tumour lysis syndrome — renal failure, arrhythmia
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.answer: Tumour lysis syndrome — renal failure, arrhythmia
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Tumour lysis syndrome is massive cell death after chemo → raised K⁺, raised phosphate, low Ca²⁺, raised uric acid → renal failure and arrhythmia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: How is tumour lysis syndrome prevented?
options: Bisphosphonates given before the first cycle of chemotherapy
IV fluids + allopurinol or rasburicase before chemotherapy
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.answer: IV fluids + allopurinol or rasburicase before chemotherapy
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Tumour lysis syndrome is prevented with IV fluids plus allopurinol for standard-risk patients, or rasburicase for high-risk disease (bulky/high-grade lymphoma such as Burkitt, high LDH, renal impairment). Rasburicase is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency — it causes severe haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia — and is not given alongside allopurinol.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: In Ann Arbor staging, what defines stage II?
options: Nodal regions on both sides of the diaphragm
≥2 nodal regions, same side of diaphragm
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.answer: ≥2 nodal regions, same side of diaphragm
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Ann Arbor stage II is ≥2 nodal regions on the same side of the diaphragm.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: In Ann Arbor staging, what defines stage IV?
options: A single nodal region on one side of the diaphragm, with no extralymphatic involvement at all
Diffuse or disseminated involvement of one or more extralymphatic organs (liver, bone marrow, lung)
≥2 nodal regions, same side of diaphragm
Nodal regions on both sides of the diaphragm
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.answer: Diffuse or disseminated involvement of one or more extralymphatic organs (liver, bone marrow, lung)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Ann Arbor stage IV is diffuse or disseminated involvement of one or more extralymphatic organs (liver, bone marrow, lung), with or without nodal disease. Two traps: E denotes limited extranodal extension contiguous with an involved nodal site (e.g. stage IIE) and is NOT stage IV; and S denotes splenic involvement, which is not stage IV either, because the spleen is lymphoid tissue.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: What do the A and B suffixes mean in Ann Arbor staging?
options: A = early stage; B = late stage
A = no B symptoms; B = B symptoms present
A = above diaphragm; B = below diaphragm
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.answer: A = no B symptoms; B = B symptoms present
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: In Ann Arbor staging, A means no B symptoms and B means B symptoms are present (fever >38°C, drenching night sweats, >10% weight loss in 6 months).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: EXAM PEARL: Which marker are Reed-Sternberg cells NOT positive for?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Reed-Sternberg cells are CD15+ and CD30+ but NOT CD20.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: EXAM PEARL: What are the translocations for Burkitt's and follicular lymphoma?
options: Burkitt's = t(14;18) BCL-2; follicular = t(8;14) MYC
Burkitt's = t(8;14) MYC; follicular = t(14;18) BCL-2
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.answer: Burkitt's = t(8;14) MYC; follicular = t(14;18) BCL-2
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Burkitt's is t(8;14) MYC; follicular is t(14;18) BCL-2.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the significance of H. pylori eradication in MALT lymphoma?
options: It is used after R-CHOP only
It is unrelated to MALT lymphoma
It can cure early gastric MALT lymphoma
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.answer: It can cure early gastric MALT lymphoma
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: H. pylori eradication can cure early gastric MALT lymphoma.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: EXAM PEARL: Match the chemotherapy toxicities.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Bleomycin causes pulmonary fibrosis; doxorubicin causes cardiomyopathy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: A 22-year-old man presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy, fever, night sweats, and a mediastinal mass on CXR. Biopsy shows Reed-Sternberg cells. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Classical HL: young adult, painless lymphadenopathy with B symptoms, mediastinal mass, Reed-Sternberg cells (large binucleate cells with prominent 'owl-eye' nucleoli). Bimodal age distribution — peaks in the 20s and again in the 60s. Highly curable.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: What is the classic appearance of Reed-Sternberg cells?
options: Large binucleate cells with prominent owl-eye nucleoli
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.answer: Large binucleate cells with prominent owl-eye nucleoli
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Reed-Sternberg cells in the right nodal context define classical Hodgkin lymphoma. They are large, binucleate (or multinucleate) B cells with prominent eosinophilic 'owl-eye' nucleoli, CD15+ and CD30+. RS-like cells can appear in infectious mononucleosis and some non-Hodgkin lymphomas, which is exactly why the diagnosis needs a whole-node excision biopsy showing the architecture and the reactive background, not an aspirate.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: What is the most common subtype of non-Hodgkin lymphoma in adults?
options: Mantle cell lymphoma, an aggressive B-cell subtype
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: DLBCL is the most common NHL (~30% of cases). It is an aggressive lymphoma but potentially curable with R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisolone). ~60–70% achieve complete remission.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: Which translocation is associated with follicular lymphoma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Follicular lymphoma has t(14;18), juxtaposing BCL-2 (anti-apoptotic) with the IgH promoter. BCL-2 overexpression prevents apoptosis. Follicular lymphoma is indolent but incurable with standard therapy; often transforms to DLBCL.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: What is the starry sky appearance on histology associated with?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Burkitt lymphoma shows a 'starry sky' pattern — sheets of monomorphic MEDIUM-sized B cells punctuated by tingible-body macrophages containing apoptotic debris (pale 'stars' in a dark 'sky'). Associated with t(8;14) c-MYC; the endemic African form is EBV-driven, while sporadic Burkitt is usually EBV-negative. It is highly aggressive with a very high tumour lysis risk.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: What is the treatment backbone for Hodgkin lymphoma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: ABVD (Adriamycin/doxorubicin, Bleomycin, Vinblastine, Dacarbazine) is standard first-line for EARLY-stage HL, with combined-modality therapy (ABVD + involved-field radiotherapy). In ADVANCED-stage disease, brentuximab vedotin + AVD is now recommended for untreated stage 3–4 CD30-positive disease (NICE); nivolumab + AVD has outperformed it in trials but is not yet recommended for NHS use. >80% cure rate overall.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: What staging investigation is most important in lymphoma workup?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: PET-CT is the gold standard for initial staging and response assessment in lymphoma. It detects FDG-avid disease above and below the diaphragm and identifies extranodal involvement. Bone marrow biopsy is additionally required for some NHL subtypes.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: What is the IPI used for?
options: Prognosis in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.answer: Prognosis in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: The International Prognostic Index (IPI) is used for DLBCL prognosis. Five factors: age >60, stage III/IV, raised LDH, ECOG PS ≥2, >1 extranodal site. Score 0–1 = low risk (5-year OS ~90%); 4–5 = high risk (~50%).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: What is the treatment for rituximab-naive CD20+ DLBCL?
options: Autologous stem cell transplant given as the first-line treatment
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: R-CHOP is the standard first-line for DLBCL. Rituximab (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody) adds ~10% survival benefit over CHOP alone. 6 cycles every 21 days. ~60–70% achieve durable remission.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: EXAM PEARL: What are the B symptoms in lymphoma?
options: Fever >38°C, drenching night sweats, weight loss >10% in 6 months
Pruritus, alcohol-induced nodal pain and splenomegaly on examination
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.answer: Fever >38°C, drenching night sweats, weight loss >10% in 6 months
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: B symptoms are: fever >38°C, drenching night sweats, and weight loss >10% body weight over 6 months. They indicate systemic disease, are staged as 'B' suffix (e.g. stage IIB), and confer worse prognosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: A 24-year-old woman has painless cervical lymphadenopathy and a bulky mediastinal mass. Excision biopsy shows a lymph node divided into nodules by broad fibrous bands, containing scattered CD15+ CD30+ Reed-Sternberg cells. Which subtype is this?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Nodular sclerosis is the commonest subtype of classical Hodgkin lymphoma. The classic picture is a young adult, often a woman, with a mediastinal mass, and a node partitioned into nodules by fibrous bands. Mixed cellularity is the most strongly EBV-associated subtype and affects older or immunosuppressed patients; lymphocyte-depleted is the rarest and most aggressive.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: A 32-year-old man has a single enlarged cervical node. Biopsy shows a nodular infiltrate containing large cells with polylobated 'popcorn' nuclei that are CD20 positive but CD30 and CD15 negative. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: The 'popcorn' or LP cell with a CD20 positive, CD30 negative, CD15 negative phenotype defines NLPHL — a separate entity from classical Hodgkin lymphoma, whose Reed-Sternberg cells are the mirror image (CD15+, CD30+, CD20 negative). NLPHL is indolent, usually presents early-stage, relapses late, and because it is CD20 positive it responds to rituximab.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: A student states that all Hodgkin lymphomas are CD15 positive, CD30 positive and CD20 negative. Which correction is right?
options: The statement is correct for every subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma
All Hodgkin lymphomas are in fact CD20 positive
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma is CD20 positive and CD30 negative
NLPHL and classical Hodgkin lymphoma share an identical immunophenotype on immunohistochemical staining
That profile defines CLASSICAL Hodgkin lymphoma; NLPHL is the mirror image — CD20 positive, CD30 and CD15 negative
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.answer: That profile defines CLASSICAL Hodgkin lymphoma; NLPHL is the mirror image — CD20 positive, CD30 and CD15 negative
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: The CD15+/CD30+/CD20-negative profile belongs to the Reed-Sternberg cell of classical Hodgkin lymphoma. NLPHL is a distinct entity whose 'popcorn' LP cells are CD20 positive, CD30 negative, CD15 negative and CD45 positive. Scoping the rule to classical HL is what makes the CD20-positive, rituximab-sensitive behaviour of NLPHL make sense.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: A 68-year-old man is diagnosed with follicular lymphoma. He is asymptomatic, has a few small non-bulky nodes, a normal LDH, no organ compromise and no marrow failure. What is the appropriate initial management?
options: Watch and wait with regular clinical review
Involved-field radiotherapy to every nodal site
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.answer: Watch and wait with regular clinical review
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Follicular lymphoma is indolent, and in asymptomatic low-bulk disease immediate chemotherapy does not improve overall survival — so watch and wait with regular review is standard. Treatment is triggered by symptoms or B symptoms, bulky nodal masses, organ compression or threat, marrow failure, or steady progression, and is then rituximab plus chemotherapy followed by rituximab maintenance.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: A woman with follicular lymphoma has been on watch and wait for four years. Over three weeks a single cervical node enlarges rapidly out of keeping with her other nodes; she has new drenching night sweats and her LDH has risen sharply. What is the most important next step?
options: Reassure her — this is the expected waxing and waning of follicular lymphoma
Re-biopsy the rapidly enlarging node, using PET-CT to target the most avid site
Repeat the original histology report and continue observation
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.answer: Re-biopsy the rapidly enlarging node, using PET-CT to target the most avid site
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Sudden rapid growth of one node out of keeping with the rest, a rising LDH, or new B symptoms in follicular lymphoma should raise transformation to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Confirm it histologically by re-biopsy, using PET-CT to target the most FDG-avid site. Transformed disease is treated as an aggressive lymphoma, not as follicular lymphoma.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: A 23-year-old man with stage IIA Hodgkin lymphoma is due to start ABVD next week. Which action is most important to take BEFORE the first cycle?
options: Refer him for early breast cancer screening
Discuss fertility preservation and offer sperm banking
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.answer: Discuss fertility preservation and offer sperm banking
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Fertility preservation must be discussed before the first cycle of chemotherapy — once treatment has started the opportunity is largely gone. Sperm banking is offered to any man whose treatment could affect fertility, and low counts at diagnosis are a reason to bank rather than not to. Annual TFTs and cardiovascular surveillance matter, but they belong to long-term follow-up, not to the week before treatment starts.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.question: A 38-year-old woman who received mediastinal radiotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma at the age of 19 asks what long-term surveillance she needs. Which specific programme is she owed?
options: Annual chest X-ray to screen for pulmonary fibrosis
Entry into a dedicated early breast cancer screening programme
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.answer: Entry into a dedicated early breast cancer screening programme
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.explanation: Breast cancer arising in the radiotherapy field is the classic late second malignancy in women irradiated to the mediastinum when young, and the excess risk is large enough to justify a dedicated screening programme starting years before population screening would. She also needs annual thyroid function tests (hypothyroidism after neck or mediastinal radiotherapy) and lifelong attention to cardiovascular risk after anthracycline and radiotherapy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: What is leukaemia?
options: Malignant proliferation of lymph node architecture, with effacement of the normal nodal structure
Malignancy of haematopoietic stem cells → marrow replaced by clonal cells → other lineages suppressed
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.answer: Malignancy of haematopoietic stem cells → marrow replaced by clonal cells → other lineages suppressed
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: Leukaemia is a malignancy of haematopoietic stem cells; marrow is replaced by clonal cells and other lineages are suppressed (anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: What is the two-axis classification of leukaemia?
options: Blast percentage × spleen size at presentation
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: Leukaemia is classified on two axes: speed (acute/chronic) and lineage (myeloid/lymphoid).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: How do lymphoma and leukaemia differ in what they affect?
options: Lymphoma affects marrow; leukaemia affects nodes
Lymphoma affects nodes; leukaemia affects marrow/blood
Lymphoma affects blood; leukaemia affects skin
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.answer: Lymphoma affects nodes; leukaemia affects marrow/blood
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: Lymphoma affects nodes; leukaemia affects marrow/blood.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: Which leukaemia is the commonest acute leukaemia, occurs >75y, and shows Auer rods?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: AML is the commonest acute leukaemia, occurs predominantly >75y, shows Auer rods, and carries raised risk after MDS/myeloproliferative disease.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: Which leukaemia is the commonest childhood cancer and is associated with Down's syndrome and CNS spread?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: ALL occurs in children (<5) and >45y, is associated with Down's syndrome and CNS spread, and is the commonest childhood cancer.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: Which leukaemia is the commonest leukaemia overall and shows smudge cells?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: CLL is the commonest leukaemia overall, occurs >55y, shows smudge cells, and can undergo Richter's transformation.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: What is the age mnemonic for the four leukaemias?
options: ALL <5 & >45 · CLL >55 · CML ~65 · AML >75 (rises across the alphabet)
AML <5 · CML >45 · CLL ~65 · ALL >75 (falls across the alphabet)
All present at the same age
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.answer: ALL <5 & >45 · CLL >55 · CML ~65 · AML >75 (rises across the alphabet)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: The age mnemonic: ALL <5 & >45, CLL >55, CML ~65, AML >75 — the age rises across the alphabet.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: Which buzzword–leukaemia pairing is correct?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: The buzzword associations are: Auer rods → AML; Philadelphia t(9;22)/BCR-ABL → CML; smudge cells → CLL; Down's syndrome & CNS spread → ALL.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: Which trigger is specifically linked to secondary AML?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: Triggers include benzene, alkylating agents (→ secondary AML), radiation, HTLV-1, and Down's syndrome (10–20× risk; both ALL and AML).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: What does t(9;22) Philadelphia → BCR-ABL signify, and how is it targeted?
options: >95% CML and some ALL → target with imatinib (TKI)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.answer: >95% CML and some ALL → target with imatinib (TKI)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: t(9;22) Philadelphia → BCR-ABL is present in >95% CML and some ALL, and is targeted with imatinib (a TKI).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: What does t(15;17) → PML-RARα signify, and how is it targeted?
options: ALL → intrathecal methotrexate for CNS prophylaxis
APML (AML subtype) → blocks differentiation → target with ATRA
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.answer: APML (AML subtype) → blocks differentiation → target with ATRA
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: t(15;17) → PML-RARα defines APML (an AML subtype), blocks differentiation, and is targeted with ATRA.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: What is the biochemical picture of tumour lysis syndrome?
options: Raised urate, raised K⁺, raised phosphate, low Ca²⁺ → AKI
Low urate, low K⁺, raised Ca²⁺
Raised Ca²⁺, low phosphate and low urate with a normal K⁺
Low K⁺, raised Ca²⁺, raised urate
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.answer: Raised urate, raised K⁺, raised phosphate, low Ca²⁺ → AKI
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: Chemo lyses cells → raised urate, raised K⁺, raised phosphate, low Ca²⁺ → AKI (urate crystals).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: How is laboratory tumour lysis syndrome defined?
options: ≥4 abnormalities, and only after chemotherapy has started
≥2 abnormalities within 3 days pre / 7 days post chemo
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.answer: ≥2 abnormalities within 3 days pre / 7 days post chemo
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: Laboratory TLS is ≥2 abnormalities within 3 days pre / 7 days post chemo.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: What is the key distinction between allopurinol and rasburicase in tumour lysis prevention?
options: Allopurinol breaks down the existing urate; rasburicase prevents its formation much further upstream
Allopurinol works upstream/preventatively; rasburicase works on already-formed urate — never give both together
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.answer: Allopurinol works upstream/preventatively; rasburicase works on already-formed urate — never give both together
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: Allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibitor) prevents urate formation; rasburicase (urate oxidase) breaks down existing urate to allantoin. They are never given together. And check G6PD status before rasburicase: it is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency, where it causes severe oxidative haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia (BSH).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: How does acute leukaemia present?
options: Painless cervical lymphadenopathy alone, with an entirely normal full blood count
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: Acute leukaemia presents with marrow failure: anaemia (low RBC), bleeding/petechiae (low platelets), infection (low neutrophils), ± lymphadenopathy/hepatosplenomegaly.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: A child presents with a non-blanching rash. Which differential list fits?
options: Anaemia, iron deficiency, thalassaemia and sideroblastic anaemia
Leukaemia, meningococcaemia, ITP, HSP, vasculitis, NAI
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.answer: Leukaemia, meningococcaemia, ITP, HSP, vasculitis, NAI
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: Non-blanching rash differentials include leukaemia, meningococcaemia, ITP, HSP, vasculitis, and NAI.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: What is the definitive investigation in acute leukaemia, and what confirms AML on it?
options: Bone marrow aspirate + film; Auer rods are pathognomonic for AML
FBC alone; smudge cells confirm AML
LP; blasts in CSF confirm AML
Hb electrophoresis; a raised HbF fraction confirms AML
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.answer: Bone marrow aspirate + film; Auer rods are pathognomonic for AML
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: Bone marrow aspirate + film is definitive; Auer rods are pathognomonic for AML.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: What does MRD by flow cytometry guide in acute leukaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: MRD (minimal residual disease) by flow cytometry guides relapse risk and de-escalation.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: What is the chemotherapy regimen for AML?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: AML induction is cytarabine + an anthracycline (daunorubicin) — the "7+3" regimen — but only for patients FIT for intensive chemotherapy. Patients unfit for intensive induction receive lower-intensity therapy such as venetoclax + azacitidine. Transplant is for intermediate/high-risk cytogenetics. It is fitness, not age, that decides.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: A ~35-year-old develops an AML subtype with t(15;17) and DIC that worsens with cytotoxic chemotherapy. Which subtype is this, and what drives differentiation?
options: CML — imatinib blocks the BCR-ABL fusion kinase
APML — ATRA reverses bleeding and drives differentiation
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.answer: APML — ATRA reverses bleeding and drives differentiation
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: APML has t(15;17)/PML-RARα and presents with DIC. ATRA is started immediately on clinical suspicion, before genetic confirmation — it IMPROVES the coagulopathy and drives differentiation. It is cytotoxic chemotherapy (blast lysis) that worsens the DIC, not ATRA. Watch for differentiation syndrome.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: A child with ALL has CNS involvement. How is this managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: CNS spread in ALL is managed with LP + intrathecal methotrexate.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: What is the chemotherapy and maintenance in ALL?
options: Cytarabine + daunorubicin, with no maintenance phase afterwards
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: ALL chemotherapy is vincristine, dexamethasone, asparaginase, and daunorubicin, with 2-year maintenance.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: How is Philadelphia+ ALL managed beyond standard chemo, and which monoclonals are used in B-ALL?
options: Add intrathecal methotrexate; venetoclax and obinutuzumab
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: Philadelphia+ ALL adds a TKI (imatinib); B-ALL monoclonals are rituximab (anti-CD20) and blinatumomab (CD19/CD3).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: What are the three phases of CML?
options: Blast crisis first, then chronic phase, then an accelerated phase
