Chronic phase, then remission, then cure once a TKI is established
An acute phase followed by a chronic phase and then resolution
Indolent disease, then Richter's transformation, then DLBCL
Chronic → accelerated → blast crisis (≥20% blasts, usually transforms to AML)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.answer: Chronic → accelerated → blast crisis (≥20% blasts, usually transforms to AML)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: CML has three phases: chronic (~5 years if untreated, often incidental raised WCC — on a TKI most patients remain in chronic phase indefinitely) → accelerated → blast crisis (≥20% blasts in blood or marrow by WHO criteria, usually transforms to AML, often fatal). Note the same ≥20% threshold defines acute leukaemia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: A middle-aged patient has insidious fever, weight loss and sweats with massive splenomegaly; the film shows leucocytosis with myeloid precursors and basophilia. Which leukaemia is this, and what is first-line treatment?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: CML presents insidiously with fever, weight loss, sweats, massive splenomegaly, and a film showing leucocytosis with myeloid precursors and basophilia; first-line is imatinib (TKI blocking BCR-ABL).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: What is the immunophenotype of CLL?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: The immunophenotype of CLL is CD5, CD19, CD20, CD23.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: An elderly patient with known CLL develops a rapidly enlarging high-grade lymphoma. What is this transformation called, and to what?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: Richter's transformation in CLL is transformation to a high-grade lymphoma (DLBCL); CLL is also associated with AIHA (warm antibody).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: What is the modern first-line management of CLL?
options: FCR (fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, rituximab) in all cases
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: Modern first-line CLL treatment is BTK inhibitors (ibrutinib/acalabrutinib) or venetoclax ± obinutuzumab; watch-and-wait is used for early/asymptomatic disease, and FCR is now largely second-line.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: EXAM PEARL: What do imatinib and ATRA target?
options: Imatinib targets CD20; ATRA targets CD19/CD3
Imatinib targets PML-RARα in APML; ATRA targets BCR-ABL in CML
Imatinib targets BCR-ABL in CML/Ph+ ALL; ATRA targets PML-RARα in APML
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.answer: Imatinib targets BCR-ABL in CML/Ph+ ALL; ATRA targets PML-RARα in APML
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: Imatinib (TKI) targets BCR-ABL in CML and Ph+ ALL; ATRA targets PML-RARα in APML.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: EXAM PEARL: Which two 'commonest' facts should be remembered?
options: AML = commonest childhood cancer; CML = commonest leukaemia overall
ALL = commonest childhood cancer; CLL = commonest leukaemia overall
CLL = commonest childhood cancer; ALL = commonest leukaemia overall
CML = commonest childhood cancer; AML = commonest leukaemia overall
Both ALL and AML are commonest overall
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.answer: ALL = commonest childhood cancer; CLL = commonest leukaemia overall
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: ALL is the commonest childhood cancer; CLL is the commonest leukaemia overall.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: A 3-year-old girl presents with pallor, bone pain, lymphadenopathy, and a WBC of 85 × 10⁹/L with lymphoblasts on film. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: ALL is the most common childhood leukaemia (peak 2–5 years). Lymphoblasts on film, lymphadenopathy and bone pain from marrow infiltration are characteristic; the white cell count may be low, normal or very high, while the red cells and platelets fall. Prognosis is excellent in children (~90% cure with chemotherapy).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: What is the Philadelphia chromosome and in which leukaemias is it found?
options: t(9;22) BCR-ABL fusion — found in CML (>95%) and ALL (~25% of adults, ~3–5% of children)
t(8;14) c-MYC fusion — found in Burkitt lymphoma and in some cases of DLBCL
t(11;14) cyclin D1 — found in mantle cell lymphoma
t(14;18) BCL-2 — found in follicular lymphoma
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.answer: t(9;22) BCR-ABL fusion — found in CML (>95%) and ALL (~25% of adults, ~3–5% of children)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: The Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) creates the BCR-ABL fusion oncogene encoding a constitutively active tyrosine kinase. It is present in over 95% of CML and about 25% of ADULT ALL — but only 3–5% of childhood ALL. In CML it is the defining lesion; in ALL it is an adverse prognostic marker, and outcomes improved substantially once a TKI (imatinib) was added to chemotherapy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: What is the treatment of choice for chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML)?
options: Allogeneic stem cell transplant as first-line
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: Imatinib revolutionised CML treatment by specifically inhibiting the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase. 10-year survival is around 85%. Second-generation TKIs (dasatinib, nilotinib) are alternative first-line options, and allogeneic SCT is reserved for TKI-resistant disease or blast crisis. Response is tracked by BCR-ABL1 transcript level on RT-qPCR — a confirmed rise or loss of response means check adherence and send kinase-domain mutation analysis before switching TKI.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: What is the classic presentation of CLL?
options: Young adult with lymphoblasts and pancytopenia
Splenomegaly with basophilia and a BCR-ABL positive film
Elderly patient, incidental lymphocytosis, smudge cells on blood film
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.answer: Elderly patient, incidental lymphocytosis, smudge cells on blood film
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: CLL is the most common adult leukaemia. Typically diagnosed incidentally with lymphocytosis >5 × 10⁹/L in an elderly patient. Smudge cells (lymphocytes crushed in processing) are the classic film finding.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: What do Auer rods on a blood film most strongly indicate?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: Auer rods are crystallised azurophilic granules in the cytoplasm of myeloblasts and indicate MYELOID lineage — in exam terms, AML. They are most prominent in APML (AML M3), where cells packed with them are called 'faggot cells'. Strictly they are not unique to AML: they can also appear in MDS with excess blasts and in myeloid blast crisis of CML.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: Which translocation is pathognomonic for acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APML)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: APML (AML M3) has the t(15;17) translocation creating PML-RARA fusion protein. Treated with ATRA (all-trans retinoic acid) + arsenic trioxide — most curable AML subtype. Associated with DIC at presentation.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: What is the 5-year survival of ALL in children vs adults?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: ALL has dramatically different outcomes by age. Children (especially ages 2–10) have ~90% cure rates. Adults have worse prognosis (~40–50% 5-year survival) due to more adverse cytogenetics (Philadelphia-positive more common) and poorer chemotherapy tolerance.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: What is the Richter transformation in CLL?
options: Transformation of CLL to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL)
Development of autoimmune haemolytic anaemia in CLL
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.answer: Transformation of CLL to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: Richter transformation occurs in ~5% of CLL, where indolent CLL transforms to aggressive DLBCL. It presents with rapidly enlarging lymph nodes, fever, and weight loss. Prognosis is poor.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: What is the treatment for APML (AML M3)?
options: Allogeneic stem cell transplant as first-line
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: APML is uniquely responsive to ATRA (differentiates promyelocytes) + arsenic trioxide. This combination achieves >90% complete remission — making APML the most curable AML subtype, despite presenting with dangerous DIC.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the blast threshold defining acute leukaemia?
options: ≥10% blasts in the marrow or blood
≥20% blasts in bone marrow or peripheral blood
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.answer: ≥20% blasts in bone marrow or peripheral blood
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: By WHO criteria, acute leukaemia is defined by ≥20% blasts in the marrow or blood — except the AML-defining genetic abnormalities (t(15;17), t(8;21), inv(16) and NPM1 mutation), which are AML regardless of blast count. <20% blasts otherwise = MDS territory. This exception matters: calling a t(15;17) patient "MDS" because the blast count is 14% misses APL, the one haematological diagnosis where hours of delay kill.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: A 34-year-old woman with newly diagnosed AML has an ECOG performance status of 0 and no comorbidity. What is the appropriate induction regimen?
options: '7+3' - 7 days of cytarabine plus 3 days of an anthracycline
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.answer: '7+3' - 7 days of cytarabine plus 3 days of an anthracycline
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: A young patient with excellent performance status and no comorbidity is fit for intensive therapy, so induction is '7+3': 7 days of continuous cytarabine plus 3 days of an anthracycline (daunorubicin or idarubicin). Non-intensive options such as azacitidine-based therapy or best supportive care are reserved for patients unsuitable for intensive chemotherapy. FCR is a CLL regimen.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: Which statement about outcome in AML is most accurate?
options: Outcome is essentially the same at all ages
AML has the best prognosis of the four leukaemias
Outcome falls steeply with age and fitness; cytogenetic risk group is the other main driver
Prognosis depends only on the white cell count that was measured at presentation
Nearly all patients are cured with a single cycle of induction
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.answer: Outcome falls steeply with age and fitness; cytogenetic risk group is the other main driver
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: AML has the worst outlook of the four leukaemias overall, and survival falls steeply with age. Long-term survival is a realistic aim in fit younger adults given intensive induction, but is uncommon in the older, unfit majority treated non-intensively. Fitness for intensive therapy and cytogenetic risk group are the two dominant drivers; secondary AML (post-MDS or post-alkylating agent) does worse. APML is the curable exception.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: A 71-year-old woman with early-stage CLL on watch-and-wait has had three episodes of pneumococcal pneumonia in 12 months. Her IgG is low. What is the underlying mechanism?
options: Neutropenia caused by CLL infiltration of the bone marrow
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: The CLL clone is a useless B-cell clone: it expands while normal antibody production collapses, producing progressive hypogammaglobulinaemia - a secondary immunodeficiency. Low IgG means failed opsonisation, so encapsulated organisms (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae) cause recurrent pneumonia, sinusitis and otitis. Infection accounts for roughly half of all CLL-related deaths. Her disease is still early-stage, so this is not marrow failure or transformation.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: The same patient continues to have severe bacterial chest infections despite prophylactic antibiotics, and her IgG remains low. What should be considered next?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: Immunoglobulin replacement is considered for recurrent or severe bacterial infection despite prophylactic antibiotics in a patient with a low IgG. It reduces infection frequency rather than prolonging survival, so it is a reserved rather than routine therapy. Recurrent infection alone is not an indication to start anti-leukaemic treatment, and corticosteroids would worsen immunosuppression.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: Which vaccination advice is correct for a patient with CLL?
options: No vaccines should be given as responses are blunted
Live vaccines are preferred, as they give a stronger and much longer-lasting immunity
Annual influenza and pneumococcal vaccination should be given; live vaccines are contraindicated
BCG should be given to reduce infection risk
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.answer: Annual influenza and pneumococcal vaccination should be given; live vaccines are contraindicated
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: Patients with CLL are immunocompromised by progressive hypogammaglobulinaemia and by treatment. Annual influenza and pneumococcal vaccination are recommended - antibody responses are blunted but still worthwhile - while live vaccines are contraindicated.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: A 66-year-old man is found incidentally to have a lymphocyte count of 60 x 10^9/L with smudge cells; flow cytometry confirms CLL. He is asymptomatic, has no palpable nodes or spleen, Hb 141 g/L and platelets 240 x 10^9/L. What is the correct management?
options: Start a BTK inhibitor because the count is above 50 x 10^9/L
Watch-and-wait with clinical review and FBC
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine to confirm the diagnosis
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.answer: Watch-and-wait with clinical review and FBC
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: This is early-stage, asymptomatic disease with no indication for treatment. A high lymphocyte count on its own is never an indication - it is the trajectory (lymphocyte doubling time under 6 months) or a consequence (marrow failure, bulk, autoimmune cytopenia, B symptoms) that triggers therapy. Treating early asymptomatic CLL gives no survival benefit and only brings forward toxicity. The diagnosis was already made on peripheral-blood flow cytometry, so no marrow is required.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.question: A 70-year-old woman with known CLL now has Hb 87 g/L and platelets 74 x 10^9/L due to marrow infiltration by CLL, plus drenching night sweats. Which statement is correct?
options: The cytopenias are too mild to matter and observation should continue
Cytopenias caused by CLL marrow failure are themselves an indication to start treatment
She should be treated only if her lymphocyte count rises above 100 x 10^9/L
Corticosteroids alone are the definitive treatment
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.answer: Cytopenias caused by CLL marrow failure are themselves an indication to start treatment
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.explanation: Progressive anaemia or thrombocytopenia caused by CLL infiltrating the marrow is one of the recognised indications to start treatment, as are constitutional (B) symptoms such as drenching night sweats. Lymphocyte count alone never triggers treatment, and Richter's transformation presents with rapidly enlarging nodal disease rather than isolated cytopenias.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: What characterises myeloproliferative disorders (MPDs)?
options: Reactive expansion of mature lymphocytes in response to a chronic infection
Uncontrolled clonal proliferation of a single myeloid stem cell line — cells still mature
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: Uncontrolled clonal proliferation of a single myeloid stem cell line — cells still mature
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: MPDs are uncontrolled clonal proliferation of a single myeloid stem cell line, with cells still mature — contrasting acute leukaemia where blasts fail to differentiate.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: What is the unifying genetic mutation of MPDs, and what can they all transform to?
options: JAK2 (also MPL, CALR) in the BCR-ABL-negative MPNs; all can transform to AML
BCL-2 rearrangement; all of them transform to follicular lymphoma
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: JAK2 (also MPL, CALR) in the BCR-ABL-negative MPNs; all can transform to AML
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: The unifying genetics of the BCR-ABL-negative MPNs (PV, ET, MF) is JAK2, CALR or MPL; CML is instead BCR-ABL-positive. All can transform to AML.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: Which proliferating line is raised in each of the three classical MPDs?
options: PV — HSC; ET — erythroid; MF — megakaryocyte
PV — megakaryocyte; ET — erythroid; MF — lymphoid line proliferation
PV — erythroid; ET — megakaryocyte; primary myelofibrosis — HSC → marrow fibrosis
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: PV — erythroid; ET — megakaryocyte; primary myelofibrosis — HSC → marrow fibrosis
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: The three classical types: PV (erythroid line raised), ET (megakaryocyte line raised), and primary myelofibrosis (HSC → marrow fibrosis).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: How does CML relate to the MPDs?
options: It is not an MPD at all
It uses JAK2 like the others
It transforms to ALL rather than to AML, unlike each of the others
It is the 4th classical MPD but uses BCR-ABL, not JAK2 — the key discriminator
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: It is the 4th classical MPD but uses BCR-ABL, not JAK2 — the key discriminator
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: CML is the 4th classical MPD but uses BCR-ABL, not JAK2 — the key discriminator.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: A patient has a true raised red cell mass driven by a JAK2 mutation. Which polycythaemia subtype is this, and what is the EPO?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: Primary = PV; EPO low
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: Absolute (true raised red cell mass) that is marrow-driven by a JAK2 mutation is primary polycythaemia = PV, with a LOW EPO.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: A heavy smoker with chronic lung disease has an absolute polycythaemia. What is the subtype and EPO level?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: Secondary; EPO high
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: Secondary absolute polycythaemia (chronic hypoxia from lung disease, high altitude, R→L shunt, heavy smoking, or an EPO-secreting tumour) has a HIGH EPO.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: A middle-aged obese man who smokes, drinks alcohol and is hypertensive has a normal red cell mass with low plasma volume. What is this?
options: Essential thrombocythaemia with a reactive picture
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: Gaisböck syndrome (relative/apparent polycythaemia)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: Gaisböck syndrome is relative/apparent polycythaemia (normal red cell mass, low plasma volume) in middle-aged obese men with smoking, HTN, and alcohol; EPO is normal.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: What single value separates dangerous clonal polycythaemia (PV) from reactive secondary causes?
options: Haematocrit — only raised in secondary causes
EPO — low in PV, high in secondary polycythaemia
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: EPO — low in PV, high in secondary polycythaemia
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: EPO is low in PV (marrow autonomy suppresses EPO) but high in secondary polycythaemia — this single value separates the clonal disease from reactive causes.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: What proportion of patients are JAK2-positive in PV versus ET and MF?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: JAK2 positivity is ~95% in PV and ~50% in both ET and MF.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: What is the hallmark of PV versus ET versus MF in the discriminator table?
options: PV: massive splenomegaly; ET: aquagenic pruritus and plethora; MF: thrombosis and bleeding
PV: aquagenic pruritus/ruddy plethora/raised Hct; ET: thrombosis ± bleeding; MF: massive splenomegaly
PV: thrombosis; ET: marrow fibrosis; MF: ruddy plethora
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: PV: aquagenic pruritus/ruddy plethora/raised Hct; ET: thrombosis ± bleeding; MF: massive splenomegaly
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: Hallmarks: PV — aquagenic pruritus, ruddy plethora, raised Hct; ET — thrombosis ± bleeding; MF — massive splenomegaly.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: What is the blood film clue in PV versus ET versus MF?
options: PV: Auer rods; ET: Heinz bodies; MF: target cells
PV: teardrop poikilocytes; ET: a raised haematocrit; MF: abnormally large circulating platelets
PV: raised haematocrit; ET: abnormal large platelets; MF: teardrop poikilocytes, leucoerythroblastic
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: PV: raised haematocrit; ET: abnormal large platelets; MF: teardrop poikilocytes, leucoerythroblastic
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: Blood film clues: PV — raised haematocrit; ET — abnormal large platelets; MF — teardrop poikilocytes and leucoerythroblastic picture.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: What is the first-line treatment in PV versus ET versus MF?
options: PV: venesection (PCV <0.45) + aspirin; ET: aspirin, cytoreduction only if high-risk; MF: supportive, a JAK1/2 inhibitor, allogeneic BMT (only cure)
PV: aspirin alone; ET: venesection to a target haematocrit below 0.45; MF: aspirin only, with no transplant option ever available at all
PV: ruxolitinib; ET: venesection; MF: aspirin
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: PV: venesection (PCV <0.45) + aspirin; ET: aspirin, cytoreduction only if high-risk; MF: supportive, a JAK1/2 inhibitor, allogeneic BMT (only cure)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: First-line: PV — venesection (PCV <0.45) + aspirin; ET — aspirin for all, with cytoreduction only if high-risk; MF — supportive, a JAK1/2 inhibitor (ruxolitinib, fedratinib or momelotinib), allogeneic BMT (only cure).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: A patient describes intense itching after a hot bath, with a ruddy complexion. What is the hallmark feature, and which condition?
options: Aquagenic pruritus after a hot bath — polycythaemia vera
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: Aquagenic pruritus after a hot bath — polycythaemia vera
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: Aquagenic pruritus after a hot bath is a classic clue to polycythaemia vera (present in ~40%), though it is suggestive rather than diagnostic — it also occurs in other MPNs and in Hodgkin lymphoma. The ruddy complexion here makes PV the answer.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: A PV patient develops a hepatic vein thrombosis. Which complication of hyperviscosity is this an example of?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: Thrombosis (e.g. stroke, DVT, Budd-Chiari)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: Hyperviscosity in PV causes thrombosis — including stroke, DVT, and Budd-Chiari (hepatic vein thrombosis).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: What confirms a diagnosis of polycythaemia vera?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: JAK2+ with a raised haematocrit
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: JAK2 V617F positivity with a raised haematocrit (>0.52 in men, >0.48 in women) confirms polycythaemia vera — note this diagnostic threshold is not the <0.45 venesection target. If V617F-negative but PV is still suspected, test JAK2 exon 12.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: Which ESR finding is described in polycythaemia vera, and why is it notable?
options: Low ESR — a high viscosity paradox
ESR is not used in PV
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: Low ESR — a high viscosity paradox
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: PV shows a low ESR, described as the high viscosity paradox.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: Which intervention is used first to lower the haematocrit in polycythaemia vera?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: Venesection (PCV <0.45)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: First-line PV management is venesection (target PCV <0.45); aspirin is given as an antithrombotic, with cytoreduction and ruxolitinib as further options.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: Which agent is added as antithrombotic therapy in PV?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: Aspirin
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: Aspirin is given as antithrombotic therapy in PV, 75 mg od for all patients unless contraindicated. The exception to know: at platelets >1000–1500 x10^9/L check von Willebrand factor activity first — acquired von Willebrand syndrome develops at extreme counts and aspirin then causes bleeding, so withhold it and cytoreduce until the count falls (BSH).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: What is the pathophysiology of myelofibrosis?
options: BCR-ABL fusion → uncontrolled myeloid precursor expansion progressively filling up the whole marrow cavity
Stem cell proliferation → abnormal megakaryocytes release TGF-beta (and PDGF) → fibroblast activation → marrow fibrosis
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: Stem cell proliferation → abnormal megakaryocytes release TGF-beta (and PDGF) → fibroblast activation → marrow fibrosis
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: Myelofibrosis: stem cell proliferation → abnormal megakaryocytes release TGF-beta (the principal fibrogenic cytokine, with PDGF contributing) → fibroblast activation → marrow fibrosis; can arise de novo or evolve from PV/ET.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: What is the commonest symptom of myelofibrosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: Fatigue (from anaemia)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: Fatigue (from anaemia) is the commonest symptom of myelofibrosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: Why does myelofibrosis cause massive hepatosplenomegaly?
options: Iron deposition within the red pulp of the spleen
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: Extramedullary haemopoiesis → portal hypertension
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: Massive hepatosplenomegaly in myelofibrosis is due to extramedullary haemopoiesis, leading to portal hypertension.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: A patient has a leucoerythroblastic film with teardrop poikilocytes, and the marrow aspirate yields a dry tap. Which condition is this?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: Myelofibrosis
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: Leucoerythroblastic film + teardrop poikilocytes with a dry tap → trephine biopsy is the classic pairing for myelofibrosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: How is myelofibrosis managed, and what is the only cure?
options: Aspirin alone, with allopurinol added; the only cure is long-term interferon alfa therapy given indefinitely
Transfusions, allopurinol, and a JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor (ruxolitinib, or fedratinib/momelotinib); allogeneic BMT = only cure
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: Transfusions, allopurinol, and a JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor (ruxolitinib, or fedratinib/momelotinib); allogeneic BMT = only cure
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: Myelofibrosis is managed with transfusions, allopurinol, and a JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor — ruxolitinib, with fedratinib and momelotinib as alternatives (momelotinib where anaemia is prominent); allogeneic BMT is the only cure.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: What is the characteristic blood picture of essential thrombocythaemia?
options: Teardrop poikilocytes with a leucoerythroblastic film and a dry tap on aspiration
Isolated raised platelets with a normal or near-normal Hb and a normal or mildly raised WCC
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: Isolated raised platelets with a normal or near-normal Hb and a normal or mildly raised WCC
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: ET shows isolated raised platelets with a normal or near-normal Hb and a normal or mildly raised WCC; the platelets are abnormal in size/function → thrombosis > bleeding.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: Why is essential thrombocythaemia a diagnosis of exclusion?
options: It requires a dry tap to diagnose
Reactive thrombocytosis (infection, iron deficiency, malignancy) must be ruled out first
It always has a completely normal platelet count at the time of presentation
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: Reactive thrombocytosis (infection, iron deficiency, malignancy) must be ruled out first
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: ET is a diagnosis of exclusion — reactive thrombocytosis (infection, iron deficiency, malignancy) must be ruled out first.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: How is essential thrombocythaemia managed?
options: Venesection in all patients to a target haematocrit below 0.45, whatever the platelet count happens to be, and whatever the calculated risk category is
Aspirin in all patients unless contraindicated; cytoreduction only if high-risk (hydroxycarbamide first-line, anagrelide second-line, interferon alfa in pregnancy)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: Aspirin in all patients unless contraindicated; cytoreduction only if high-risk (hydroxycarbamide first-line, anagrelide second-line, interferon alfa in pregnancy)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: ET is managed with aspirin in all patients unless contraindicated, plus cytoreduction only if high-risk — age >60, platelets >1500 x10^9/L, or previous thrombosis or haemorrhage (BSH) — with hydroxycarbamide first-line, anagrelide second-line and interferon alfa in pregnancy. At extreme platelet counts (>1000-1500 x10^9/L) check von Willebrand factor activity before aspirin, as acquired von Willebrand syndrome causes bleeding.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the signature pairing for myelofibrosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: Teardrop poikilocytes + dry tap
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: Teardrop poikilocytes + dry tap is the signature pairing for myelofibrosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: EXAM PEARL: What are the treatment backbones for PV and ET?
options: BMT = PV backbone; ruxolitinib = ET backbone
Aspirin alone = PV backbone; venesection = ET backbone
Venesection + aspirin = PV backbone; aspirin alone = ET backbone
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: Venesection + aspirin = PV backbone; aspirin alone = ET backbone
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: Venesection + aspirin is the PV backbone; aspirin alone is the ET backbone.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: EXAM PEARL: Which statements about MPD transformation and categories are correct?
options: ET is never a diagnosis of exclusion
Gaisböck syndrome is an absolute rather than a relative polycythaemia, with a genuinely raised red cell mass on formal measurement
All MPDs can transform to AML; myelofibrosis can be the end-stage of PV/ET; ET = diagnosis of exclusion; Gaisböck = relative polycythaemia
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: All MPDs can transform to AML; myelofibrosis can be the end-stage of PV/ET; ET = diagnosis of exclusion; Gaisböck = relative polycythaemia
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: All MPDs can transform to AML; myelofibrosis can be the end-stage of PV/ET; ET is a diagnosis of exclusion; Gaisböck is relative (apparent) polycythaemia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: EXAM PEARL: Summarise the JAK2 rates and the CML point.
options: JAK2 ~50% PV, ~95% ET/MF; CML uses JAK2
JAK2 ~95% PV, ~50% ET/MF; CML uses BCR-ABL, not JAK2
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: JAK2 ~95% PV, ~50% ET/MF; CML uses BCR-ABL, not JAK2
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: JAK2 is positive in ~95% of PV and ~50% of ET/MF; CML uses BCR-ABL, not JAK2.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: A 58-year-old man presents with headache, facial flushing, and pruritus after hot showers. His Hb is 198 g/L and haematocrit is 0.62. What is the likely diagnosis?
options: Renal cell carcinoma with EPO production
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: Polycythaemia vera (JAK2 mutation)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: PV triad: plethora/facial flushing, pruritus after hot water (aquagenic pruritus from histamine release), and elevated haematocrit. JAK2 V617F mutation in 95%. Rule out secondary polycythaemia with EPO level (low in PV, high in secondary).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: What is aquagenic pruritus and which condition is it characteristic of?
options: Pruritus after water exposure (especially hot) — characteristic of polycythaemia vera
Pruritus from dry skin in eczema
Pruritus caused by bile salt deposition in the cholestatic liver diseases
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: Pruritus after water exposure (especially hot) — characteristic of polycythaemia vera
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: Aquagenic pruritus (itching after water exposure) is characteristic of polycythaemia vera, caused by histamine release from increased mast cells/basophils. It occurs in about 40% of PV and is often the presenting complaint, preceding the full diagnosis by years — it is suggestive rather than diagnostic, and also occurs in other MPNs and in Hodgkin lymphoma.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: What differentiates essential thrombocythaemia (ET) from reactive thrombocytosis?
options: ET: associated with bleeding only and never with thrombosis; reactive thrombocytosis: thrombosis only, and never bleeding
ET: platelet count always >1500; reactive: always <1000
ET: JAK2/CALR/MPL mutation, marrow biopsy showing megakaryocyte proliferation, persistent elevation; reactive: cause-driven, polyclonal
ET: responds to aspirin; reactive: does not
ET: low EPO; reactive: high EPO
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: ET: JAK2/CALR/MPL mutation, marrow biopsy showing megakaryocyte proliferation, persistent elevation; reactive: cause-driven, polyclonal
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: ET is a clonal disorder (JAK2 50%, CALR 25%, MPL 5%) with marrow megakaryocyte proliferation. Reactive thrombocytosis is polyclonal, secondary to iron deficiency, infection, inflammation, or post-splenectomy, and resolves with treatment of the cause.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: What is the classic blood film finding in myelofibrosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: Teardrop poikilocytes (dacrocytes) + leukoerythroblastic picture
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: Myelofibrosis blood film shows teardrop poikilocytes (red cells squeezed out of fibrosed marrow in a 'teardrop' shape) and a leukoerythroblastic picture (immature granulocytes + nucleated RBCs). Massive splenomegaly from extramedullary haematopoiesis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: Among the BCR-ABL-negative MPNs, which has the highest risk of transformation to AML?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: Myelofibrosis (~20% at 10 years)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: Myelofibrosis has the highest AML transformation risk (~20% at 10 years), and also carries risk of 'spent phase' with worsening anaemia. PV has ~5% 10-year AML risk; ET has ~1%.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: What is the role of ruxolitinib in myelofibrosis?
options: It reverses the established fibrosis within the bone marrow
JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor — reduces splenomegaly and constitutional symptoms
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor — reduces splenomegaly and constitutional symptoms
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: Ruxolitinib (JAK1/2 inhibitor) dramatically reduces massive splenomegaly and constitutional symptoms (night sweats, pruritus, weight loss) in MF. It does not reverse fibrosis or reduce AML transformation but improves survival.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: What EPO level differentiates primary from secondary polycythaemia?
options: Low/subnormal EPO = primary (PV) — feedback suppression; high EPO = secondary
JAK2 testing now replaces EPO measurement in the workup entirely
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: Low/subnormal EPO = primary (PV) — feedback suppression; high EPO = secondary
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: In PV, autonomous JAK2-driven red cell production suppresses EPO via negative feedback → low/subnormal EPO. Secondary polycythaemia (COPD, renal tumours, altitude) has high EPO as the driving force.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: What is the CALR mutation associated with?
options: Polycythaemia vera and the other erythroid-driven MPNs
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: Essential thrombocythaemia and myelofibrosis (JAK2-negative cases)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: CALR (calreticulin) mutations are found in ~25% of ET and ~25–35% of MF — mostly in JAK2-negative cases. CALR-mutant ET has lower thrombosis risk than JAK2-positive ET. Testing order: JAK2 first, then CALR, then MPL.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: A young patient with unprovoked portal vein thrombosis is investigated. What haematological condition should be excluded?
options: Factor V Leiden mutation alone, and nothing else
JAK2 V617F mutation — associated with MPDs and thrombophilia
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: JAK2 V617F mutation — associated with MPDs and thrombophilia
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: JAK2 V617F causes thrombophilia in addition to MPD features. It is found in ~25–40% of unexplained splanchnic vein thromboses (Budd-Chiari, portal vein thrombosis) even without overt polycythaemia — low-grade MPD.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.question: EXAM PEARL: What are the four 'classical' myeloproliferative neoplasms?
options: PV, ET, MF, CML (all driven by constitutive kinase activation)
PV, ET, MDS and aplastic anaemia grouped together
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.answer: PV, ET, MF, CML (all driven by constitutive kinase activation)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.explanation: The four classical MPNs: polycythaemia vera (JAK2), essential thrombocythaemia (JAK2/CALR/MPL), myelofibrosis (JAK2/CALR/MPL), and CML (BCR-ABL). All feature constitutive myeloid proliferation from kinase mutations.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: What is the defining paradox of myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS)?
options: Hypercellular marrow with raised peripheral counts across all three lineages, and without any dysplasia
Hypercellular marrow + peripheral pancytopenia — clonal cells die by premature apoptosis before reaching the blood
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Hypercellular marrow + peripheral pancytopenia — clonal cells die by premature apoptosis before reaching the blood
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: The defining paradox of MDS is a hypercellular marrow with peripheral pancytopenia: clonal cells proliferate but die by premature apoptosis before reaching the blood (marrow full, periphery empty).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: What is MDS?
options: A group of acquired clonal bone marrow disorders → ineffective haematopoiesis → progressive marrow failure
A reactive marrow response to infection
An over-production of mature myeloid cells that then survive normally in the peripheral blood
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: A group of acquired clonal bone marrow disorders → ineffective haematopoiesis → progressive marrow failure
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: MDS is a group of acquired clonal bone marrow disorders causing ineffective haematopoiesis and progressive marrow failure.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: Where does MDS sit on the disease spectrum?
options: Cytopenias → MDS → AML — the pre-leukaemic middle ground
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Cytopenias → MDS → AML — the pre-leukaemic middle ground
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: MDS sits on the spectrum cytopenias → MDS → AML and is the pre-leukaemic middle ground.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: What is the key blast cut-off separating MDS from AML?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: <20% blasts = MDS; ≥20% blasts = AML
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: The cut-off is <20% blasts = MDS and ≥20% blasts = AML. The AML-defining genetic abnormalities override the count: t(15;17)/PML::RARA, t(8;21), inv(16) and NPM1 mutation are AML at any blast %, and missing t(15;17) means missing APL, an emergency needing immediate ATRA.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: How does MDS contrast with MPN?
options: MPD = ineffective production with dysplasia; MDS = over-production of mature cells — the same origin, the same output
MPN = over-production of mature cells; MDS = ineffective production with dysplasia — same myeloid origin, opposite output
MPD is pre-leukaemic; MDS is not
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: MPN = over-production of mature cells; MDS = ineffective production with dysplasia — same myeloid origin, opposite output
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: MPN (myeloproliferative neoplasm) is over-production of mature cells while MDS is ineffective production with dysplasia — same myeloid origin, opposite output. Overlap MDS/MPN entities such as CMML show both.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: What is the typical demographic and primary nature of MDS?
options: Children under 5 years, mostly inherited marrow failure
Elderly — median onset >70 years, mostly primary/idiopathic
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Elderly — median onset >70 years, mostly primary/idiopathic
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: MDS is a disease of the elderly with a median onset >70 years, mostly primary/idiopathic.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: What is the key secondary (therapy-related) cause of MDS?
options: Chronic Helicobacter pylori infection of the stomach
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Prior chemotherapy (alkylating agents) or radiotherapy
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: The key secondary cause of MDS is therapy-related: prior chemotherapy (alkylating agents) or radiotherapy; benzene exposure is an environmental cause.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: How does MDS typically present?
options: Always with a dramatic acute bleed at first presentation, never as an incidental finding on a routine count
Often incidental — asymptomatic abnormal FBC; symptoms arise from one or more cytopenias, anaemia commonest
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Often incidental — asymptomatic abnormal FBC; symptoms arise from one or more cytopenias, anaemia commonest
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: MDS is often incidental (asymptomatic abnormal FBC); symptoms arise from one or more cytopenias — anaemia is the commonest and often the only one, with full pancytopenia in a minority.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: Which MCV pattern is the classic examinable film clue to the anaemia of MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Macrocytic anaemia (raised MCV)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: The anaemia of MDS is classically macrocytic (raised MCV) — the examinable film clue. It can also be normocytic, so a normal MCV does not exclude MDS.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: A blood film in suspected MDS shows bilobed neutrophils and hypogranular neutrophils. What are these named findings?
options: Auer rods within circulating blasts, indicating myeloid lineage
Pseudo-Pelger–Huët cells and hypogranular neutrophils — dysplasia findings
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Pseudo-Pelger–Huët cells and hypogranular neutrophils — dysplasia findings
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: Pseudo-Pelger–Huët cells (acquired bilobed neutrophils) and hypogranular neutrophils are the named, examinable dysplasia findings in MDS; blasts are <20%. The inherited Pelger–Huët anomaly is a benign mimic.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: What is the definitive investigation in MDS, and what does it confirm?
options: Blood film alone — confirms the dysplasia and makes the diagnosis outright
Bone marrow aspirate + biopsy — confirms hypercellular marrow, dysplastic lines, blast %
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Bone marrow aspirate + biopsy — confirms hypercellular marrow, dysplastic lines, blast %
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: Bone marrow aspirate + biopsy is definitive, confirming a hypercellular marrow, dysplastic lines, and blast %.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: What drives prognosis in MDS?
options: Cytogenetics — isolated del(5q) good, complex karyotype and monosomy 7 poor
Plasma viscosity, measured at diagnosis and on every follow-up
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Cytogenetics — isolated del(5q) good, complex karyotype and monosomy 7 poor
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: Cytogenetics drive prognosis in MDS — isolated del(5q) carries a good prognosis while a complex karyotype or monosomy 7/del(7q) carries a poor one. Isolated del(5q) is separately the lenalidomide-responsive subtype.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: Which score guides treatment intensity in MDS?
options: The Wells score for pre-test probability of thrombosis
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: IPSS-R (Revised International Prognostic Scoring System)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: The IPSS-R (Revised International Prognostic Scoring System) guides treatment intensity in MDS.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: How is low-risk MDS managed?
options: Immediate allogeneic stem cell transplantation for every patient at diagnosis, regardless of their risk score or of their fitness
Watchful waiting, transfusions, EPO/ESA in selected patients, luspatercept for ring-sideroblast anaemia, infection management, iron chelation
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Watchful waiting, transfusions, EPO/ESA in selected patients, luspatercept for ring-sideroblast anaemia, infection management, iron chelation
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: Low-risk/supportive MDS management includes watchful waiting, RBC transfusions for anaemia, an ESA in selected patients, luspatercept for transfusion-dependent ring-sideroblast/SF3B1 anaemia after ESA failure, infection management (neutropenic sepsis is an emergency), and iron chelation for transfusion overload.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: Why is iron chelation used in MDS?
options: To treat the anaemia directly by raising the haemoglobin
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: For transfusion overload (cross-ref haemochromatosis/thalassaemia)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: Iron chelation is used in MDS for transfusion overload (cross-referencing haemochromatosis/thalassaemia).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: A patient with MDS has the 5q- subtype. What is the targeted treatment?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Lenalidomide (a thalidomide analogue)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: The isolated del(5q) subtype is treated with lenalidomide (a thalidomide analogue) — the targeted exam fact. It is teratogenic, so the UK Pregnancy Prevention Programme applies, and it causes marked early neutropenia/thrombocytopenia needing close FBC monitoring.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: How is high-risk MDS (or younger/fit patients) managed?
options: Hypomethylating agents (azacitidine), intensive chemo; allogeneic stem cell transplant = only cure
Watchful waiting only, with no active treatment offered at any stage of the illness at all
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Hypomethylating agents (azacitidine), intensive chemo; allogeneic stem cell transplant = only cure
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: High-risk/younger fit patients are managed with hypomethylating agents (azacitidine) and intensive chemo; allogeneic stem cell transplant is the only cure.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: What is the only cure for MDS, and why is it limited?
options: Azacitidine — limited by its cumulative haematological and gastrointestinal toxicity
Allogeneic stem cell transplant — reserved for younger/fit patients given the elderly demographic
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Allogeneic stem cell transplant — reserved for younger/fit patients given the elderly demographic
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: Allogeneic stem cell transplant is the only cure, reserved for younger/fit patients given the elderly demographic of MDS.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: On the discriminator table, what is the marrow cellularity in MDS versus aplastic anaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: MDS hypercellular; aplastic anaemia hypocellular
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: MDS has a usually hypercellular marrow whereas aplastic anaemia is hypocellular. Aplastic anaemia is pancytopenic by definition; MDS shows one or more cytopenias — anaemia commonest and often the only one.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: On the discriminator table, what is the blood picture in AML compared with MDS?
options: AML: pancytopenia with no blasts; MDS: blasts dominate the film
AML: blasts dominate; MDS: one or more cytopenias, anaemia commonest
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: AML: blasts dominate; MDS: one or more cytopenias, anaemia commonest
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: In AML blasts dominate the blood picture, whereas MDS shows one or more cytopenias — anaemia commonest and often the only one, with pancytopenia in a proportion.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: On the discriminator table, what is the blast % in aplastic anaemia vs MDS vs AML?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Aplastic: not increased; MDS: <20%; AML: ≥20%
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: Blast %: aplastic anaemia not increased; MDS <20%; AML ≥20%.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: On the discriminator table, dysplasia separates MDS from which condition?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: MDS
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: Dysplasia is present in MDS and absent in aplastic anaemia — that is what the discriminator table uses it for. Note that dysplasia can also be present in AML (AML with myelodysplasia-related changes); it is the blast count of 20% or more that defines AML, not the dysplasia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: What is the trajectory of MDS?
options: → may transform to AML (~30%); most lower-risk patients die of cytopenia complications
→ progression to aplastic anaemia with a fatty, hypocellular marrow instead
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: → may transform to AML (~30%); most lower-risk patients die of cytopenia complications
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: MDS may transform to AML in about 30% of cases, with the risk driven by IPSS-R; most lower-risk patients die of the complications of cytopenias rather than of leukaemia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: An elderly patient with prior chemotherapy presents with an incidental pancytopenia; marrow is hypercellular with dysplastic lines and 8% blasts. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: MDS
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: A hypercellular marrow with dysplasia and blasts <20% (here 8%) in an elderly post-chemotherapy patient with pancytopenia is MDS.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: A patient previously labelled MDS now has 25% blasts in the marrow. What has happened?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Transformation to AML (≥20% blasts)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: Blasts ≥20% means transformation from MDS to AML — MDS is the pre-leukaemic middle ground.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: EXAM PEARL: State the MDS paradox.
options: Hypercellular marrow + raised peripheral counts in all three lineages = MDS
Hypercellular marrow + peripheral pancytopenia = MDS (premature intramedullary apoptosis)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Hypercellular marrow + peripheral pancytopenia = MDS (premature intramedullary apoptosis)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: The MDS paradox: hypercellular marrow + peripheral pancytopenia due to premature intramedullary apoptosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: EXAM PEARL: In which context is MDS classic?
options: Pre-leukaemic — classic in the elderly or post-chemo/radiotherapy
Only ever as an inherited marrow failure disorder of childhood
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Pre-leukaemic — classic in the elderly or post-chemo/radiotherapy
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: MDS is pre-leukaemic and classic in the elderly or post-chemo/radiotherapy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: EXAM PEARL: What are the dysplasia clues on the film?
options: Schistocytes and teardrop poikilocytes seen on the film
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Macrocytic anaemia; pseudo-Pelger–Huët / hypogranular neutrophils
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: Dysplasia clues on the MDS film are macrocytic anaemia and pseudo-Pelger–Huët / hypogranular neutrophils.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: EXAM PEARL: How does MDS differ from aplastic anaemia?
options: Aplastic anaemia is hypercellular, with marked dysplastic change
MDS is hypocellular with no dysplasia
Same pancytopenia but hypocellular marrow and no dysplasia in aplastic anaemia
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Same pancytopenia but hypocellular marrow and no dysplasia in aplastic anaemia
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: Versus aplastic anaemia: same cytopenias, but aplastic anaemia has a hypocellular marrow with no dysplasia (MDS is usually hypercellular with dysplasia). Cellularity usually separates them, but ~10–15% of MDS is hypoplastic and overlaps — dysplasia, excess blasts and clonal cytogenetics are definitive.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the blast cut-off separating MDS from AML?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: <20% blasts = MDS; ≥20% = AML
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: The general cut-off is <20% blasts = MDS and ≥20% = AML. The AML-defining genetic abnormalities override the count: t(15;17)/PML::RARA, t(8;21), inv(16) and NPM1 mutation are AML at any blast %, and missing t(15;17) means missing APL, an emergency needing immediate ATRA.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: A 72-year-old woman is found to have isolated del(5q) on cytogenetics, normal-to-high platelet count, and MDS on biopsy. What targeted treatment is available?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Lenalidomide
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: 5q- syndrome responds specifically to lenalidomide (thalidomide analogue). It achieves transfusion independence in about two-thirds and a cytogenetic response in about 70% of del(5q) MDS — a better response than other MDS subtypes. Note that although it is licensed for transfusion-dependent anaemia in lower-risk del(5q) disease and accepted for use in Scotland, it is not recommended by NICE for use in England.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: What is the role of azacitidine in MDS?
options: Hypomethylating agent used in higher-risk MDS to improve survival and delay AML transformation
Reserved for relapsed acute myeloid leukaemia only, with no established role at all in MDS
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Hypomethylating agent used in higher-risk MDS to improve survival and delay AML transformation
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: Azacitidine (hypomethylating agent) is the standard treatment for higher-risk MDS in patients not eligible for allogeneic stem cell transplantation (NICE). It improves survival and delays AML transformation compared with conventional care, but is not curative.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: Which MDS subtype is associated with SF3B1 mutation and has a better prognosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: MDS with ring sideroblasts (MDS-RS)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: SF3B1 mutation is found in >80% of MDS-RS cases (ring sideroblasts on Prussian blue stain). It is associated with better prognosis and predicts luspatercept response — lenalidomide is the targeted agent for isolated del(5q), not for MDS-RS.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: What is the significance of a rising blast count from 8% to 22% in a patient previously diagnosed with MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Transformation to AML (blasts ≥20%)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: MDS transforms to AML in ~30% of cases. The threshold is ≥20% blasts (WHO criteria). Once transformation occurs, management shifts to AML protocols — intensive chemotherapy or palliation depending on fitness.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: A patient with MDS on regular transfusions develops cardiac and hepatic complications despite adequate haematological management. What is the likely cause?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Transfusional iron overload
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: Repeated RBC transfusions deposit ~250 mg iron per unit. Iron accumulates in heart, liver, and endocrine organs. Cardiac complications (arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy) and hepatic cirrhosis result. Iron chelation (deferasirox oral or desferrioxamine SC/IV) is indicated.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: What EPO level predicts response to ESA therapy in MDS?
options: EPO <500 IU/L, but only where ring sideroblasts are also present on the marrow
EPO level is irrelevant to response
Low serum EPO — best response <200 IU/L, and an ESA is generally not offered above 500 IU/L
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Low serum EPO — best response <200 IU/L, and an ESA is generally not offered above 500 IU/L
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: ESAs (EPO/darbepoetin) are offered in lower-risk MDS with serum EPO <500 IU/L and a low transfusion burden, and work best when EPO is <200 IU/L. A high endogenous EPO suggests the marrow is already maximally stimulated, so ESAs add little above 500 IU/L.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: Why is allogeneic SCT limited in MDS despite being the only cure?
options: MDS is predominantly a disease of the elderly with comorbidity, so most are not fit enough for transplant — selection is by fitness, not a fixed age cut-off
Donor availability is never an issue
SCT carries no treatment-related mortality in this age group, so fitness and comorbidity are entirely irrelevant to the decision to proceed with it
MDS is always cured with azacitidine
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: MDS is predominantly a disease of the elderly with comorbidity, so most are not fit enough for transplant — selection is by fitness, not a fixed age cut-off
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: Allogeneic SCT carries significant treatment-related morbidity/mortality (10–20%). Since MDS predominantly affects patients >70 years, most are ineligible. Reduced-intensity conditioning expands eligibility to older/fitter patients.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: What differentiates MDS from aplastic anaemia (AA) on bone marrow biopsy?
options: MDS: usually hypercellular with dysplasia; AA: hypocellular without dysplasia
MDS: normal cellularity without dysplasia; AA: hypercellular marrow
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: MDS: usually hypercellular with dysplasia; AA: hypocellular without dysplasia
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: The key bone marrow distinction: MDS = usually hypercellular with dysplastic cell lines and ±increased blasts (about 10–15% of MDS is hypocellular, so cellularity alone does not exclude it). AA = hypocellular (fatty marrow replacement) with no dysplasia. Both cause cytopenias via opposite marrow patterns — aplastic anaemia is pancytopenic by definition, MDS often only anaemic.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: A 68-year-old man has Hb 82 g/L, MCV 104 fL, platelets 68 and neutrophils 0.9. B12, folate, TFTs and LFTs are normal and he does not drink excessively. What should be suspected?
options: Folate deficiency alone, with a normal marrow
MDS with pancytopenia and macrocytic anaemia
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: MDS with pancytopenia and macrocytic anaemia
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: Pancytopenia with macrocytic anaemia in an older patient, once nutritional, thyroid, liver and alcohol causes are excluded, suggests MDS and mandates a bone marrow aspirate and trephine — the blood picture raises the suspicion but does not itself make the diagnosis. Macrocytosis is a classic MDS finding.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: EXAM PEARL: A 74-year-old man post-chemotherapy for bladder cancer presents 3 years later with fatigue, pancytopenia, and hypercellular dysplastic marrow with 12% blasts. What is the diagnosis?
options: Primary/idiopathic MDS unrelated to the chemotherapy
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Therapy-related MDS (MDS-EB2) — alkylating agent-induced
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: Alkylating-agent or radiotherapy-related MDS typically presents around 5–10 years after exposure (this case at 3 years is early), often with -5/del(5q) or -7. Blasts 10–19% = MDS with excess blasts 2 (MDS-EB2, renamed MDS-IB2 in the current WHO classification). Topoisomerase-II-inhibitor-related disease has a shorter 1–3 year latency and presents as AML with KMT2A rearrangement. t-MDS carries a worse prognosis than primary MDS.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: Which is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder, and what is its usual inheritance?
options: Von Willebrand disease — mostly autosomal dominant
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Von Willebrand disease — mostly autosomal dominant
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Von Willebrand disease is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder and is mostly autosomal dominant.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: Which factor is deficient in haemophilia A versus haemophilia B?
options: A = factor VIII; B = factor IX
A = factor IX; B = factor VIII
A = factor VII; B = factor IX
A = factor IX; B = factor XI
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: A = factor VIII; B = factor IX
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Haemophilia A is factor VIII deficiency; haemophilia B is factor IX deficiency (Christmas disease).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: What are the two jobs of VWF, and why does this explain haemophilia-like features in severe VWD?
options: Carrier of factor IX and platelet inhibition
Platelet adhesion/aggregation and carrier/stabiliser of factor VIII — so severe VWD lowers VIII and raises APTT
Complement activation, and degradation of factor VIII in the circulation, shortening its half-life
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Platelet adhesion/aggregation and carrier/stabiliser of factor VIII — so severe VWD lowers VIII and raises APTT
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: VWF has two jobs: platelet adhesion/aggregation at the vessel wall, and carrier/stabiliser of factor VIII. That dual role explains why severe VWD can produce haemophilia-like features (low VIII, raised APTT).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: What is the core pathophysiology of von Willebrand disease?
options: Factor IX deficiency → impaired intrinsic pathway
Consumption of clotting factors and platelets, with secondary activation of fibrinolysis
VWF deficiency → defective platelet function + secondary factor VIII deficiency
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: VWF deficiency → defective platelet function + secondary factor VIII deficiency
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: VWD is VWF deficiency → defective platelet function + secondary factor VIII deficiency.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: Which VWD type accounts for ~80% of cases, is mildest, and is autosomal dominant?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Type 1 (partial reduction in VWF quantity)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Type 1 is a partial reduction in VWF quantity, ~80% of cases, mildest, and autosomal dominant.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: Which VWD type is a total absence of VWF, autosomal recessive, and mimics haemophilia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Type 3
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Type 3 is a total absence of VWF, autosomal recessive, severe, and mimics haemophilia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: A young woman presents with gum bleeding on brushing, epistaxis, easy bruising and heavy periods, with a positive family history. What is often the presenting complaint of VWD?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Menorrhagia
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Menorrhagia is often the presenting complaint of VWD, alongside mucocutaneous bleeding (gum bleeding, epistaxis, easy bruising) and a positive family history.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: What is the specific diagnostic test for von Willebrand disease?
options: The skin bleeding time performed alone at the bedside
The Bethesda assay, which titrates the inhibitory antibody
Reduced ristocetin cofactor activity (VWF:RCo) alongside VWF antigen
Prolongation of the prothrombin time on the coagulation screen
A factor IX assay showing a reduced circulating factor IX level
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Reduced ristocetin cofactor activity (VWF:RCo) alongside VWF antigen
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: The diagnosis is made on the VWF panel: VWF antigen plus a ristocetin-based VWF activity assay (VWF:RCo or GPIbM), with factor VIII. Ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation (RIPA) and multimer analysis are used to SUBTYPE, not to diagnose — and in type 2B, low-dose RIPA is increased rather than reduced, which is the subtype where desmopressin is contraindicated.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: Which investigation pattern fits VWD?
options: Normal VWF antigen with a markedly reduced factor IX level
Normal platelet function testing, a low platelet count and a raised PT
A raised PT in isolation, with a normal APTT, normal platelet function and normal VWF antigen
A low platelet count with abnormal VWF and a prolonged prothrombin time
Prolonged PFA closure time; PT and platelets normal; low VWF antigen + activity; moderately low factor VIII
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Prolonged PFA closure time; PT and platelets normal; low VWF antigen + activity; moderately low factor VIII
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: VWD shows a prolonged PFA-100 closure time, normal PT, normal platelets (except type 2B, where they are low), low VWF antigen and activity, and a moderately low factor VIII. The APTT may be normal or raised — commonly normal in type 1. The diagnosis rests on the VWF panel, not on the APTT.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: What is the first-line treatment for minor bleeding or pre-procedure cover in type 1 von Willebrand disease?
options: VWF concentrate ± factor VIII, given as the initial treatment for every type
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Desmopressin (DDAVP) — releases endogenous VWF
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Desmopressin (DDAVP), which releases endogenous VWF, is first-line for minor bleeding and procedural cover in type 1. VWF concentrate (± factor VIII) is what a severe or life-threatening bleed needs, and is also the treatment in type 2/3. Tranexamic acid is an adjunct for mucosal bleeding.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: Which non-hormonal drug is used for menorrhagia in von Willebrand disease, in place of the NSAID used for heavy periods in the general population?
options: Mefenamic acid, at the dose used for heavy periods in the general population
Norethisterone or the combined oral contraceptive pill
Low-dose aspirin, taken through the first three days of each period
Von Willebrand factor concentrate given at the start of each period
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Tranexamic acid
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Tranexamic acid is the non-hormonal drug used here. Mefenamic acid and other non-selective NSAIDs — standard for heavy periods in the general population — are AVOIDED in a bleeding disorder, because they impair platelet function on top of the existing defect. Note the options are not a fixed ladder: a levonorgestrel intrauterine system is the first treatment to consider where it is suitable [NICE], with tranexamic acid and hormonal options used as alternatives or alongside it.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: Which is the most common of the two haemophilias, and is desmopressin useful in it?
options: Haemophilia A — desmopressin useful in mild disease
Haemophilia B — desmopressin useful in mild disease
Both equally common — desmopressin equally effective
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Haemophilia A — desmopressin useful in mild disease
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Haemophilia A (factor VIII) is the most common of the two, and desmopressin is useful in mild disease.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: Why is haemophilia B called 'Christmas disease'?
options: Because the first case was described in a paper published on Christmas Day
Named after Stephen Christmas, the first patient described
After the doctor who described it
Because of the festive rash it causes
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Named after Stephen Christmas, the first patient described
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Haemophilia B is 'Christmas disease', named after Stephen Christmas, the first patient described.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: A boy with haemophilia has spontaneous haemarthroses and muscle haematomas from infancy. What factor level defines this severe grade?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Severe haemophilia is a factor level <1%, with spontaneous bleeds — haemarthroses and muscle haematomas from infancy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: A patient with haemophilia bleeds only with significant trauma or surgery. Which severity grade and factor level is this?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Mild — 5–40%
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Mild haemophilia has a factor level of 5–40% and bleeds only with significant trauma or surgery.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: What is the hallmark clinical feature of haemophilia, and which joints are typically affected?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Haemarthroses — knees, ankles, elbows
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Haemarthroses are the hallmark of haemophilia, typically affecting the knees, ankles, and elbows.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: Which investigation pattern fits haemophilia?
options: Raised APTT; PT, TT, PFA closure time, platelets, VWF all normal; low factor VIII (A) or IX (B) confirms
A low platelet count with a raised PFA closure time and a normal APTT throughout the illness
Raised PFA closure time with normal APTT
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Raised APTT; PT, TT, PFA closure time, platelets, VWF all normal; low factor VIII (A) or IX (B) confirms
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Haemophilia shows a raised APTT with PT, TT, PFA closure time, platelets, and VWF all normal; low factor VIII or factor IX confirms the diagnosis. The Bethesda assay detects inhibitor antibodies.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: What does the Bethesda assay detect in haemophilia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Inhibitor antibodies
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: The Bethesda assay detects inhibitor antibodies.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: How is factor replacement given in severe haemophilia?
options: Desmopressin given on alternate days for both haemophilia A and haemophilia B, from infancy onwards, with factor concentrate held in reserve
IV factor VIII or IX concentrate as prophylaxis from early childhood to protect joints — factor VIII about 3×/week, factor IX about twice weekly
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: IV factor VIII or IX concentrate as prophylaxis from early childhood to protect joints — factor VIII about 3×/week, factor IX about twice weekly
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Severe disease is managed with IV recombinant factor VIII or IX concentrate as prophylaxis from early childhood to protect the joints. Factor VIII is given roughly 3× weekly or alternate days; factor IX has a longer half-life, so haemophilia B prophylaxis is typically around twice weekly.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: What is emicizumab (Hemlibra), and what is its role?
options: A factor IX concentrate for haemophilia B
A bispecific antibody mimicking factor VIII; standard prophylaxis in haemophilia A including inhibitor patients
A VWF concentrate for type 3 VWD
A monoclonal antibody targeting complement C5, used to prevent intravascular haemolysis in PNH patients
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: A bispecific antibody mimicking factor VIII; standard prophylaxis in haemophilia A including inhibitor patients
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Emicizumab (Hemlibra) is a bispecific antibody mimicking factor VIII, now standard prophylaxis in haemophilia A, including inhibitor patients. It is prophylaxis only — a breakthrough bleed still needs factor, or a bypassing agent if there is an inhibitor — and it does nothing in haemophilia B, which lacks factor IX rather than VIII.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: Which complication of haemophilia therapy causes treatment to fail?
options: Cardiac iron deposition from repeated factor concentrate infusions
Inhibitor antibodies developing against infused factor
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Inhibitor antibodies developing against infused factor
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Inhibitor antibodies develop against infused factor, causing treatment to fail; chronic arthropathy from repeated haemarthroses and historically HIV/HCV from plasma-derived products are other complications.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: In the discriminator table, what is the inheritance of VWD vs Haemophilia A/B vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Autosomal dominant (mostly); X-linked recessive; acquired
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Inheritance: VWD is autosomal dominant (mostly), haemophilia A/B is X-linked recessive, and DIC is acquired.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: In the discriminator table, what is the bleeding type of VWD vs Haemophilia A/B vs DIC?
options: All three produce a purely mucocutaneous pattern
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Mucocutaneous; deep (joints/muscle); mixed
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Bleeding type: VWD is mucocutaneous, haemophilia A/B is deep (joints/muscle), and DIC is mixed.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: In the discriminator table, how do platelets compare across VWD, Haemophilia A/B, and DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Normal; normal; low
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Platelets are normal in VWD — except type 2B, where the abnormal VWF binds platelets and causes a thrombocytopenia — normal in haemophilia A/B, and low in DIC.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: In the discriminator table, how does PT compare across VWD, Haemophilia A/B, and DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Normal; normal; raised
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: PT is normal in VWD, normal in haemophilia A/B, and raised in DIC.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: In the discriminator table, how does the VWF / ristocetin result compare across VWD, Haemophilia A/B, and DIC?
options: Normal in VWD; abnormal in Haemophilia A/B
Abnormal in VWD; normal in Haemophilia A/B; not applicable in DIC
Not applicable in VWD; abnormal in Haemophilia A/B; normal in DIC
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Abnormal in VWD; normal in Haemophilia A/B; not applicable in DIC
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: VWF / ristocetin is abnormal in VWD, normal in haemophilia A/B, and not applicable in DIC.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: EXAM PEARL: A patient has mucocutaneous bleeding. What level of the haemostatic system does this point to, versus haemarthrosis?
options: Mucocutaneous → VWF/platelet problem; haemarthrosis → coagulation factor (haemophilia)
Mucocutaneous points to a coagulation factor problem; haemarthrosis points to a platelet problem
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Mucocutaneous → VWF/platelet problem; haemarthrosis → coagulation factor (haemophilia)
