conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Bleeding pattern tells you the level: mucocutaneous → VWF/platelet problem; haemarthrosis → coagulation factor (haemophilia).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: EXAM PEARL: An isolated raised APTT with normal everything else (including PT) suggests what?
options: Vitamin K deficiency affecting the extrinsic pathway
Haemophilia (or mild VWD) — intrinsic pathway only
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Haemophilia (or mild VWD) — intrinsic pathway only
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: An isolated raised APTT with normal everything else (and normal PT) points to haemophilia or mild VWD — the intrinsic pathway only.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: EXAM PEARL: In which conditions does desmopressin work, and where does it NOT work, and why?
options: Works in haemophilia B; does not work in haemophilia A because there is no stored VIII to release
Works in all haemophilia and all VWD types
Works in haemophilia A (mild) and VWD type 1; does NOT work in haemophilia B — no stored IX to release
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Works in haemophilia A (mild) and VWD type 1; does NOT work in haemophilia B — no stored IX to release
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Desmopressin works in mild haemophilia A and VWD type 1, but does NOT work in haemophilia B because there is no stored factor IX to release.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the single fact explaining the VWD/haemophilia overlap, and which VWD type mimics haemophilia A?
options: VWF carries factor IX; type 1 VWD → mimics haemophilia B
VWF carries factor VIII; type 3 VWD → very low VIII → mimics haemophilia A
Factor VIII carries VWF; type 2 VWD → very low VWF → mimics haemophilia A
VWF degrades factor VIII; type 3 VWD → mimics DIC
VWF and factor VIII are unrelated
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: VWF carries factor VIII; type 3 VWD → very low VIII → mimics haemophilia A
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: VWF carries factor VIII — the one fact explaining the VWD/haemophilia overlap; type 3 VWD gives very low VIII and so mimics haemophilia A.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: A 7-year-old boy presents with spontaneous haemarthrosis and a prolonged APTT with normal PT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Haemophilia A presents with spontaneous haemarthroses, deep muscle bleeds, and prolonged APTT with normal PT. It is X-linked recessive (males affected). Haemophilia A (factor VIII) is 4× more common than haemophilia B (factor IX).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: What is the inheritance pattern of haemophilia A and B?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: X-linked recessive
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Both haemophilia A (factor VIII) and haemophilia B (factor IX) are X-linked recessive. Males are affected; females are carriers. Daughters of affected males are obligate carriers.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: Which clotting test is abnormal in haemophilia A?
options: Both the PT and the APTT are prolonged, reflecting a common pathway defect
The PT is prolonged while the APTT remains within the normal range
PT prolonged with a normal APTT and a prolonged PFA closure time
Platelet function testing is abnormal in isolation, with a normal APTT
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: APTT prolonged; PT normal
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Factor VIII sits in the intrinsic pathway, which the APTT measures. The PT measures the extrinsic pathway (factors VII, X, V, II) and is unaffected. Platelet function is normal, so the PFA closure time is normal.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: What is the treatment for acute haemarthrosis in a patient with severe haemophilia A?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Recombinant factor VIII concentrate
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Recombinant factor VIII concentrate is the treatment of choice for haemophilia A bleeds. Target factor VIII level >50% for joint bleeds, >80–100% for life-threatening bleeds. DDAVP can be used for mild haemophilia A only.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: How does DDAVP (desmopressin) help in mild haemophilia A?
options: Directly replaces circulating factor VIII from a recombinant source
Stimulates release of stored factor VIII and vWF from endothelial cells
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Stimulates release of stored factor VIII and vWF from endothelial cells
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: DDAVP causes endothelial cells to release stored factor VIII and vWF, temporarily raising levels 2–4 fold. Useful for minor bleeds or procedures in mild haemophilia A and type 1 vWD. Not effective in severe haemophilia A.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: What is the most common inherited bleeding disorder?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Von Willebrand disease
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: vWD is the most common inherited bleeding disorder: around 1% of the population have a low VWF level on laboratory testing, though clinically significant disease is nearer 1 in 1,000. Most cases are type 1 (partial quantitative deficiency of vWF). Inheritance is mostly autosomal dominant — type 3 and type 2N are recessive — unlike haemophilia, which is X-linked.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: A young woman presents with menorrhagia, easy bruising, and prolonged bleeding after dental extraction. The PFA closure time is prolonged and the APTT is mildly prolonged. What is the likely diagnosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Von Willebrand disease type 1
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: vWD classically presents with mucocutaneous bleeding (menorrhagia, gum bleeding, easy bruising, epistaxis, post-procedure bleeding). The PFA closure time is prolonged because VWF is needed for platelet adhesion. The APTT may be prolonged because VWF carries factor VIII — but note it is commonly NORMAL in type 1, so a normal APTT does not exclude the diagnosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: What is type 3 von Willebrand disease?
options: Complete absence of vWF — most severe form, behaves like haemophilia A
Loss of the high-molecular-weight vWF multimers, with normal total antigen
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Complete absence of vWF — most severe form, behaves like haemophilia A
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Type 3 vWD is rare (autosomal recessive) with complete vWF absence. Secondary factor VIII deficiency occurs (vWF stabilises VIII), causing haemophilia A-like bleeds in addition to mucocutaneous bleeding.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: What is the prophylaxis strategy in severe haemophilia A?
options: On-demand treatment only when bleeding occurs
Regular prophylactic factor VIII infusions 3× weekly
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Regular prophylactic factor VIII infusions 3× weekly
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Prophylactic factor VIII (3× weekly or every other day) prevents haemarthroses and joint damage in severe haemophilia A. Extended half-life factor VIII products (PEGylated or Fc-fusion) allow less frequent infusions. Emicizumab is a separate class — a subcutaneous bispecific antibody that MIMICS factor VIII rather than replacing it, given weekly to four-weekly, and now widely used first-line prophylaxis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: EXAM PEARL: What differentiates haemophilia A from vWD on lab testing?
options: Haemophilia A prolongs both PT and APTT; vWD prolongs the PT alone
Haemophilia A: prolonged APTT with normal platelet function tests; vWD: abnormal platelet function (PFA closure time), APTT normal or prolonged
Haemophilia A has a normal APTT, whereas vWD characteristically prolongs the PT
Both conditions produce an identical pattern on every coagulation and platelet function test available, so the two cannot be told apart in the laboratory
Haemophilia A lowers the platelet count, whereas in vWD the platelet count is normal
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Haemophilia A: prolonged APTT with normal platelet function tests; vWD: abnormal platelet function (PFA closure time), APTT normal or prolonged
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Haemophilia A: APTT prolonged (factor VIII deficiency) with normal primary haemostasis. vWD: primary haemostasis is defective, so the PFA closure time is prolonged — but the APTT is normal OR prolonged, depending on how far factor VIII has been dragged down by loss of its carrier, and in type 1 (about 80% of cases) it is commonly normal. The definitive discriminator is the VWF panel (VWF antigen and activity), not the APTT.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: A 4-year-old boy with severe haemophilia A has received factor VIII for a knee bleed. Over recent months his usual dose has become progressively less effective, and today a standard dose produced no rise in his factor VIII level. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Progression to severe von Willebrand disease with loss of VWF
Development of an inhibitor (alloantibody) against factor VIII
Conversion of haemophilia A to haemophilia B
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Development of an inhibitor (alloantibody) against factor VIII
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: A previously effective dose that stops working, with no expected post-infusion rise, is the clinical signature of an inhibitor. Inhibitors are far commoner in severe haemophilia A than B and usually appear early - within the first several dozen exposures, hence in young children. A mixing study flags it (failure to correct on mixing) and the Bethesda assay quantifies it. Haemophilia A does not convert to B, and vitamin K deficiency prolongs the PT rather than abolishing a factor VIII increment.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: A 19-year-old woman with type 2B von Willebrand disease attends for dental extraction. Which treatment is contraindicated?
options: Planning the procedure with the haemophilia centre
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Desmopressin (DDAVP)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Desmopressin is contraindicated in type 2B. The abnormal VWF in 2B binds platelets excessively, and releasing more of it worsens the thrombocytopenia. VWF concentrate is the appropriate replacement, and tranexamic acid mouthwash, local measures and planning with the centre are all appropriate. Desmopressin is also ineffective in type 3, where there is no stored VWF to release.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: A 27-year-old man with severe haemophilia A is brought to the emergency department after a fall with a scalp haematoma. He is alert with a normal neurological examination. CT is available in 40 minutes. What should happen first?
options: Await the CT before giving any treatment
Give tranexamic acid alone and observe for 4 hours
Discharge with head injury advice as the examination is normal
Request a Bethesda assay before treating
Give factor VIII replacement immediately, then proceed to CT
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Give factor VIII replacement immediately, then proceed to CT
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: In a known haemophiliac with a suspected intracranial bleed, factor replacement is given first and imaging follows. Intracranial haemorrhage is the leading cause of bleeding death, and a normal initial examination does not exclude it - waiting for a scan wastes the window in which treatment is most effective. Tranexamic acid is an adjunct, not a substitute for factor, and a Bethesda assay is irrelevant to the immediate emergency.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: A 10-year-old with haemophilia B is due routine immunisations. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Omit all vaccinations because of bleeding risk
Give subcutaneously where possible, or intramuscularly under factor cover, with firm pressure afterwards
Give all vaccinations intramuscularly with no special precautions, no factor cover and no pressure afterwards
Give only oral vaccines and defer the rest indefinitely
Give intramuscularly after a dose of aspirin for discomfort
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Give subcutaneously where possible, or intramuscularly under factor cover, with firm pressure afterwards
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Vaccination is actively encouraged in bleeding disorders, not avoided. The route is adjusted: subcutaneous where an equivalent exists, or intramuscular under factor cover, with firm pressure applied afterwards. Routine IM injection without cover risks a muscle haematoma. Aspirin is contraindicated because it adds a platelet defect to the existing factor defect.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: A 34-year-old man with moderate haemophilia A develops left groin pain after lifting. He lies with the left hip flexed and resists extension. Observations show a tachycardia and a falling haemoglobin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Iliopsoas haemorrhage
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: An iliopsoas bleed classically causes groin or hip pain with the hip held flexed and resistance to extension, and the retroperitoneum accommodates a large volume of blood, so tachycardia and a falling haemoglobin follow. It is a well-recognised mimic of appendicitis and of hip pathology. It needs urgent factor replacement and imaging. Compartment syndrome affects a fascial compartment of the limb rather than the retroperitoneum.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: Which statement about desmopressin in bleeding disorders is correct?
options: It causes hyponatraemia, so fluid intake should be restricted and sodium monitored
It is effective in haemophilia B because it releases stored factor IX
It can be given repeatedly at short intervals with undiminished effect
It is the treatment of choice in type 3 von Willebrand disease
It has no relevant contraindications in von Willebrand disease
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: It causes hyponatraemia, so fluid intake should be restricted and sodium monitored
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Desmopressin is an ADH analogue, so hyponatraemia - occasionally causing seizures, particularly in children - is a genuine hazard, and fluid restriction with sodium monitoring is required. It is ineffective in haemophilia B (no stored factor IX) and in type 3 VWD (no stored VWF), it shows tachyphylaxis with repeated dosing, and it is contraindicated in type 2B.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: Which of the following is NOT appropriate advice for a patient with haemophilia?
options: Avoid aspirin and non-selective NSAIDs unless agreed with the haematologist
Plan dental extractions in advance with the haemophilia centre
Carry an alert card and a treatment plan
Attend a designated comprehensive care centre for follow-up
Take ibuprofen regularly for joint pain from previous bleeds
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Take ibuprofen regularly for joint pain from previous bleeds
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Regular ibuprofen is inappropriate: non-selective NSAIDs impair platelet function and add a second haemostatic defect to the existing factor deficiency. Paracetamol and opioids are the acceptable analgesics. All the other options are standard advice - avoid antiplatelet drugs, plan procedures with the centre, carry an alert card, and receive care through a designated comprehensive care centre.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: What is the guiding principle of transfusion strategy?
options: Transfuse to a target Hb of 120 g/L in every patient, whatever the underlying cause of the anaemia
Always transfuse two units before reassessing
Restrictive transfusion strategy (lower thresholds) → better outcomes; one unit at a time, then reassess
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Restrictive transfusion strategy (lower thresholds) → better outcomes; one unit at a time, then reassess
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: A restrictive transfusion strategy (lower thresholds) leads to better outcomes; give one unit at a time, then reassess.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A patient without ACS has symptomatic anaemia. At what Hb threshold should red cells be transfused, and to what target?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Transfuse if Hb <70, target 70–90 g/L
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: In non-ACS patients, transfuse if Hb <70 with a target of 70–90 g/L.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A patient with acute coronary syndrome is anaemic. What is the red cell transfusion threshold and target?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Transfuse if Hb <80, target 80–100 g/L
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: In ACS, transfuse if Hb <80 with a target of 80–100 g/L.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Which set of practical facts is correct for red cell transfusion?
options: Infuse over 6 h; stored at 2–6°C; each unit completed within 48 h of leaving the blood fridge on the ward
Infuse over 30 min; stored at 20–24°C; each unit completed within 24 h
Infuse over 4 h; stored at room temperature; each unit completed within 1 h
Infuse over 10 min; stored at −20°C; each unit completed within 6 h
Infuse over 90–120 min; stored at 2–6°C; each unit completed within 4 h of leaving controlled-temperature storage
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Infuse over 90–120 min; stored at 2–6°C; each unit completed within 4 h of leaving controlled-temperature storage
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Red cells are infused over 90–120 min and stored at 2–6°C in a controlled-temperature blood fridge. Each unit must be COMPLETED within 4 hours of leaving controlled-temperature storage — the clock starts when the unit leaves the fridge, not when it is connected.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Which blood group is the universal donor for red cells?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: O negative
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: O negative is the universal donor for red cells.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: What is the indication for FFP?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Clotting factor deficiency (PT/APTT >1.5× normal)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: FFP is indicated for clotting factor deficiency (PT/APTT >1.5× normal).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Which statement about FFP is correct?
options: Contains all clotting factors; universal donor = AB; avoid in fluid overload (large volume)
Contains only fibrinogen; universal donor = O; stored at room temperature in the lab
Contains factors II, VII, IX, X only
Is the fastest option for warfarin reversal
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Contains all clotting factors; universal donor = AB; avoid in fluid overload (large volume)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: FFP contains all clotting factors, its universal donor is AB (no anti-A or anti-B), and it is a large volume so should be avoided in fluid overload.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A patient with DIC has a fibrinogen of 1.0 g/L. Which product is indicated, and what does it contain?
options: PCC — factors II, VII, IX, X
Cryoprecipitate — fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF, factor XIII
Platelets — one adult dose raises the count by roughly 20–30×10⁹/L
Red cells — for acute blood loss
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Cryoprecipitate — fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF, factor XIII
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Cryoprecipitate is indicated for low fibrinogen (<1.5 g/L) — DIC, liver failure, massive transfusion — and contains fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF, and factor XIII.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Why is cryoprecipitate called 'cryo'?
options: It is stored on dry ice
It is frozen at -80°C before use
It is the precipitate of FFP at 4°C
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: It is the precipitate of FFP at 4°C
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Cryoprecipitate is the precipitate of FFP at 4°C — hence 'cryo'.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: What is the prophylactic platelet transfusion threshold in a stable, non-bleeding patient with no planned procedure?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Platelets are indicated for severe thrombocytopenia with bleeding, and prophylactically if <10×10⁹/L in a stable patient. Higher thresholds apply in other settings: <50×10⁹/L before an invasive procedure, and <100×10⁹/L for CNS or ophthalmic surgery.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: How are platelets stored, and why are they not refrigerated?
options: Stored at 37°C, to mimic normal body temperature
Stored at 4°C, which prevents them from aggregating within the pack itself
Stored frozen at −20°C, which preserves their function best
Stored at 20–24°C, because chilling activates platelets and shortens their survival
Stored at 0°C, to prevent them from clotting during storage
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Stored at 20–24°C, because chilling activates platelets and shortens their survival
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Platelets are stored at 20–24°C with continuous gentle agitation, for up to 7 days. They are not refrigerated because chilling activates them and causes rapid clearance by the liver — they lose post-transfusion survival.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: By how much does one adult dose of platelets typically raise the platelet count?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: One adult dose of platelets raises the platelet count by ~20–30×10⁹/L.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A patient on warfarin presents with an intracranial haemorrhage. Which product gives the fastest reversal, and which factors does it contain?
options: PCC — factors II, VII, IX, X (reversal within 1h)
Platelets — factors II, VII, IX, X
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: PCC — factors II, VII, IX, X (reversal within 1h)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: PCC gives the fastest reversal (within 1h) for emergency warfarin reversal and contains factors II, VII, IX, X.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Why must IV vitamin K always be given alongside PCC for warfarin reversal?
options: Vitamin K reverses the action of platelets
Vitamin K speeds up PCC infusion
Vitamin K prevents an allergic reaction to the PCC during the infusion
Factor VII has a short half-life, so without vitamin K the INR creeps back up
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Factor VII has a short half-life, so without vitamin K the INR creeps back up
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Always give PCC with IV vitamin K because factor VII has a short half-life — without it, new factors won't be synthesised and the INR will rebound.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Which patients still require CMV-seronegative components in the UK, now that all components are leucodepleted?
options: All immunocompromised patients, including solid-organ transplant recipients
Intrauterine transfusion, neonates up to 28 days, and elective transfusion in pregnancy
Anyone receiving a transfusion who is known to be CMV-seronegative themselves
All patients with HIV, regardless of CD4 count or viral load
All patients receiving chemotherapy for a haematological malignancy
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Intrauterine transfusion, neonates up to 28 days, and elective transfusion in pregnancy
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: CMV is leucocyte-transmitted, so universal leucodepletion makes standard UK components "CMV-safe". CMV-seronegative components are now reserved for intrauterine transfusion, neonates up to 28 days, and elective (non-emergency) transfusion in pregnancy. Transplant recipients and HIV patients no longer routinely require them.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: What do irradiated blood products prevent, and how?
options: Antibodies are removed, which prevents haemolysis of the transfused cells
Leucocytes are removed, which prevents transmission of cytomegalovirus
Plasma proteins are removed, which prevents allergic reactions
Donor T-cells are inactivated by irradiation → prevents TA-GVHD
Fibrinogen is added to the component, which prevents bleeding
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Donor T-cells are inactivated by irradiation → prevents TA-GVHD
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Irradiation INACTIVATES donor T-cells so they cannot proliferate (it does not remove them), preventing TA-GVHD, which is almost always fatal. UK indications are specific: Hodgkin lymphoma, purine analogues and alemtuzumab, stem cell transplant, congenital T-cell immunodeficiency, intrauterine and neonatal exchange transfusion, granulocytes, HLA-matched platelets and directed donations from relatives — not any haematological malignancy, and not HIV.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Why does a restrictive transfusion strategy give better outcomes than a liberal one?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Fewer reactions, less fluid overload
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: A restrictive strategy (lower threshold) results in fewer reactions, less fluid overload, and better outcomes than liberal.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: In warfarin reversal, how quickly does vitamin K work by the IV versus oral route?
options: IV works in 24h; oral works in 4–6h
IV works in 4–6h; oral works in 24h
IV works in 1h; oral works in 12h
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: IV works in 4–6h; oral works in 24h
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Vitamin K works in 4–6h by IV and in 24h orally; it should always be given.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: What is the universal first step for every transfusion reaction?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: STOP the transfusion
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Stopping the transfusion is the universal first step for every reaction.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A patient develops a temperature rise of 1.2°C to 38.4°C with mild chills during transfusion, with no rigors and otherwise stable. Which reaction is this, and what is the cause?
options: Minor allergic reaction — a response to donor plasma proteins
Febrile non-haemolytic — anti-leucocyte antibodies → cytokine release
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Febrile non-haemolytic — anti-leucocyte antibodies → cytokine release
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Febrile non-haemolytic reaction is caused by anti-leucocyte antibodies → cytokine release. Mild means a temperature rise of 1–2°C to below 39°C with no other features: STOP and assess, give paracetamol, and restart cautiously at a slower rate only if mild and the patient is stable. Rigors, a temperature ≥39°C or a rise ≥2°C is a moderate reaction — do not simply restart; exclude bacterial contamination and haemolysis first (BSH).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A patient develops urticaria and pruritus during transfusion with no systemic compromise. What is the management?
options: STOP; IM adrenaline 0.5mg; ABC; IV fluids
STOP immediately; check ID + bag label; Coombs + recross-match
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Stop temporarily; antihistamine; can restart
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: A minor allergic reaction (to donor plasma proteins) causes urticaria and pruritus with no systemic compromise; manage by stopping temporarily, giving an antihistamine, and can restart.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A patient with IgA deficiency develops hypotension, bronchospasm and angioedema of rapid onset during transfusion. What is the immediate management?
options: STOP; IM adrenaline 0.5mg; ABC; IV fluids
Slow/stop; paracetamol; can restart if stable
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: STOP; IM adrenaline 0.5mg; ABC; IV fluids
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Anaphylaxis (IgA deficiency + anti-IgA antibodies) causes hypotension, bronchospasm, angioedema of rapid onset; manage by STOP, IM adrenaline 0.5mg, ABC, and IV fluids.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Minutes into a transfusion, a patient develops fever, loin/back pain, hypotension and dark urine. What is the cause, and the immediate action?
options: Donor plasma proteins — antihistamine; can restart
ABO incompatibility (wrong blood — human error) — STOP; keep the line open with saline; recheck ID against the bag; telephone the transfusion laboratory at once
Donor antibodies causing a capillary leak — give oxygen and respiratory support, sit the patient up, and give NO diuretics at all in this particular setting
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: ABO incompatibility (wrong blood — human error) — STOP; keep the line open with saline; recheck ID against the bag; telephone the transfusion laboratory at once
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Acute haemolytic reaction is due to ABO incompatibility (wrong blood — human error), with fever, loin/back pain, hypotension and dark urine within minutes. STOP immediately, keep IV access open with 0.9% saline and resuscitate to maintain urine output, recheck the patient's identity against the bag label, and telephone the transfusion laboratory at once — another patient may be about to receive the swapped unit. Return the unit and giving set with fresh clotted and EDTA samples for DAT, repeat group and crossmatch; monitor for AKI and DIC (BSH).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Within 6h of transfusion a patient develops non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, hypoxia, HYPOtension and fever. Which reaction is this, and how is it managed?
options: TACO — slow/stop; furosemide + O₂; sit upright
Acute haemolytic — STOP; check ID + bag label
TRALI — STOP; O₂ + supportive; NO diuretics
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: TRALI — STOP; O₂ + supportive; NO diuretics
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: TRALI (donor antibodies → neutrophil activation → capillary leak) causes non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, hypoxia, HYPOtension and fever within 6h; manage with STOP, O₂ + supportive, NO diuretics.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A patient with pre-existing heart failure develops pulmonary oedema, HYPERtension, raised JVP and orthopnoea during transfusion. Which reaction is this, and how is it managed?
options: TACO — STOP; sit upright; O₂ + IV furosemide
Acute haemolytic — check ID + bag label
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: TACO — STOP; sit upright; O₂ + IV furosemide
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: TACO (volume overload — too fast / pre-existing HF/renal failure) causes pulmonary oedema, HYPERtension, raised JVP and orthopnoea (cardiogenic). STOP the transfusion, sit the patient upright, and give oxygen with IV furosemide. It is the commonest cause of transfusion-related death and is largely preventable with a pre-transfusion risk assessment, single units transfused slowly, and a prophylactic diuretic where indicated (SHOT).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Both TRALI and TACO cause pulmonary oedema during/after transfusion. What is the key discriminator between them?
options: Urine colour — TRALI causes dark urine
Onset — TRALI is always delayed, whereas TACO is immediate
Blood pressure — TRALI causes hypotension, TACO causes hypertension
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Blood pressure — TRALI causes hypotension, TACO causes hypertension
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Both cause pulmonary oedema; the key difference is blood pressure (and mechanism): TRALI = hypotension, TACO = hypertension.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: How do the oedema mechanisms differ between TRALI and TACO?
options: TRALI = immune-mediated capillary leak (non-cardiogenic); TACO = volume overload (cardiogenic)
TRALI = volume overload (cardiogenic); TACO = a capillary leak (non-cardiogenic)
TRALI = ABO incompatibility; TACO = IgA deficiency
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: TRALI = immune-mediated capillary leak (non-cardiogenic); TACO = volume overload (cardiogenic)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: TRALI is immune-mediated capillary leak producing non-cardiogenic oedema; TACO is volume overload producing cardiogenic oedema.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Which management contrast between TRALI and TACO is correct?
options: TRALI = furosemide + O₂; TACO = O₂ + supportive, NO diuretics
TRALI = O₂ + supportive, NO diuretics; TACO = furosemide + O₂
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: TRALI = O₂ + supportive, NO diuretics; TACO = furosemide + O₂
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: TRALI is managed with O₂ + supportive and NO diuretics; TACO is managed with furosemide + O₂.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Which memory hook correctly matches the reaction?
options: Both — leaky lungs + low BP → no diuretics
TRALI — too much fluid + high BP → diurese; TACO — leaky lungs + low BP → no diuretics
TRALI — ABO mismatch → check ID; TACO — IgA deficiency → adrenaline
TRALI — high BP → furosemide; TACO — low BP → fluids
TRALI — leaky lungs + low BP → no diuretics; TACO — too much fluid + high BP → diurese
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: TRALI — leaky lungs + low BP → no diuretics; TACO — too much fluid + high BP → diurese
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: The hooks are: TRALI — leaky lungs + low BP → no diuretics; TACO — too much fluid + high BP → diurese.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: In the warfarin reversal sequence, what is the role of FFP?
options: An older alternative; large volume, avoid in fluid overload
Contains factors II, VII, IX, X only
Replaces the need for vitamin K
First-line in all warfarin reversal, ahead of PCC
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: An older alternative; large volume, avoid in fluid overload
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: In the warfarin reversal steps, FFP is an older alternative — large volume, so avoid in fluid overload; PCC is preferred for emergency reversal.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A 70-year-old man receiving his third unit of blood develops sudden hypotension, loin pain, and dark urine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction (ABO incompatibility)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Acute haemolytic reactions present with fever, loin pain, haemoglobinuria and hypotension due to ABO incompatibility causing intravascular haemolysis. Stop the transfusion immediately, keep the line open with saline, recheck identity against the bag, telephone the transfusion laboratory at once (another patient may be at risk), and return the unit and giving set with fresh samples.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: What is TRALI?
options: Non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema within 6h of transfusion due to anti-leukocyte antibodies
Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema from volume overload
An acute haemolytic reaction from ABO incompatibility missed at the bedside check
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema within 6h of transfusion due to anti-leukocyte antibodies
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: TRALI presents within 6h of transfusion as acute respiratory distress with bilateral infiltrates; PCWP is normal (differentiating from TACO). Anti-HLA or anti-HNA antibodies from donor activate recipient neutrophils.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Which blood product contains all clotting factors including fibrinogen?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Fresh frozen plasma (FFP)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: FFP contains all clotting factors. Cryoprecipitate is enriched in fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF, and factor XIII but lacks other factors.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A patient needs urgent reversal of warfarin before emergency surgery. What is the first-line treatment?
options: Cryoprecipitate, given on its own without vitamin K
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) + vitamin K
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: PCC (Beriplex/Octaplex) provides rapid reversal of warfarin by replenishing factors II, VII, IX, X. IV vitamin K is given concurrently for sustained reversal. FFP takes longer and requires more volume.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: What is the storage temperature and shelf life of platelets?
options: 2–6°C for up to 35 days, in a controlled-temperature blood fridge
Frozen at −30°C, giving a shelf life of about one year
4°C for 7 days, with gentle agitation throughout storage
Room temperature without agitation, for up to 10 days
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: 20–24°C with agitation, up to 7 days
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Platelets are stored at 20–24°C with continuous gentle agitation. UK shelf life is up to 7 days, extended from 5 once bacterial screening was introduced. They are never refrigerated because chilling activates platelets and causes rapid clearance by the liver, destroying post-transfusion survival. Room-temperature storage is also why bacterial contamination is commoner with platelets than any other component.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: When should irradiated blood products be used?
options: Patients who have had an ABO-incompatible transfusion
Immunocompromised patients at risk of transfusion-associated GvHD
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Immunocompromised patients at risk of transfusion-associated GvHD
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Irradiation INACTIVATES donor T-lymphocytes so they cannot proliferate — it does not remove them — preventing TA-GvHD, which is almost always fatal. The UK indications are specific: Hodgkin lymphoma (lifelong), purine analogues and alemtuzumab, stem cell transplant, congenital T-cell immunodeficiency, intrauterine and neonatal exchange transfusion, granulocytes, HLA-selected platelets and directed donations from relatives — not a haematological malignancy per se, and not HIV (BSH).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: What is the Hb threshold for red cell transfusion in a stable, asymptomatic adult without cardiac disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Hb <70 g/L
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Transfuse at Hb <70 g/L in stable patients, target 70–90 g/L (NICE). A threshold of <80 g/L with a target of 80–100 g/L applies specifically in acute coronary syndrome — a raised threshold for chronic cardiovascular disease is not a NICE recommendation.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: What is cryoprecipitate particularly rich in?
options: Fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF, factor XIII
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF, factor XIII
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Cryoprecipitate is the cold-precipitate from FFP, concentrated in fibrinogen (most important), factor VIII, vWF, and factor XIII. It is used for hypofibrinogenaemia in DIC and massive haemorrhage.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A patient develops a temperature rise of 1.2°C to 38.4°C with mild chills 30 minutes into a blood transfusion, with no rigors, no rash, no haemodynamic compromise and no respiratory distress. What is the most likely reaction?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Febrile non-haemolytic reactions are the most common transfusion reaction, caused by cytokines in stored blood or anti-leukocyte antibodies. Mild means a 1–2°C rise to below 39°C with no other features; rigors, a temperature ≥39°C or a ≥2°C rise makes it a moderate reaction that should not simply be restarted (BSH). Stop and assess, give paracetamol, and restart cautiously at a slower rate if mild and the patient is stable. Urticaria and pruritus would instead indicate a minor allergic reaction, treated with an antihistamine.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the complication of repeated red cell transfusions in haemoglobinopathies?
options: Vitamin B12 deficiency caused by repeated transfusion
Platelet refractoriness developing after repeated red cell units
Transfusion-related acute lung injury occurring cumulatively
Progressive worsening of the underlying anaemia
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Iron overload requiring chelation therapy
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Repeated transfusions in thalassaemia/sickle cell disease cause iron overload (haemosiderosis) — each unit delivers ~250 mg iron. Chelation with desferrioxamine (IV/SC) or deferasirox (oral) is required.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: You are asked to start a 2-unit red cell transfusion on the ward. Baseline observations were recorded 20 minutes ago. When must the next full set of observations be taken?
options: 15 minutes after the start of the first unit only
15 minutes after the start of each unit
Hourly from the start of the transfusion
Only at the end of the second unit
30 minutes after the start of each unit
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: 15 minutes after the start of each unit
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Pulse, BP, temperature and respiratory rate are recorded within 60 minutes before starting, 15 minutes after the start of EVERY unit, and within 60 minutes of each unit finishing, with visual observation throughout. The 15-minute check is repeated for each unit because acute haemolytic, septic and anaphylactic reactions declare themselves in the first few minutes.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A unit of red cells is collected from the blood fridge, but the patient is then taken to CT and returns 45 minutes later. The nurse asks whether the unit can be put back in the fridge. What is the correct answer?
options: Yes, provided it has not been spiked
Yes, if it is returned within 2 hours
No — a unit out of controlled-temperature storage for more than 30 minutes cannot be returned
Yes, if the ward fridge is temperature-monitored
No — no component may ever be returned to the fridge once it has been issued at all
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: No — a unit out of controlled-temperature storage for more than 30 minutes cannot be returned
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: The 30-minute rule: once a component has been out of controlled-temperature storage for more than 30 minutes it cannot go back into the blood fridge and must be transfused or discarded. Collect units only when you are ready to start.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A unit of red cells left the blood fridge at 08:00 and the transfusion began at 08:30. At 12:15 roughly a third of the unit remains. What should be done?
options: Continue — the 4-hour clock starts when the transfusion is first connected to the patient, not when it leaves storage
Continue at a faster rate to finish the unit
Stop the unit and discard the remainder, because it must be completed within 4 hours of leaving controlled-temperature storage
Return the remainder to the laboratory for reissue later that day
Continue for up to 6 hours provided observations are normal
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Stop the unit and discard the remainder, because it must be completed within 4 hours of leaving controlled-temperature storage
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: The 4-hour rule: each unit must be COMPLETED within 4 hours of leaving controlled-temperature storage (JPAC), because bacteria proliferate once the pack warms. Here the clock started at 08:00, so the unit should have finished by 12:00; the remainder is discarded and the incident documented.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A patient is midway through a unit of red cells and is due IV co-amoxiclav. There is a single peripheral cannula. What is the correct action?
options: Give the antibiotic through the same line, flushing with 5% glucose
Add the antibiotic to the blood pack
Run the antibiotic in Hartmann's alongside the blood
Do not give drugs or other fluids through the transfusion line — only 0.9% sodium chloride may share it; site a second access or wait
Pause the transfusion for 30 minutes and give the antibiotic through the same line, flushing the line before and afterwards
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Do not give drugs or other fluids through the transfusion line — only 0.9% sodium chloride may share it; site a second access or wait
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Nothing but 0.9% sodium chloride may go through a blood administration line. Calcium-containing fluids such as Hartmann's override the citrate anticoagulant and clot the line, and drugs must not be added to a component. Obtain separate access or give the drug once the unit is complete.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A medical student offers to help by pre-labelling the crossmatch tube at the nurses' station before you take the sample. Why must this be refused?
options: Pre-printed labels are not accepted by most laboratories
The tube label must be handwritten at the bedside after positive patient identification — pre-labelling is the classic route to 'wrong blood in tube'
Labels applied early peel off in transit
Only the phlebotomy team may label transfusion samples
The label must be applied only after the sample has reached the laboratory and been formally booked in by a member of the laboratory staff
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: The tube label must be handwritten at the bedside after positive patient identification — pre-labelling is the classic route to 'wrong blood in tube'
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: The pre-transfusion sample requires positive patient identification (the patient states name and date of birth, checked against the wristband) and the tube is then hand-labelled at the bedside, before leaving the patient. Pre-labelling or labelling away from the bedside is the classic mechanism of a wrong blood in tube incident.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Twenty minutes into a platelet transfusion, a 62-year-old man develops a temperature of 39.8°C, violent rigors and a blood pressure of 80/45 mmHg. What is the most likely cause and the key immediate step beyond stopping the transfusion?
options: Febrile non-haemolytic reaction — give paracetamol and restart the same unit at a slower infusion rate afterwards
Bacterial contamination of the unit — take cultures from the patient and the unit and give broad-spectrum antibiotics
Minor allergic reaction — give an antihistamine
TRALI — give oxygen and avoid diuretics
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Bacterial contamination of the unit — take cultures from the patient and the unit and give broad-spectrum antibiotics
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Platelets are stored at room temperature, which makes bacterial contamination far more likely than with other components. High fever, rigors and shock soon after starting the unit point to a septic reaction: stop, take blood cultures from the patient AND the unit, start broad-spectrum antibiotics and resuscitate.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Nine days after a red cell transfusion for a gastrointestinal bleed, a woman returns with jaundice and a Hb that has fallen from 98 to 74 g/L. The DAT is positive. What has happened?
options: Delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction from an anamnestic alloantibody response
Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia triggered by the transfusion episode itself
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction from an anamnestic alloantibody response
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: A delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction: an alloantibody from earlier transfusion or pregnancy was below the detection threshold at crossmatch and is boosted by re-exposure. Falling Hb, jaundice and a positive DAT appear days to about 2 weeks later. Management is supportive, but the antibody must be identified so future units avoid that antigen.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A patient receives an ABO-incompatible unit because of a bedside identification error and requires intensive care. Beyond informing the hospital transfusion team, which report is a statutory legal requirement?
options: A SHOT report only, since SHOT reporting is itself a legal requirement
A report to the MHRA via SABRE under the Blood Safety and Quality Regulations 2005
A report to the coroner only if the patient dies
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: A report to the MHRA via SABRE under the Blood Safety and Quality Regulations 2005
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Serious adverse reactions and serious adverse events must be reported to the MHRA through SABRE (Serious Adverse Blood Reactions and Events) — this is statutory under the Blood Safety and Quality Regulations 2005. SHOT reporting is the professionally mandated UK haemovigilance scheme and is submitted through the same portal, and a local incident report and duty of candour discussion are also required.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Ten days after a transfusion following a hip replacement, a 68-year-old woman with four previous pregnancies presents with widespread purpura and a platelet count of 6 x 10^9/L. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
options: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia — stop heparin and start argatroban
Delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction — supportive care
Disseminated intravascular coagulation — give platelets and cryoprecipitate
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Post-transfusion purpura — give IVIg
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Post-transfusion purpura: profound thrombocytopenia about 5–12 days after transfusion, classically in a previously pregnant HPA-1a negative woman, in whom platelet-specific alloantibodies destroy autologous as well as donor platelets. IVIg is the treatment; further platelet transfusions are largely ineffective.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Under UK blood safety legislation, for how long must the fate of every blood component issued be traceable?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: 30 years
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: The Blood Safety and Quality Regulations 2005 require full traceability from donor to recipient, with records kept for 30 years. This is why the transfusion tag must be returned to the laboratory and the fate of every unit recorded.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: What is the clinical significance and typical timing of neutropenic sepsis?
options: A complication only of radiotherapy, not of systemic chemotherapy
A chronic complication seen months after chemotherapy has finished
A benign self-limiting fever that settles without any treatment
A medical emergency — the commonest serious complication of chemotherapy, typically 7–14 days post-cycle (the nadir)
A hypersensitivity reaction seen during the chemotherapy infusion itself, which resolves as soon as it is stopped
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: A medical emergency — the commonest serious complication of chemotherapy, typically 7–14 days post-cycle (the nadir)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Neutropenic sepsis is a medical emergency and the commonest serious complication of chemotherapy, typically occurring 7–14 days post-cycle (the nadir).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: What is the definition of neutropenic sepsis?
options: Neutrophils ≤0.5 ×10⁹/L on anticancer treatment PLUS temp >38°C or clinical signs of sepsis
Neutrophils below 2.0 ×10⁹/L accompanied by a fever of any degree
Any fever arising in a patient who has a diagnosis of cancer
Neutrophils ≤0.5 ×10⁹/L on its own, whatever the temperature or clinical state
A platelet count below 10 ×10⁹/L together with a temperature above 38°C
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Neutrophils ≤0.5 ×10⁹/L on anticancer treatment PLUS temp >38°C or clinical signs of sepsis
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Neutropenic sepsis is defined as a neutrophil count of 0.5 ×10⁹/L OR LOWER in a patient on anticancer treatment, PLUS either a temperature above 38°C or other signs/symptoms consistent with clinically significant sepsis. Note the boundary: a count of exactly 0.5 with a fever meets the definition.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: Why are the signs of neutropenic sepsis often blunted?
options: Because the infection in this setting is almost always viral
Because patients are routinely taking regular antipyretics
Without neutrophils there is less inflammatory response, so fever may be the only sign
Because concurrent corticosteroid therapy masks all of the clinical signs
Because the neutrophil count is too high to mount a response
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Without neutrophils there is less inflammatory response, so fever may be the only sign
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Without neutrophils there is less inflammatory response, so fever may be the only sign; the patient may be hypothermic, confused, or hypotensive instead — maintain a low threshold to treat.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: A chemotherapy patient at day 10 post-cycle is hypothermic and confused with no fever. What should you do?
options: Only treat once the blood cultures have returned positive
Reassure and observe him on the ward without giving any antibiotics
Wait for a documented fever above 38°C before treating
Discharge with oral analgesia and open access to return
Treat as neutropenic sepsis — maintain a low threshold, as signs may be blunted
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Treat as neutropenic sepsis — maintain a low threshold, as signs may be blunted
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Signs may be blunted — without neutrophils, a patient may be hypothermic, confused, or hypotensive rather than febrile; maintain a low threshold to treat.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: What is the commonest organism in neutropenic sepsis, and its usual source?
options: Pseudomonas aeruginosa — usually arising from the gut by translocation
Staph epidermidis (coagulase-negative Gram-positive) — usually from indwelling lines
Escherichia coli — usually from the urinary tract
MRSA — usually from a colonised skin site or wound
Candida species — usually from the lungs and airways
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Staph epidermidis (coagulase-negative Gram-positive) — usually from indwelling lines
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: The commonest organism is Staph epidermidis (coagulase-negative Gram-positive), usually from indwelling lines in cancer patients.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: Why is piperacillin-tazobactam (Tazocin) chosen over narrow Gram-positive cover?
options: It is the cheapest broad-spectrum option available
It covers only Staph epidermidis from indwelling lines
It is an antifungal with useful antibacterial activity
Empirical cover must target Gram-negatives including Pseudomonas
It deliberately avoids covering Pseudomonas species
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Empirical cover must target Gram-negatives including Pseudomonas
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Empirical cover must target Gram-negatives including Pseudomonas, which is why Tazocin is chosen over narrow Gram-positive cover.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: What is the key principle of the emergency response in neutropenic sepsis?
options: Antibiotics are NOT delayed for investigations — give Tazocin first, take cultures around it
Always await the blood culture results before giving the patient any antibiotics at all
Imaging of the chest and abdomen must precede antibiotics
Start empirical antifungal therapy before antibacterials
Give oral antibiotics first and reserve IV for deterioration
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Antibiotics are NOT delayed for investigations — give Tazocin first, take cultures around it
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Antibiotics are not delayed for investigations — give Tazocin first and take cultures around it.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: What is the first action in the emergency response, and within what timeframe?
options: IV vancomycin within 1 hour of presentation
IV meropenem within 6 hours of presentation
IV amphotericin within 1 hour of presentation
Oral ciprofloxacin given orally within 24 hours of the patient first presenting
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: IV piperacillin-tazobactam (Tazocin) immediately — within 1 hour ('door-to-needle')
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Step 1 is IV piperacillin-tazobactam (Tazocin) immediately — within 1 hour ('door-to-needle'), before cultures if needed.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: Which investigations make up the cultures + septic screen (Step 2)?
options: Haemoglobin electrophoresis with a reticulocyte count and a peripheral blood film
A bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy only
JAK2 V617F mutation testing on peripheral blood
A serum erythropoietin level, taken before treatment
Blood (peripheral and line), FBC, CRP, U&E, LFT, clotting, lactate; CXR, urine/sputum/stool
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Blood (peripheral and line), FBC, CRP, U&E, LFT, clotting, lactate; CXR, urine/sputum/stool
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Step 2 is cultures + septic screen: blood (peripheral and line), FBC, CRP, U&E, LFT, clotting, lactate, plus CXR and urine/sputum/stool.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: A neutropenic sepsis patient remains febrile and unwell at 48 hours on Tazocin. What is the next step?
options: Stop all antibiotics and observe off treatment
Escalate to meropenem ± vancomycin (vancomycin if line infection/MRSA suspected)
Switch to oral ciprofloxacin and plan an early discharge home the same day
Repeat the same course of Tazocin unchanged
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Escalate to meropenem ± vancomycin (vancomycin if line infection/MRSA suspected)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: If still febrile/unwell at 48h, escalate to meropenem ± vancomycin (vancomycin if line infection/MRSA suspected).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: When is vancomycin added during escalation?
options: Only if the patient is apyrexial
Only if fungal infection is found
If line infection / MRSA is suspected
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: If line infection / MRSA is suspected
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Vancomycin is added (to meropenem at the 48h escalation) if a line infection or MRSA is suspected.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: A neutropenic sepsis patient remains unresponsive to antibiotics at 4–6 days. What should be done?
options: Investigate fungal infection → empirical mould-active antifungal (liposomal amphotericin B, or an echinocandin such as caspofungin)
Stop the antibiotics and discharge with oral follow-up
Restart Tazocin at the same dose for a further course
Give a blood transfusion to improve oxygen delivery
Switch to oral antibiotics and arrange ambulatory review, with no further investigation of the persistent fever at all
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Investigate fungal infection → empirical mould-active antifungal (liposomal amphotericin B, or an echinocandin such as caspofungin)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: At 4–6 days unresponsive, investigate fungal infection and start an empirical mould-active antifungal — liposomal amphotericin B or an echinocandin such as caspofungin. Note that unqualified 'amphotericin' means the conventional deoxycholate formulation, which is markedly nephrotoxic and is not what UK units give.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: What does NICE say about de-escalating antibiotics in neutropenic sepsis?
options: Continue intravenous antibiotics for a full 6 weeks, whatever the clinical response
Stop antibiotics as soon as the first dose has been given and cultures are taken
Switch IV→oral at 48 h if the risk of septic complications has been reassessed as low, and stop once the sepsis has responded — irrespective of the neutrophil count
Once apyrexial for 48h, continue a fixed 10-14 day total course whatever the risk assessment shows, stopping only once the neutrophil count has fully recovered
Never de-escalate — the intravenous course runs until the neutrophil count recovers
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Switch IV→oral at 48 h if the risk of septic complications has been reassessed as low, and stop once the sepsis has responded — irrespective of the neutrophil count
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: NICE ties the 48-hour IV→oral switch to a REASSESSED LOW RISK of septic complications, judged by a competent professional using a validated risk score — not to apyrexia alone. It ties stopping antibiotics to the sepsis having responded, irrespective of the neutrophil count, rather than to a fixed 10–14 day course. The familiar apyrexia-plus-fixed-course shorthand is the trap here.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: What prophylaxis is given when neutrophils are anticipated to fall to 0.5 or lower?
options: Meropenem during the expected period of neutropenia
Vancomycin given throughout the expected period of neutropenia
Liposomal amphotericin during the expected nadir
Fluoroquinolone prophylaxis (e.g. ciprofloxacin) during the expected nadir
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Fluoroquinolone prophylaxis (e.g. ciprofloxacin) during the expected nadir
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: When anticipated neutrophils are 0.5 ×10⁹/L or lower, fluoroquinolone prophylaxis (e.g. ciprofloxacin) is given during the expected period of neutropenia (NICE).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: What is the role of G-CSF (filgrastim) in prophylaxis?
options: It eliminates the need for empirical antibiotics
Shortens the duration of neutropenia in high-risk chemotherapy regimens
It treats established invasive fungal infection
It replaces venesection in myeloproliferative disease
It raises the platelet count as well as the neutrophil count
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Shortens the duration of neutropenia in high-risk chemotherapy regimens
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: G-CSF (filgrastim) shortens the duration of neutropenia in high-risk chemotherapy regimens.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: EXAM PEARL: How is the diagnosis of neutropenic sepsis best summarised?
options: It needs imaging confirmation before treatment can start
It requires clinical judgement well beyond the stated criteria, since the numbers alone do not make the diagnosis
It needs a positive blood culture before it can be diagnosed
Neutrophils ≤0.5 + temp above 38°C (or sepsis signs) on chemo = neutropenic sepsis — the definition is the diagnosis
It can only be diagnosed formally by the oncology team
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Neutrophils ≤0.5 + temp above 38°C (or sepsis signs) on chemo = neutropenic sepsis — the definition is the diagnosis
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Neutrophils 0.5 ×10⁹/L or lower plus a temperature above 38°C (or other signs or symptoms consistent with clinically significant sepsis) in a patient on anticancer treatment = neutropenic sepsis (NICE). The definition is the diagnosis — and note the boundary: a count of exactly 0.5 with a fever meets it.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the rule about Tazocin timing?
options: Tazocin within 1 hour — do NOT wait for cultures, imaging, or the neutrophil count
Tazocin only once the blood cultures have returned
Tazocin within 24 hours of presentation is perfectly acceptable practice
Tazocin only after imaging has identified a source
Tazocin is not first-line — start meropenem instead
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Tazocin within 1 hour — do NOT wait for cultures, imaging, or the neutrophil count
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Give Tazocin within 1 hour — do NOT wait for cultures, imaging, or the neutrophil count. You are treating SUSPECTED neutropenic sepsis; the FBC confirms it afterwards, and waiting for it is the commonest reason the hour is breached.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the escalation ladder in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Tazocin → meropenem ± vancomycin (48h) → antifungals (4–6 days)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: The escalation ladder is Tazocin → meropenem ± vancomycin (48h) → antifungals (4–6 days).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the commonest organism versus what empirical cover targets?
options: Commonest organism: MRSA (skin); empirical cover targets viruses
Commonest organism: Pseudomonas (gut); cover targets Staph epidermidis
Commonest organism: Candida (from the lungs); cover targets Gram-positive organisms
Commonest organism: E. coli (urine); empirical cover targets fungi
Commonest organism: Staph epidermidis (lines); empirical cover targets Pseudomonas/Gram-negatives
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Commonest organism: Staph epidermidis (lines); empirical cover targets Pseudomonas/Gram-negatives
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: The commonest organism is Staph epidermidis (from lines), but empirical cover targets Pseudomonas/Gram-negatives.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the prophylaxis, and which complications does the note cross-reference?
options: Tazocin ± vancomycin; cross-ref anaemia and marrow failure
Fluoroquinolone ± G-CSF; cross-ref chemo complications (TLS, marrow failure)
Amphotericin ± G-CSF; cross-ref thrombosis and bleeding
Venesection ± aspirin; cross-ref polycythaemia and hyperviscosity
Meropenem ± antifungals; cross-ref lymphoma and marrow failure
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Fluoroquinolone ± G-CSF; cross-ref chemo complications (TLS, marrow failure)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Prophylaxis is fluoroquinolone ± G-CSF; the note cross-references chemo complications (tumour lysis syndrome, marrow failure).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: A patient on chemotherapy presents with a temperature of 38.5°C and neutrophils of 0.3 ×10⁹/L. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Neutropenic sepsis
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Neutrophils 0.5 ×10⁹/L or lower (here 0.3) on anticancer treatment with a temperature above 38°C meets the NICE definition of neutropenic sepsis. Treat now — do not wait for a second reading or for cultures.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: Within what timeframe must the first dose of antibiotics be given in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Within 1 hour
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: The 'door-to-needle' target is to give IV Tazocin within 1 hour, before cultures if needed.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: Which best describes the inflammatory response in neutropenic sepsis?
options: Identical to that of a non-neutropenic patient with sepsis
Exaggerated — a florid inflammatory response is always present clinically
Muted — fewer neutrophils mean less inflammation, so fever may be the only sign
Absent fever is reassuring and excludes significant sepsis
Always accompanied by a characteristic widespread rash
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Muted — fewer neutrophils mean less inflammation, so fever may be the only sign
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: The inflammatory response is muted because there are fewer neutrophils, so fever may be the only sign and hypothermia/confusion/hypotension may occur instead.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: What should be done with antibiotics relative to taking cultures in suspected neutropenic sepsis?
options: Withhold antibiotics until imaging has been completed
Take all cultures and wait for the results before antibiotics
Take cultures only after 48 hours of empirical treatment
Give empirical antifungals before taking any cultures
Give Tazocin first and take cultures around it — do not delay antibiotics
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Give Tazocin first and take cultures around it — do not delay antibiotics
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Antibiotics are not delayed for investigations — give Tazocin first and take cultures around it.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: Which agent is used if fungal infection is suspected after 4–6 days of unresponsiveness?
options: Vancomycin, to broaden Gram-positive cover at the 4–6 day point
Ciprofloxacin, adding a second agent for Gram-negative cover
Filgrastim (G-CSF), to shorten the duration of the neutropenia
A further course of piperacillin/tazobactam at an increased dose
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Liposomal amphotericin B
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Persistent fever at 4–7 days (≈96 hours) of broad-spectrum antibiotics with ongoing neutropenia prompts an empirical mould-active antifungal: liposomal amphotericin B or an echinocandin such as caspofungin. Unqualified "amphotericin" means the conventional deoxycholate formulation, which is markedly nephrotoxic and is not what UK units give; fluconazole is inadequate because it lacks Aspergillus cover.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: According to NICE, when may a patient with neutropenic sepsis be switched to oral antibiotics?
options: Only after a full 6 weeks of intravenous therapy has been completed
Immediately at presentation, in place of the first intravenous dose
Never — the intravenous course must be completed in full as an inpatient, whatever the risk assessment happens to show at 48 hours
After 48 hours, once the risk of septic complications has been reassessed as low by a competent professional using a validated risk score
Once empirical antifungal therapy has been started alongside them
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: After 48 hours, once the risk of septic complications has been reassessed as low by a competent professional using a validated risk score
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: NICE ties the switch to a reassessed low risk of septic complications after 48 hours rather than to apyrexia alone, and ties stopping to the sepsis having responded rather than to a fixed course length. The apyrexia shorthand is widespread but it is not the NICE criterion.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: Why is neutropenic sepsis described as 'a definition, not a judgement call'?
options: If the neutrophil and temperature/sepsis criteria are met on anticancer treatment, the diagnosis is made
Because only a senior clinician is permitted to diagnose it
Because it requires a validated risk scoring system to confirm it before any treatment is started
Because it depends on the blood culture results coming back
Because imaging is what confirms the diagnosis in practice
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: If the neutrophil and temperature/sepsis criteria are met on anticancer treatment, the diagnosis is made
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: The diagnosis is a definition, not a judgement call: meeting the neutrophil and temperature/sepsis-sign criteria in a patient on anticancer treatment makes the diagnosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: Which combination of antibiotics is the escalation choice at 48h if the patient remains unwell?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Meropenem ± vancomycin
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: At 48h, the escalation is to meropenem ± vancomycin (vancomycin if line infection/MRSA is suspected).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: Which prophylactic measure shortens neutropenia duration rather than preventing infection directly?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: G-CSF (filgrastim)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: G-CSF (filgrastim) shortens the duration of neutropenia in high-risk chemotherapy regimens, whereas fluoroquinolone prophylaxis targets infection during the nadir.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: The commonest organism ISOLATED FROM BLOOD CULTURES in neutropenic sepsis typically arises from which source?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Indwelling lines
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Staph epidermidis, the commonest organism, usually arises from indwelling lines in cancer patients.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: A 45-year-old woman on CHOP chemotherapy for DLBCL presents on day 10 with temperature 38.8°C. Her neutrophil count is 0.2 × 10⁹/L. What is the immediate management?
options: IV vancomycin alone, to cover a presumed line-associated Gram-positive organism
Oral ciprofloxacin with discharge home, as she is haemodynamically stable and otherwise entirely well on review
Wait for the blood culture results before committing to any antibiotic therapy
IV piperacillin/tazobactam within 1 hour, taking blood cultures around the first dose and never delaying it for them
Oral co-amoxiclav, reserving intravenous therapy for those who later deteriorate
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: IV piperacillin/tazobactam within 1 hour, taking blood cultures around the first dose and never delaying it for them
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Neutropenic sepsis is a medical emergency. Take blood cultures (peripheral and from each line lumen) if that can be done in minutes — but the first IV dose of piperacillin/tazobactam must be given within 1 hour of presentation, BEFORE cultures if necessary, and without waiting for the neutrophil count, imaging or culture results. Cultures are taken around the first dose, never as a gate to it.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: Which organism is the most feared in neutropenic sepsis due to its rapid fatality?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa causes fulminant, rapidly fatal sepsis in neutropenic patients. Its intrinsic antibiotic resistance and endotoxin make it particularly deadly. Piperacillin/tazobactam and meropenem provide Pseudomonas cover.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: After 5 days of IV antibiotics a neutropenic patient remains febrile with neutrophil count 0.1 × 10⁹/L. What should be added?
options: Switch to oral antibiotics and plan discharge
Double the dose of the current antibiotic
Antifungal therapy (caspofungin or voriconazole) and CT chest for Aspergillus
Add corticosteroids to dampen the fever
Stop all of the antibiotics and reculture the patient off treatment
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Antifungal therapy (caspofungin or voriconazole) and CT chest for Aspergillus
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Persistent fever after 4–7 days of antibiotics in prolonged neutropenia should prompt empirical antifungal therapy (caspofungin for Candida/Aspergillus, voriconazole if Aspergillus suspected). CT chest looks for the 'halo sign' of invasive pulmonary aspergillosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: What is the 'halo sign' on CT chest and what does it suggest?
options: Consolidation with an air bronchogram — bacterial pneumonia
Bilateral perihilar infiltrates with sparing — acute respiratory distress syndrome
Pleural thickening with a pleural effusion — mesothelioma
A ring-enhancing lesion with surrounding oedema — cerebral abscess
Ground-glass halo surrounding a pulmonary nodule — suggests invasive pulmonary aspergillosis
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Ground-glass halo surrounding a pulmonary nodule — suggests invasive pulmonary aspergillosis
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: The 'halo sign' (CT ground-glass opacity surrounding a nodule) represents haemorrhagic infarction around angio-invasive Aspergillus. Seen in immunocompromised patients with neutropenia. Treat with voriconazole IV.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: Which patient group should receive co-trimoxazole (PCP) prophylaxis?
options: Every patient under the care of a haematology service, without any exception whatsoever, from the point of diagnosis onwards to discharge
Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) patients on treatment, stem cell transplant recipients, and patients on prolonged high-dose corticosteroids
Only patients with HIV whose CD4 count has fallen below 200 cells/mm³ on treatment
Only patients who have previously undergone a surgical splenectomy for any reason
Only those who have already had a documented episode of PCP infection previously
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) patients on treatment, stem cell transplant recipients, and patients on prolonged high-dose corticosteroids
